CHINA TEAS.
Tea a id Sir Andrew Clarke.
For years. whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tet, I have Advised the Pare. old Fashioned China whlch I keep, and the advice has been appreciated.
It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion.

Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London hospital: "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, an one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the howls will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a Cup of tea.' I say ' thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours ahout R tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the fiery ins sestim unit a cup of It taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it, actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. In you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh. get Mack China Tea, putting in the rig.ht measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person aud one for the blessed pot. Thou pour on briskly boiling water, and within five , minutes you must pour It Off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." - • - -

Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this ,31d fashioned tea is like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to ita apparent insipidness ; but If its use is persisted in, It will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the syatem, and if, in a week to two after Its use, a trial is again made of the kind now In ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have oeen using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

"Au flesh is grass," but some people display more greenness than others. WHEN a man has poor cousins his relations 'With them are usually strained. IN the parable the foolish vir,-;ins neglected to put oil in their lamps. In our times the foolish virgins put oil on the fire. UNCLE—I hear sou take dancing lessons; how do you like waltzing? Nephew—Oh, vy much I But the lady is always in my way. see you later," said a persistent and threatening collector to a delinquent debtor. "Not if I see you first," was the reply. TEACHEt of Natural History—Now tell me which of the animals displays the greatest attachment to man? Pupil—The leech. MAMMA—" And how does Birdie's throat feel now ? " Birdie—" De east side's all right mamma, but de west side's, drefful sore." TOMMY (aside)—Columbus was by birth an Italian. Teacher (to teat. pupil's intelligence)—And what is an Italian? Tommy—An organ-grinder. IN Genoa the policemen wear silk hats and carry silver-headed walking-sticks. Genoa seems to be the only place where a policeman can look as big as he feels. SAID a fault-finding man to his wife, "Your bad cookery is rather apt to spoil the dinner." "It doesn't spoil it half as often as your bad temper does," was the retort MANDOLIN playing is the latest flshionable craze among young ladies. " DID you ever execute a work of art ?" asked a I Boston girl of a young man from the country. "Oh, yes," was the cheerful reply. "We Scrub- s town fellows hung Governor St John in effigy a couple of months ago." HEAD of Department (severely to clerk)—" How is it, Thomson, you were away from the office all day on Wednesday last?" "I was ill, sir," was the timid reply. "111 on a weekday ?'' thundered the chief. Pray what do you do on Sundays THE most ignorant man we ever heard of was the fellow who, having a grudge against a Kentucky colonel, threw arsenic into the latter's well. For reasons which need not be mentioned, the colonel's health was nowise affected by the experiment. HENRY returns in triumph from the junior ex- amination. "How did you get along, my son V his doting parent inquires. " First-rate," an- swered Henry. "I answered all the questions." "Good. How did you answer them ?" "I said I didn't know." A POLITICAL ORATOR, speaking of a certain general whom he professed to admire, said that on: the field of battle he was always found where the bullets were.thickeste "Where was that ?" asked one of the audience. "In the ammunition wag- gon," said another. New-York Barber's Shop.—John Chinaman (who has just had his head shaved and his tail attended to)—" How mnchee ?" Black Barber (in perplexity) —" Wal, mistah, I ha'dly knows whudder it's a shave ur a ha'r-out ; jes' wait a minit till I speak wid de boss." Teacher (to boy whose father keeps a corner grocery)—" Johnny, if your father has a hundred eggs, and twenty of them are bad, how many of them does he lose ?" Johnny—" He don't lose any of them. He sells the bad ones to the restaurant- keeper to make omelets of." "Have you read the Descent of Man ?' " asked Clara, looking over her book-shelves. "No," said George, a little timidly; "don't care for it; but I'd like to get the assent of woman." It is cur- rently reported that he got it the very next Sunday night that ever was. MRS. PLAINDAME, after looking long and thoughtfully at a plaster cast of Shakespeare, remarked:—" Poor man, how pale he was! He couldn't have been well when he was taken." ":No," replied- Fogg, "He was dead." " Ah, that accounts for it," said Mrs. P., drawing a sympathetic breath. %TINES —" Why, Finks, old boy, how are you? How you have changed !" Finks—" In what way ?" Jinks—" You seem to have grown rather careless. You used to be quite a dude." Finks— " Oh, that's it, is It? Well, I'm married." Jinks • "Not a dude any niore, then ?" Finks—" No, I'm • sub-dude." SHE was tall, dignified, spectacled, and from Boston. Her mind was jammed with metaphysical philosophy, and she couldn't help but show it. Mr. Churnpley," said she to that modest youth at a little social affair on Prospect-street, "have you read Gall?" He edged away from her in terror. "I —I don't know, ma'am," he feebly murmured; " I—l never saw it—are they usually red ?"—Cleveland Sun. AT an evening service in Edinburgh the minister, who was much given to metaphor, in the course of an eloquent sermon thundered froth, "What is that I hear ? " Upon which his old beadle, start- ing up from a surreptitious nap, called out, in a very audible voice, "'Deed, sir, it's naethin' but the clock chappin' eight." A FARMER on being asked to write a testimonial for a potent clothes wringer, produced the follow- ing : • I bought your clothes wringer and am hugely pleased with it. I bought a lot of wood which proved too green and unfit to burn. I ran the whole through your wringer, and have used the wood for kindling ever since." "SOME folks say I'm conceited," remarked young Popinjay the other day, "but I'm not. I don't believe in hiding what talent I've got under s bushel, that's all." "That's where you're right, young man," exclaimed a bystander, approvingly. "I wouldn't waste a bushel on it, if I were you. A small-sized pint measure would be amply sufficient." GENTLEMAN (who has stepped upon her dress)— A thousand pardons, madam. Lady (pleasantly— It's of no consequence, sir. What she said of him :—" Awkward, stupid fellow I My gathers are all torn out, and I have got to go home." What he said to himself : " Confoundedly ridiculous fashion these trains in the street. Make a man look like a fool, cutting up such capers with them I" IT was in the drawing-room of my uncle's house in Arlington Street (writes Lady Chatterton) that Tom Paine, who had been brought there as a sort of lion, was breakfasting with my aunt one day, received a note from one of the Prince Regent's Court to the effect that the Prince was anxious to , know if he (Tom Paine) had beer bred to the sea. The writer had, by a slip of the pen, spelt the word bread, upon which Tom Paine wrote in pencil on the cover : "No, not bread to the sea, But it was bread to me And—bad bread it be."

A WELL-KNOWN Society lady in New York has made a pet of a small turtle, which she dresses in a pink silk dress, and takes it to the Opera. She lets it walk about the velvet ledge in front of the box, and asks her gentleman friends if it hasn't got beautiful eyes, and they say "Yes,' and all the I time are aching in their hearts to take it by the tail, and fire it at the man with the trombone. A GENTLEMAN tells a good story of one of his domestics. Having employed a new housemaid, he eat down in the dining-room the evening after, to a "civil game of whist" with his wife and a couple of neighbours. The next morning "my lady," "the help," observed that "the card play- ing must be put a stop to or she would be obliged to leave—she didn't approve of the practice, and never allowed it in families where she lived." SPEAKING of Friday being theminister'9 busy day, the Rev. Alfred Goodrich, of Glasgow tells a good story, partly at his own expense. In a former charge he had amongst his flock a worthy woman who was a lady of the wash-tub. By ill-luck he chanced to pay a pastoral visit at a time when she was up to the elbows in suds. He received a sound lecture for so inopportunely timed a visit. "'r day, then are you at liberty ?" he inquired. She said Friday. "That, madam, is my washing day." "illy stars?" is a favourite expression with theatrical managers. ",DoEs your wife talk in her sleep?" asked one married man of another one day when they were compering notes. "I don't lie awake to see,' replied the heartless husband; "but she talks au thereat of the time, so I rather guess she does."

Lord and Lady Derby have left Knowsley for the season, and intend to reside for a few weeks at Dolwood, their place near Beckenham. Holwood was for many years the favourite country residence of Mr. Pitt, and it was long the abode of Lord Mancellor Cranworth.

Cht The Empress Frederick and the Emperor William are both very anxious to marry Prince George of Wales to Pincess Margaret of Prussia, and such an alliance would meet with general approval.Pripcess Margaret is bright and accomplished,intelligent,and very fond of England and of the English manner of life. The Princess was born in April, 1872. The octogenarian cattle painter, Mr. T. S. Cooper, K.A., is better. He has been seriously ill at his home, Vernon Holme, Canterbury, for some time. Every winter of late bronchitis has attacked him, but this year it was complicated with the" danger- ous and infectious disease." However, he hopes soon to be as hale and hearty as ever. Except for a slight deafness he hit no infirmitie.!, and never uses spectacles,, • Miss Jean Dalrymple, the palmist of Bond-street, who takes palmistry seriously as a science,has con- ceived rather an original idea. She is applying for leave to efamine the hands of the monkeys at the Zoo, in order to Ye if their characters and destinies are as visible in their hands as she believes to be the case with the characters anddestinies of human beings. If her prognostications are not correct,the monkeys, at least, will never betray her. On the Saturday before his death Cardinal Man- ning forwarded a sealed letter to Rome, in which he made a strong representation as to the choice of hi successor, and this dying message will be a powerful factor in the selection. The packet was forwarded by special messenger. one of the best- known priests in London being chosen for the mis- sion. The contents of the letter have not transpired but there is an impression that Dr. Gilberts qualifi- cations were strongly urged.

There died on Tuesday at Draycott, near Derby, the Rev. Samuel Antliff, D.D., one of the best known ministers in the Primitive Methodist Connexion. He entered the ministry in 1841, and was president of the conference in 1873. He filled other high positions in the Connexion, and was sent en special missions to various parts of the world. He was taken ill last year whilst on a visit to America to attend the Wesleyan (Ecumenical Conference. He was a member of the Derbyshire County Council and the Derby School Board.

There is reason for hope that the influenza is at last beginning to abate. The official return published show that last week only 436 deaths in London were primarily attributed to the malady, as compared with 506 in the previous week, and that there is a corresponding decline in cases in which influenza has been noted as a secondary cause of death. This is the first time since the epidemic assumed a seri- ous form, towards the end of last year, that there has been a decline, the numbers having, until last week, risen continuously from 19 to 506. Last year, when influenza prevailed, a similar movement was noted ; that is to say, the numbers rose from nine in one week to 319, and then gradually died away. It will be news to most' people at the present moment that the wholesale price of quinine is 10qr.l. per ounce. It has fallen to that price from 16s. in 1878, so writes a correspondent, but 80 far as we can remember there has been no corresponding fall in the retail price during the same period. An or- dinary chemist's shillingsworth of tincture, ammo- niated or otherwise,contains probably about twelve grains. At this rate an ounce of quinine,wholesale price 10id., may be retailed into about forty shil- lingsworth of tincture. It is an ill wind that blows nobody good,and and the middleman druggist must be making a fat thing out of the influenza epidemic. Even " the stores" must be retailing the drug at an enormous profit.

The opening of Parliament, will, we hope, bring a cessation of hostilities at Pastbourne. The Town Council is incorrigible. It has not ceased its law- less proceedings after the adverse decision in the Jaw courts. Something must be done to stop the disgraceful behaviour of the police and the mob. Sunday's report is that" gangs of men arrived by rail, others trudged in from the surrounding I vil- lages, and the disgraceful scenes enacted bathe description." A few Salvationists who went to a spot on the beach where they could disturb no one, essayed to play, but were set upon by the police and the mob. "Lasses " were thrown down, and fainted : every Salvationist was assaulted and lost part of his or her apparel.

The death of Lady Castlemaine calls to mind the circumstances under which the Irish 'peerage of Castlemaine was bestowed on William Hancock, the bonder of the family, for "Union services," which fully bear out Mr. Lecky's charge that the peerage in Ireland is associated with memories not of hon- our but of shame. The story is thus tersely told in the " Black List "of the supporters of the Union in the Irish House of Commons,preserved in Sir Jonah Barrington's " Rise and Fall of the Irish Nation." This is the extract :

"60, William Hancock (Athlone).—An extra- ordinary instance. He made and sang songs against the Union in 1799 at a public dinner of the Op- position, and made and sang songs for it in 1800. lie got a peerage." Mr. Harry Bates (the new A.R.A.) is, among other works, engaged upon a relief in the form of a nar- row, oblong panel, designed to fit in the upper por- tion of a mantelpiece, or, perhaps, one would rather say that the mantelpiece is designed for framing the relief, which is in Mr. Bates's best style. The subject is " Endymion," and is treated with an amazing combination of power and delicacy. The work-room of this brilliant young sculptor is an ideal place for the production of his masterpieces. Lofty and large, yet without that bare and_comfort- less appearance characteristic of most sculptors' studios, both entrances give upon a garden, where the birds sing in summer, and where the first snow- drops are now thrusting their white and green buds through the grass.

It can be authoritatively stated that there is no foundation for the rumour circulated that, against the wish of the Queen, the Prince of Wales and Prince George desire the latter's title to be the Duke of Lancaster. The story, indeed, carries its impossibility on iti face, for the Duchy of Lancas- ter is now held by the Queen in virtue of its for- feiture more than four hundred years ago to the Crown, to which it was then inseparably united by Act of Parliament. When the new Dukedom is created—and it is believed we shall not have long to wait—it is not impossible that it will be associ- ated with a title new to the English temporal peer- age, for the suggestion has been made and has re- ceived high consideration that Prince George should be the first Duke of London.

The grounding of 11.11.5. Victoria is a pretty piece of business. The Victoria is one of the largest and most powerful battle ships afloat. A model of her, if we remember rightly, formed part of the cheap and useful jubilee offering of the Royal Navy to her gracious Majesty. The cost of the ship would probably not be expressed in less than seven figures. She was commissioned only a year or two ago, and now she lies aground on a nobbly Greek promons tory, with five hundred tons of water in her fore compartments. Plenty of plausible explanations of the accident will doubtless be forthcoming, but the i British taxpayer will be a fool f he believes that gross bungling and incompetence are not some- where at the bottom of it. Perhaps we might understand how the ship came to be where she is if we knew how somebody on board came to be where he is.

The process of converting Great Britain into a purely grazing country proceeds apace. Three I years ago there were to every three acres of ;ploughed land just two acres of pasture. Now the proportions are about equal, and it is a striking fact that the corn crops of Great Britain at this time , cover an area of nearly one million acres less than they covered ten years ago—wheat alone standing for nearly three-fourths of the diminution. A more remarkable circumstance is that in spite of the enormous increase in the importation of frozen and preserved meats, our flocks and herds are rapidly augmenting in number. There were on British pastures last year nearly twenty-nine millions of sheep and lambs, showing an advance of very nearly a million-and-a-half over the number in 1890. Our total sheep stock last year, moreover, exceeded by three million head the flocks of two years ago, and by more than four millions the flocks of 1881.

son Bennett, Sir Oscar Clayton, and Sir George Paget reduces the number of our knighted physi- cians and surgeons to forty-nine, not including Sir John Tomes, the dentist. Twelve of these are mili- tary doctors and two naval. Of the military medical dozen, no fewer than eleven are surgeons. Seven others are public officials, mostly connected with lunacy and botany both at home and in the colonies; two, Sir John Kirk and Sir Rutherford Alcock, owed their honors to acting as political agents; one is a surgeon-dentist; and one, Sir Charles Cameron, an analyst and chemist. This leaves Imighthoods for twenty-four ordinary practitioners. Two of the five Irish knights owe the handles to their names to holding the mayoralties of Dublin and London- derry at the proper times. There are three Scotch knights and two colonial. Birmingham is the only English town that has two knighted medical men, Sir Walter Foster and Sir James Sawyer. Sir Geo. Paget's death leaves Cambridge with only one, the same as Norwich, where Sir Peter Eade was mayor just beforb being knighted. One veterinary sur- geon only has been so distinguished. He lives at Windsor, and doctors the Queen's horse.
ASLEEP FOR OVER FOUR MONTHS.

A peculiar case of prolonged sleep is at present occupying the attention of medical circles in Ger- many. A miner named Johan Latus is at present an inmate of a hospital at Mylsowitz, in Silesia, where he was admitted four and a half months ago, and since then all efforts to wake him have proved fruitless. Dr. Albens, the doctor attending•him, is of opinion that the apparent sleep is really a state of catalepsy, though medical science has on record no previous case of such a prolonged nature. He has arrived at this conclusion on account of all the limbs being absolutely rigid. The body lies quite still, the breathing is regular, and there is a healthy colour in the cheeks. In the last few days the body has become much less rigid, and the patient has even made some slight movement, without, how- ever, the condition of apparent sleep being in any I way disturbed. In four and a half months that sleep has lasted the hair has remained stationary. Nourishment to the extent of from two to three litres of milk is administered daily by a tube in- serted in the throat.
A grey, windless sky stretched overhead, and a grey, sullen sea boomed against the black basalt columns of the cliff whereon the castle atands. _

Under such a sky, the loneliness and sadness of the place is intensified strangely. A sense of weird and profound melancholy clings around it. As the water rushes into a gulf beneath—a rumble kirnas it is called—and tumbles about there, upheaving and churning restlessly, until it finally resolves itself into spray, a sound echoes through the hollow walls, a dismal sound like a prolonged moan. Seldom does a human footfall resound there. Within the ruined enclosure, a few sheep nibble the scanty pasturage ; seagulls flap their long wings over it; and ever and anon the plaintive cry of the plover breaks the solemn stillness. There are no cottages scattered about to suggest the presence of humanity, and to do away with utter isolation. Ruined, frowning, repellent in its desolation, has it remained for centuries since it was destroyed and dismantled by Edward VI. Nevertheless the outlines which are yet traceable, suggest a stupen- dous Border stronghold. The 'gateway, with its circular arch, portico, and inner gate, its turret crowned towers; the remains of a chapel; all these the riding party had soon explored. Lady Callerley felt awed and amazed by it, and drew nearer to her husband. It affected her imagination, and seemed to her to be peopled by the shades of the old robber chieftains and rove* who had held it in days gone by..

When they had wearied of exploring the Castle, they found a seat where they could overlook the sea, and here they rested for a while. Silvia was full of curiosity concerning the place. Was there any tradition attaching to it? Surely such a weird, strange-looking castle must have its legend? A story to match its appearance, too, she was certain! There was no lack of strange, romantic tales in the north, evidently. " Ah, Sihria, little Lady Romance, you too are beginning to be infected by the spirit of superstition which seems to be in the very air of Northum- bria 1" "One may wish to hear the legends without being obliged to believe in them." " Well for you if you stop there, ma belle cousin ? " said Mrs. Brearnish laughing. "As for we poor unfortunates who are born in the county of ghosts, witches, wangs, and bogles, there is nothing for us but to believe all we are told." Sir Lancelot Callerley gave a quick glance at his cousin, a glance that appeared to be one of warning; but if so, she declined to accept the signal, by refusing to meet his eyes. - "We shall have you a true Northumbrian ere long, Silvia," she went on, in a teasing sort of way. "You know how I hate superstitions, Dorothy ? " broke out Sir Lancelot, impatiently. "But this is such a pretty and poetic one, dear Lance; you really ought to tell it to your wife."

"Not so, my fair cousin ! I have not your gift of eloquent speech. Since you have chosen to pique my little Silvia's curiosity, you had better gratify it, or there will be no more peace; and meanwhile I will scramble down to the shore yonder, where it is too rugged for ladies to venture. When I was a boy, I knew every cave, rock, and pool about the place!" Silvia made a timid little gesture, half appealing to him to stay, but he did not notice. She had been so happy in his company that day. What did the legend matter, if he were there not to listen to it along with her? Nevertheless, the story of Sir Guy the Seeker being, as Mrs. Breamish averred, a pretty and poetic one, did not fail to interest her, and rivet her wandering attention. And the fair Dorothy told it exceedingly well. • How that the Knight Sir Guy, seeking refuge from a thunderstorm, bound his Ba.rba7y steed tc an old vew tree. which grew nt,ar to the castle, ana nimseir explorea tne interior tor Fulmer, until the hour of midnight sounded from some dis- tant monastery; and how at the last stroke the gates of the portal under which he was sheltering burst open, and the form of an ancient man ap- peared, girt about with a red hot chain, and with eyes which might have been lighted at the fires of Hell, so lurid was their glow. How this dreadful personage gave the Knight an invitation to follow, and deliver a beauteous dame from captivity, atithe same time warning him that, whatever terrible vision met his eyes, he must show no sign of fear. Sir Guy dauntlessly declared that he did not know the meaning of the word fear, and added, "Come what come will, come good, come ill, lead on! I'll follow thee!" In and out, and round about, followed Sir Guy, until they reached a winding stair, and still the ghostly guide beckoned him onward and upward. As he mounted the first flight, he heard a deep drawn sigh; at the aecond, a death bell tolled; while a boding whisper crept into his ear at the third, invoking God's mercy upon his soul. A brazen gate confronted .them when they reached the topmost height, but on the guide extending his wand, it slowly opened and allowed them to enter. Then the dauntless knight found himself in a spacious hall, where a hundred marble knights lay sleeping on the ground, each by the side ol his marble steed. Down the hall he paced, until he came to where two grim skeletons of colossal size confronted him, each crowned with the likeness of a kingly crown ; and each appearing to guard a tomb of crystal, wherein sat the most lovely lady ever beheld by mortal eye. Soon, as she saw Sir Guy, she knelt to him, and held up her hands in mute appeal. To look at was to love her, and the Knight was her own true knight for ever. "Say, lovely creature, what askest thou at my hands; and tell me what mortal can do to win thee?" he cried, but her lips were sealed, and she answered not. Then the Wizard who had guided him made answer instead, pointing to the grim guardians of the tomb, one of whom held a sword, and the other a horn. "Choose now whether thou wilt draw the sword, or sound the horn ! And be- ware ! For only by the rightful choice can you free the dame." Ah, fearful responsibility of choice ! How was Sir Guy to decide? First, he laid his fingers on the hilt of the sword, then he drew back. A mistake would be fatal ! At last, in desperation, he caught up the horn and blew a strong, shrill blast, which echoed like thunder adown the marble hall. At the sound, each marble warrior started from his centuries old sleep, and each marble horse stamped the floor impatiently. Oh, it was a terrible sight! Spears in hand, they rushed upon the luckless knight. He was not wanting in bravery, though the odds were dreadful. He threw away the horn and drew his own trusty blade. So soon as his hold on the horn relaxed, a yell of des- pair was heard, and the Wizard cried, shame on the coward who blew the horn, instead of unsheath- ing the sword," and in a moment the knight sank senseless on the ground. In the morning he found himself lying in the porch where he had taken shelter the night before, but a change had ptassed over him. In his heart ever burned a remembrance of the beautiful captive dame, with her tearful ap- pealing eyes, and his peace of mind was gone for ever. Night and day he sought for the winding stair, but always in vain, crying "Oh, could I but have one chance more, could I but find that sword again! Years oassed on. and his beard. grew
ulel not let this- daunt her, and as

soon as it stopped bleeding, she went on again. Unluckily one of the stones was in so shaky (or as the natives would say, " coggly ") a position, that as she left it, it turned over, and with a plash toppled into the deepest part of the pool, leaving an impossible leap for her return journey, though in her eagerness to proceed she did not notice this at the time. After all, when she did get across, there were no nests in the hole, only thr...e beetles, and an un- pleasantly large spider, which ran out upon her mind utilised her at once for a ladder to reach the ground by, a proceeding against which she objected strongly, and testified thereto with a scream of dismay. But this was nothing to the horror she felt when she found herself landed in the very middle of the water with a terrible gulf before, and a wall of rock behind her. What was she to do? She thought of wading, but dipping one foot down, down, as far as she dared, while clinging with might and main to her ark of safety—a strong, firm boulder—she found the water deep enough at that particular spot to take her up to the waist. And then, the way it rushed and swirled was sufficient to frighten her—why, it would carry her off her feet in an instant, and sweep her away, goodness knows where. Oh, dear ! oh, dear, should she have to stay there all day, until she was missed and a search made for her? And even when they did search, this was the last place they would think of looking at, all out of the beaten track as it was! To add to her discomfort, she was beginning to feel exceedingly hungry, and the thought of that nice luncheon safely packed away, and ready to be eaten, was the most tantalising of all. If only the basket was beside her on that big stone' she wouldn't have minded so much! It was too bad I She collapsed altogether, and drawing her feet , under her dress, for they were cold and benumbed. with their unaccustomed exposure, she crouched together, a miserable spectacle of tearful despair. But presently there appeared a deliverer on the scene, in the person of a young man fishing up the stream • who was at first exceedingly disgusted to find that the pool in which he had confidently reckoned upon finding two or three big trout, was , rendered valueless for angling purposes; but whom the sight of tears, and the sound of sobs, moved to instant pity. As he had on wading boots, it was the work of a moment to reach the stone, lift off the little girl (as he imagined Silvia to be), and Carry her across to dry land. Then he asked her : laughingly to kiss him, as payment for the timely rescue, still under the impression of her complete childishness, which her light weight helped to ' justify, and not meaning to offend a grown woman. Indeed, her simple gown and silk sash, was an unusual garb there, and to his unskilled eyes carried on the delusion. But to his intense sur- prise the little creature drew herself up, and looked at him with great hauteur. "How dare you?" she asked, in an angry tone. " Do you know who I am ?" "No, indeed, how should I?" replied the young fellow, wondering a little. "I am Lady Callerley. Now you see what an absurd thing you have asked ? " The fisherman took off his hat, and made a courtly bow, while humbly begging her pardon for his mistake; which Silvia, after a second look at lira, and a recognition that he was certainly a gentleman, was graciously pleased to grant. Nature had given this young man a passport at once into favour by bestowing upon him a handsome face and figure; though fortune, perhaps thinking this enough, had withheld her gifts. The coat he wore was threadbare and shabby in the extreme, and his hat had, too, evidently seen better days. But with such a winning expression, and a smile which broke forth like sunshine, with its flash of white teeth and a sparkle of brown eyes, who cared for threadbare clothes and battered head-gear, or could think of anything save that a creature beautiful as Antinous and radiant as Apollo stood there in the sunlight? And yet, there were faint lines of care upon that young brow, and 'hollows below the eyes, which ought not to have been there, had life dealt altogether fairly, and as it should have done with him. "Lady Callerley, alone and unattended, and at the mercy of a wandering knight errant to help her out of a dilemma. Fie, that ought not to be ! As he spoke half-mockingly, their eyes met, and they burst out laughing simultaneously, which did away effectually with any further stiffness on the lady's part. "And who is my wandering knight, pray'" asked Silvia at length, when- they had dune laughing. Only good-for-nothing Jack Breamish, at your Setwice.' 1:50 Was was Jack Breamish, of whom the ens,. Dorothy had spoken in such a contemptuous way, but of whom she had been able to say so little definite harm. He was an idler, a wastrel, a keeper of low company, a lover of horses and dogs, a ne'er-do-welL But Mrs Breamish's dispraise was not convincing to Lady Callerley, nor would the latter have been inclined to love me whom Dorothy had held up as worthy of honour. Nevertheless, Silvia had expected to find a boor, a clumsy, rude, unpleasant, lout in Squire Bre,a,mish's half-brother, and was proportionately pleased and surprised to find a person so present- able—presentable, that is to say, in everything save his sorry habiliments. As Silvia disliked Dorothy, she at once and without the slightest proof, decided that Mrs. Breamish was to blame for the poor, good looking, gentle-spoken young gentleman's poverty. "It is well you happened to fish up the stream this way," she said gratefully, "but I never ex- pected to come to harm upon Lancelot's estate ! " "But you had left it, you see! It extends half- way across the burn, and you were about two-thirds over. Will you honour me by accepting my escort aome ? "

"Yes, perhaps. Only I don't want to go home yet, and I've had no luncheon, and all those dear primroses are to gather ! I'll tell you what ! You shall share my luncheon, and help me to fill it—the basket I mean—with primroses, and then you can carry it back. But first of all you must sit down there and keep your eyes fixed straight in front of you upon the water, while I put on my shoes and stockings !" Jack Breamish obeyed. A very merry time the two of them had. It was an unconventional pro- ceeding, that luncheon in the wood, but an innocent enough one, and Silvia felt as though she would grow to like "Cousin Jack," as she dubbed him, very much indeed. Her interest was enlisted by his pleasant face, and her pity by his poverty—of which, however, he made no undue parade—and when she had drawn out 14 story, little by little, and found how he had been —kept hanging on year after year doing nothing by the hope of a com- comission, which his brother had promised their father on the latter's death-bed to procure for him, she grew very indignant indeed. Old Squire Breamish had not acted fairly when he made no provision for the child of his old age, but left him to the tender mercies of a brother, who could not be expected to feel very enthusiastic about such an interloper; however he might find it politic to disguise his sentiments_ Jack inherited nothing, save a small farm belonging to his mother, from whom came also his comeliness and the sunny nature that enabled him to find happiness and pleasure in a life where kicks were more frequent than haifpence. But the lad would have done more good fighting under Collingwood or Nelson, than kicking his heels here, and associating with his in- feriors, simply because he was too proud to play toady, and too poor to be quite independent of his equals. Often he had thought of enlisting, but, being of an easygoing nature, had drifted on ; getting used to his unpleasant position, basking in the rays of sunshine which now and again fell across his path, and taking the clouds and shadow as things to be endured philosophically, and to be forgotten as soon as possible, because they were inevitable.

One of the pleasantest things in his life, as he confided to Silvia, was the great affection which little Lance, his brother's boy, had ever shown to- wards him, much to the annoyance of the mother, who affected to imagine that poor "Uncle Jack" would instil his own depraved tastes and liking for low society into her offspring. But all her anger and admonitions on the subject were of no avail. The little rogue would steal away whenever he he could manage it, to the relative he loved, and would greet his approach with shrieks of delight, from quite babyhood. "He's a splendid little lad," said Jack enthusi- astically, "and she need not be afraid. I wouldn't do him a bit of harm. It is hard not to be allowed to have anything to care for one," he added, plain- tively, and. Lady Callerley's heart was touched. She held out her hand and shook his heartily at parting. "I like you, and I won't believe a word against you, whatever Mrs. Breamish says," she exclaimed, and don't forget please, that you've got a new friend who wants you to do something with your life ! " Jack's charming smile beamed out at this assurance. Then his face clouded.

GOOD-FOR-NOTHING JACK BREAMISIL Dorothy Breamish returned to her own home, but her words—as they were probably meant to do —rankled in Lady Callerley's Ibreast. It appeared now as though her marriage was a mistake, a great and irretrievable blunder. She could have loved her husband dearly, but he needed so little love. It was hard upon her that this should be so. She was very young and unformed, but there were , large reserves of feeling and affection lying dormant 1 in her nature. 1 Those moody, abstracted fits of her husband's— she was growing to dread them, and to shun his' society while they had possession of him. Besides this she resented a certain want of confidence of which she was vaguely conscious. It might perhaps have been as well had she been courageous enough to speak on this point at first, but she was too shy or too sensitive to do so, and the opportunity passed, and time rendered it more difficult. Still it was something to be relieved of Madam's over- powering presence, and to feel at last that the tardy spring was in the air. Yes, even to this bleak country, spring had come; and Silvia's blood began to follow the example in the sap in the gnarled and twisted old beeches forming the avenue, and to course more rapidly through her veins. Fortunately for Lady Callerley, youth is never persistently and consistently unhappy. Besides, nature had gifted her with an irresistible bent towards sunshine. Upon such a morn of May as dawned somewhere about the middle of the month, she found it easy to forget everything, save the pleasant fact that the sun shone, the birds sang joyously, and the crisp leaflets upon the above-mentioned beech trees quivered with vigorous young life, and that it was positive bliss merely to be alive The fields breathe sweet, the daisies kiss our feet, Young lovers meet, old wives a sunning sit, Li every street, these tunes our ears do greet,— "Cuckoo, jug-jug, pu-twe, to-witto-woo, Spring, the sweet spring." Sir Lancelot was away, riding to the northern boundary of his estate, to inspect some improve- ments which were going on at a farm there, se Lady Call rley was free to follow her own sweet will, and spend the day where she pleased. She =wee that tine Mould be out of doors. Me go Denton, the butler, to pack her a nice little luncheon in a basket, and of she set, quite unattended; upon her exploring expeditions. She intended to go down to Yarrop Burn, and follow the course of the stream, up through the wood until she grew tired, when there would be the luncheon basket to un- pack and empty, and to fill up with the primroses 1 which she felt pretty sure of finding by the brink of the water, and amongst the trees. When she reached the water there were a thousand things to interest and amuse her, things which came with a wonderful charm of novelty; because the town beauty had never been trained to I appreciate nature, and yet had a great tendency to 1 love and study it, and now for the first time in her life had a chance of this taste being indulged. The clear amber water, that took its colour from the beds of peat higher up among the hills, was dammed , back and hemmed in by boulders, just at the part where Silvia came upon it, and a r,cky bank rose opposite to her on the Breamish F:1 04. while on the narrow wooded slope, starred I: ::2kl there with tufts of primroses, half hidden by their great fleshy leaves, was to be scrambled down somehow by those dainty little feet, so utterly unused to rough paths. But Lady Callerley enjoyed even the scramble immensely, all the more that it seemed to have a smack of adventure about it, to the girl who had hitherto scarcely ever been allowed out of doors alone. She hung her big silk hat, with its monstrous plumes of feathers, upon an elder bush, and then sat down and deliberately took off her shoes and stockings, because the water did look so inviting, and those tiresome high heels dug into the soft earth and kept her back. Then she sat down on a stone by the water's edge, and dabbled her tiny white feet in the brown water, watching the crowds of minnows scuttling away as she splashed, and then coming again nearer when she kept perfectly stilL Beyond this post were great boulders lying in the bed of the stream; and the sunlight came through the branches of the trees, where the leafage was yet too scanty to hinder it much, and brought out the rich olive, and golden, and emerald tints of the mosses with which those boulders were gemmed; and the waving shadows of the boughs flickered and fell upon the water. Tiny birds sat on the stones, twittering and chirping, and moving about inoessantly ; water ousels and wagtails they were, though Silvia did not know this. The swallows, too, had arrived, and swept in graceful arches over the burn, dipping their wings in it, and then off again, swift as lightning. In the trees above, the chaffinches kept up a brisk lively noise; now and again the mellow notes of a thrush broke through their puny din with a glorious bar or so of rich melody; and from the distance came the monotonous, incessant cry of the cuckoo, that cry which, though in itself harsh and discordant, sug- gests spring so forcibly that all else is forgotten, and from the mere acc:dent of association, what is really a discord becomes a harmony. Sillvia was charmed. She watched the milk white blossoms fall from a wild cherry tree that drooped over the stream, and as they drifted away, looking like flashes of foam on the golden brown water, she was pleased to fancy each one laden with a new-born wish, and anxiously followed its course and hoped it would sail along free and fair, and not be wrecked in the shallows, or swamped in the rapids. Then it behoved her to try and cross the burn, by some stones immediately below the pool. She noticed some swallows flying in and out of a hole in the rock opposite, and imagined that there they might have a nest--quite a fallacy on her part, and showing ignorance of natural history—and oh, what a delight it would be to find young swallows! Considering her total want of practice in the difficult art of jumping barefooted from boulder to boulder' she got on pretty well, except that she cut oaaof tite vow little Jee l,il lit

div.p: WAR IN BEA VEN

In "My Mission to Abyssinia," Mr. Gerald 11. Portal, her Majesty's Agent and Consul-General at Zanzibar, gives an interesting description of a meteorological phenomenon. He says: The plateau of Godofelassi, about 7,500 feet above the sea, is in , a sort of cup formed by a wall of lofty mountains 'which nearly surround the plain, leaving,open only the gap through which we had entered. We were almost in the centre of the plain, and the moun- tain walls were from' a mile to two miles distant. . . . . About nine o'cloch th first muttering of a thunderstorm was heard in the hills on our ex- treme right. Rapidly gaining strength as it rolled forward towards our front, the flashes soon became incessant, and the corresponding reports like thei Ifiring of many heavy guns. Suddenly, with a crash which must have shaken the hills, this bombard- ment is answered by another mighty storm on our extreme left, which, firing its heavy artillery with ever-increasing rapidity, bears on along the moun- tains to meet the aggressor. Storm No. I appar- ently calls up its reserves, No. 2 does the same for as these two original combatants meet with a terrific crash straight before uq, two fresh thunder- clouds on the right,and three on the left,are hurry- ing up with all speed, each firing all its available guns as quickly as possible, and converging on the centre point, where the two first combatants are flashing and crashing in their death struggle. At one moment we could see seven separate storms banging away simultaneously. The noise was tremendous, the flashes incessant; within the space of one minute by the watch, Beech and I counted seventy-five flashes of lightning. . . . . While this panorama was being enacted before and all round us not a drop of rain had fallen where we sat, not a breath of wind had stirred the embers of the fire; we lay in a dead calm, as though all the forces of Nature were concentrated on the struggle going on before us, utterly neglecting the rest of the world.

WHAT SHOULD BE DONE FOR THE LABOURER? In the "Nineteenth Century" Lord Thring writes, as his wont, intelligently and lucidly, as to what is necessary to be done in order to settle the land question. His own summary of his paper is to be found in the following paragraph, which should be committed to heart by Parliamentary candidates in every rural constituency at the coming election : "Comparatively small amendments of the stattbte- book would remove the legal obstacles in the way of a complete scheme of improvement. Arouse the Revenue authorities and the Board of Agriculture, and you have brought into the market from time to time parcels of land of a size eminently adapted to the labourer. Moreover, they will not be huddled together in large unmanageable lumps, but distri- buted in small holdings throughout the rural pa- rishes. Create district registers of title by making every County Council a registry office for titles and a sale office of land,and you have the machinery for selling the land. Make the post office an advertis- ing instrument and their officers collectors of the instalments of purchase-motley, and there arises a complete organisation for bringing home to the peasant a knowledge of the land he can buy, and a perception of the easy mode in which he can ac- quire that land, pay the purchase money, and deal with it cheaply. Create village councils, and you invest the peasant with a status which will give him an interest in his village, and a position which he will not readily exchange for that of a town re- sident. It is not, however, the interest of the well- to-do labourer which is alone to be considered. Dives and Lazarus may well both claim sympathy. Make it the duty of the parish in the first instance, and of the County Council as a secondary authority, to assert the right of the public to the footpaths and the roadside wastes, and the blessing of the ar- tist, the stranger, and the ploughman shall rest on the head of the Government who cares for such things, small in themselves but large in their effects."
THE KAISER'S KNIFE AND FORK.

An incident which occurred two or three years ago, on the occasion of the young German Em- peror's visit to Greece, illustrates anew the fact, which no one ever doubted, that the etiquette of a Court may bring as much discomfort to the king as to the people who surround him. The Kaiser holds the honorary rank of adiniral in the British navy. The commander of the British squadron in Greek waters tendered his Majesty a dinner on board his ship. Of course the banquet was to be a most elaborate and magnificent affair. The hour arrived, and the Royal guest and his suite and offiecrs, all in brilliant uniform, were as- sembled. Then it was discovered that an important implement was missing. Where was the Emperor's knife and fork. For the Kaiser, baying but one arm that he can use—his left arm is withered—can wield the sceptre, the sword, or the pen ; but cannot use a knife and fork as other people use them. In their place be empleys an ingenious contrivance which combines in one implement both knife and fork, and does very well with it. Just at the last moment it was discovered that the imperial knife and fork had not been placed by the imperial plate. It was sought for but could not be found. The Emperor's attendants were inquired of ; no one knew where it was. _ _

Then the knife and fork might have been left ashore, perhaps. A picked crew were put into one of the ship's boats, and brawny backs bent over the oars ; for the errand was one that called for despatch. The Emperor's quarters in the city were searched, but no knife and fork could be found. All this time the dinner was spoiling. The search had been made with all possible energy, but it was now two hours since the table had lacked only the Kaiser's knife and fork. But the dinner could not be eaten until the Kaiser was ready to eat, and his eating implement must be found.' Perhaps before this time the happy thought had occurred to more that one person, " the Emperor may know where it is." But up to this time no one had ventured to ask him. Would he, under the melancholy circumstances, take it amiss if he were questioned? Hunger rendered the host bold; with decorous delicacy the Emperor was approached,and the momentous question was put. Could he tell where his knife and fork could be found?

" Why, yes, here it 18," replied William 11. ; and reaching inside his uniform, he produced the much sought implement from an inner pocket. The host forthwith led the way to the table, not only greatly relieved in mind, but deeply impressed with the fact that the affairs of Germany weie in safe hands.

_ The annual St. Paul's Congregational tea party and concert were held in the Co-operative Hall, , Sankey-street, Warrington, on Monday evening. The hall was handsomely decorated for the occasion.. About 360 persons partook of tea, and there was a large attendance at the subsequent concert. Mr. Robert Davies presided, and was supported by the Rev. H. V. Pigot, vicar of St. Paul's, the Rev. T. AL R. Young Hughes, his curate, Alderman Sutton, and. .`es Mr. Thomas Morris. The CHeimeax, who was received with applause, said ....., —.- before calling upon the vicar to speak to them on the condition of the parish in which he and his wife worked so hard, he would like to take his audience back 50 or 60 years, and tell them what he recollected of the churchee lin Warrington. He was sure it would interest them, because it always interested him very much indeed to hear what his ancestors had done. When he was a little boy there was only the old church at the top of Church-street, though not the old church they' now knew. There were then no Mount SchoolS and no National Schools. Services were held in the morning and afternoon, and there was no evening service in Warrington. He recollected even- ing services being got up many years after, and there being sconces with tallow candles in them for light. (Laughter.) He recollected going to the church with his father and mother,and sisters and brothers, and he was sorry to say that, with the cxception of Major Pickmere, he did not know a single gentleman now living who went to the church at that time. He remembered three ladies who did, who were still alive, but ladies being a little particular about their ages sometimes, he would mention none of their names except one. (Laughter.) An old lady now living, who was 98 years of age, and in possession of her faculties, a vigorous old lady, in fact, used to come to the Warrington Parish Church when he was a very little boy. He referred to Miss Lloyd, for- merly of Sankey. At that time there was no such thine as a parochial tea : it had never been dreamed of. The seats in the body of the church were free, whilst the pews were in the gallery and sides. People were very friendly in those days, and there were few people in the town whom his father did not know. But considering that the popalation of the town had more than trebled, it was no wonder that he did not know everybody now. Trinity Church was in those days the church for what might be called the better off class, who used to have pews with their names on, and there were only a few free seats. St. Paul's had only just been built, St. James's, Latchford, shortly before. There were no such things as mission rooms or schools, except Sunday schools. On the last Sunday in the month bread used to be distributed in the Parish Church. His father was always in office at the church as warden, sidesman, or in some other capacity, and he remembered from the earliest times seeing three large square pews full of loaves of bread, which were distributed after the service to the poor people who came for them. In the morning the men mostly came to church,and in the afternoon the ladies. After church they walked home through the pleasant Howley fields by footpaths across a clear brook from which boys caught small fish. The church wag surrounded by beautiful lime trees, and the rectory was hidden by trees, and a very pretty place it was. The walks were quite the pleasure of going to church on Sun- day afternoon and half the congregation streamed over the meadows round by the mill and weir, and back into • the town. In the morning when they came out of ...,, church they went straight home to dinner. (Laughter.) He remembered what he supposed they never saw now that they used to meet a procession of little girls carry- ing home pork, mutton, or pies from the bakehouse for ' dinner. His father was then a:Guardian. Occasionally they called at the old white workhouse in Church.st., where the inmates had boiled beef, carrots, and turnips for dinner every Sunday. He thought the inmates must have got tired of this, but they had as much as they could eat. The women were dressed in wincey petti- coates, with bedgowns on. (Laughter.) The services inside the church, he might say, were conducted on very primitive principles, and such a thing as a hymn was absolutely unknown. What was used was a metrical translation of the Psalms by Hop- kins. He remembered the rector, the Rev. Horace Powys, trying to introduce a book with about a dozen hymns, includinc, "Awake my soul" and "Glory to my God this night' but many of the congregation resented even that. One old gentleman was heard to mutter when they struck up one of the hymns, "What is this? David was a fool to this man." (Laughter.) There were two pews in the church with fireplaces in, and when the parson spoke too long the people used to poke the fire as a hint. (Laughter.) Over the end of the chancel were two colours, one of these being that of the Warrington Volunteers. Perhaps it might" be said he ought to think a great deal of the present days. Well, he did in some respects but not in others, when he thought of these old days, when Warrington was an old country town with little smoke and little stir. He Wag delighted to see so many there that evening, and he hoped it was a sign that Mr. and Mrs. Pigot were ap- preciated, and it gave him great pleasure to meet them. Though he did not live in the parish his office was in it, and he had something to do with the living, and when in Warrington he considered himself a parishioner of St. Paul's. The Rev. H. V. PIGOT, the vicar, then addressed the meeting. He reminded the audience that at the last congregational meeting the Rev. Mr. Wilkinson, for- , merly of St. Paula was present, and hoped to have been, this year,but was disappointed. The parish, it was weli known, had been worked thoroughly by Lim, when ke was in it, but it could not be expected that they could show a great deal of progress during the year that had passed. A high level had been reached, and they had done all they could to maintain that high level, during part of the time he had been connected with the church he had been single handed,and some work had to be neg- lected. He thanked very heartily those friends who had helped him to carry on the work,until the Rev.Mr.Young Hughes was appointed curate. Since he came they had' made decided progress. He thanked also Mrs. Beaman for having taken upon herself the responsibility of Pre; viding him with help. The rev. gentleman then referre to a presentation to be made that night to Mr. George, Bebington, the chief ringer of St. Paul's, of a set of hane bells for the ringers. The concert was then proceeded with, and we"! as follows :—Part song, "Up quit thy bower, the choir ; songs "The old cathedral," Mr. Parkinson ; and "The children's home," Miss Picton ; humoroul Irish song," She'd like to be Queen of the May," encorl Mr. Mentgomey ; songs, "The new kingdom," IVlisd Cosgrove ; "The mighty deep," Mr. Sherlock, .ani " Ages ago," Miss Oxley; humorous musical reel ', encored,Mr.Montgornery ; songs, "The armourer's gi;;L' Mr. G. The Committee had been much gratified by that donation, but he Should like to mention that while they were ac- tually giving in Warrington instruction to pupil teachers and assistant masters and mistresses from the county of Chester, the County Council were asking Warrington teachers and assistant masters and mistresses to go to Manchester for the same kind of instruction. He should have thought that if Warrington was a proper centre for the instruction of students from Cheshire it would have been a properly situated centre for the same purpose for its own population. 'the Committee hoped soon to have this rectified. The Council would observe that it was pro- ' posed to increase the curator's salary by £l5 a year. Mr. Madeley was appointed ha the year 1674, and since then had had only one advance, £l5. During that period the work of the museum and library had considerably increased, and that of the library had still further in- creased in consequence of that institution being made free. The Committee believed that they had in Mr. Madeley one of the most ably constituted men for the position that there were to be found in Lancashire, and were unanimous in askine the Council to grant the slight increase. It did not involve any increase in the rates, because their expenditure was limited to the amount of the museum rate, and that could not be added to. The Council would notice that the salary of the secretary of the Technical Instruction Committee was fixed at the sum of £5O a year. tin March last they appointed Mr. Madeley secretary of that Committeeeton- sidering him the best man for the post, and circum- stances had fully justified his selection. The work was very onerous and responsible; they had over 500-students and V. distinct classes and the whole of the manage- ment, as to finances and in every ether respect was car- riedlon by the secretary. Councillor GREENING secendedthe motion. Councillor BOLTON proposed an amendment that the salary of Mr. Madeley be not increased £l5, and that he betnot paid £5O for the secretaryship. He did not think tkot the Council should establish the precedent of in- creasing salaries from 12 months back, from last instead ce next March. The MAYOR: He has done the work ;he was not en- gaged to do that work. Councillor BOLTON said Mr. Madeley Was a public ser- tvant of the Corporation, and if certain work came in ffor the Committee to do he was responsible for doing it, and if he did not do it, ought to be removed. He did not • see that there was any increase of work in the museum, and there had been more assistance. According to the regular pay of the Corporation officers, he thought Mr. Madeley bad quite sufficient. Councillor Dritoe seconded the amendment. Councillor BROWNS asked if Mr.Madeley did not under- take the duties free. (Cries of" No," by Mr. Roberts and others.) He had certainly been under the impression that he did. He would remind them that Mr. Madeley in addi- tion to £155 a year, had a house, coals, and gas, no rates to pay, and assistance for cleanine,therefore, the Com- mittee were proposing to make his salary something like £275 a year. If they were going to tarry that night all the increases of salaries brought forward they were go- ing to increase the rates something like a third of a penny in the Z. Councillor Bocrox, said he would divide his 'notion, and moved an amendment fast that the £l5 increase be not given. Councillor DIXON seconded. Alderman PLATT considered the proposed increases of Mr. Madeley's remuneration byoas6s a year, at one time, too much. He preferred that the matter shoald be ! re-considered. Councillor SHAW GREEN considered that Mr. Madeley, was possessed of very 'considerable organising skill and ability and carried his work to a high pitch of perfection. He did not think there was any technical F ehlol being ! carried on so perfectly as that at Warringt on. 4,Coun- cillor Shaw Green strongly advocated both increases. Councillor MONWS eapported the original proposition. Councillor Hint supported the ,amendment. He re- marked that Mr. Madttiley (must as secretary of the Technical Instruction Committee, be using time that he ought to devote to other (Corporation works, and ought not to be paid £5O for doing that. Councillor GREENING supported the original proposi- tion. He mentioned in Mr. Madeley's favour,that in the classification of the museums of the country, the War- ! rington museum had been placed in the first class. Councillor H. Roamers replied on the discussion. He said Mr. Madeley in point of his intimate acquaintance both with literature and with natural history was an ex- ceptionally able man. A division then took .place, and the votiug was as follows :—For the amendment, Alderman Platt, Coun- cillors Bolton, Hill, Connell, Smethurst, Ashton,Browne, Blackhurst, and Dixon.-. Against,AlderinenFrancomb, Sutton, Harrison, Hdlmes, Burgess, and Chandley, and Councillors lit. T. Fairclough, Shaw-Green, Hepherd, Garner, H. They had been told that the in- crease involved no extra rates, but he was remember of the Museum Committee for two or three years, and al- ways found they were in debt, and they managed so well that they were always likely to be. Councillor DIXON seconded. Alderman I'LATT considered the increase too much. It was continually drummed into their ears, he said, that it would cost the ratepayers nothing, hut it was not very long since the library rate was increased fromlld.to in the 2, and they would no doubt increase it to 2d. in time. Alderman tPtartr : Not about the extra halfpenny, but because by-and-bye they-will want more. Councillor BOLTON next moved that a resolution on , the minutes of the Committee to the effect that the news- papers should, not in tuture be supplied with copies of , the Council summons before the meetings of the Council to' which they relate, should not be adopted. He con- tended that the newspapers had a, perfect right to let the public know what they were doing. oHear, hear.) They were there simply as representatives of the public. Councillor H. ROSEATE; seconded the proposal. He thought the Council should not forget the fact that they were there merely as the representatives and trustees of the general body of ratepayers. He was one of those who believed that the more thoroughly the matters of the Council were discussed by the public the more effici- ently would the work of the Corporation be carried out. Ele looked upon the press as perhaps the greatest educa- tional faculty that this country possessed, and it was a happy thing that as a rule the press of the country was Largely actuated by the highest and best of motives, and as long as that was so they could not put themselves too thoroughly in its hands as to their conduct and actions 'in municipal business. (Hear, hear.) , Alderman Sorrow also supported the amendment, as he believed they ought to afford every opportunity for the public to know what the Council was doing. Alderman Hotmas said he should not support the I proposal of the Committee. He did not know how the ' resolution came to be passed. It must have been passed after he left the Committee, for he should certainly not have supported it for a moment. Alderman HARRISON rose to support the amendment, an announcement which was greeted with much laugh- ter. When the apparently astonished Alderman inquired what caused the laughter, somebody replied that he voted for the resolution in Committee. He however, begged to say most distinctly that he did 'IA vote for it, but if he did he asserted his right to change his opinion. ( Laughter.) Alderman FRANECOIR '(%vho had now taken the chair, the Mayor having left to catch a train) said they I seemed to be all of one opinion against the resolution. Alderman HARRISON Who is the putative father ? (Much laughter.) THE BOROUGH SURVEYOR'S SALARY. -AN ,EXTRAORDINARY RESOLU noN WHICH NOBODY 'OWNS.
The minutes of the General Purposes Committee which contained various resolutions given in our columns last week, were moved by the Maroa, and teconded by Alderman HARRISON.
Alderman PLArr moved as an ameadment that the ,proposal to increase the salary of the borough Surveyor ;from £4OO to £5OO per annum be not adopted. . . . . .
Councillor BOLTON seconded, as he thought a rise of ..£lOO was too much at once. He would support a rise of 1.£50.

Couucillor SUOMI:MST also opposed the proposal. Alderman CILILNDLET was decidedly of opinion that Mr. Longdin deserved the increase. lie referred to the extra architectural work which Mr. Longdin hadvendered the Corporation, in devising the markets, and the new 'baths. In addition to this his duties in connection with the Longford works had beau of a very onerous character. _ .

Alderman HARRISON also supported the proposed increase. He remarked that Mr. Vawser, the former surveyor, was offered a salary of £5OO a year ,on condi- tion that he would give up private practice but this he declined to do. Through the instrumentality of Mr. Longdin there had been effected a saving to the town of upwards of £2,000 a year, in forcing excreta through subterranean pipes to Longford instead of taking it by cart and horse as formerly. Alderman Surrox said they must not forget that, dur- ing the past few years,the work of the officials had very materially increased. He supported the increase. Councillor Him. opposed the proposed increase, and pointed out that, if it were given, they should be paying £665 a year for work that was done by Mr. Vawser for £5OO. . . _

Councillor BROWNE was surprised that the officials had not gone in for an increase all round, considering how generous the Council was. He pointed out that Mr. Vawser had no paid assistant, ,while Mr. Lougdin had Mr. Walker and others. He opposed so large an increase as £loo,but would be in favour of -£5O being given. Councillor Dixon opposed the proposed increase, and referred to the extraordinary expenses incurred at Long- ford.

Councillor FLOOD referred to-the great increase in the size of the town since Mr. Vawser was surveyor, miles of streets having been added. if he had ever complained of Mr. Longdin it was because he was attempting to do too much. He spoke with some ,experience of the work done, and if some of the other officials in the borough surveyor's office had comie forward in the same manner as Mr. Longdin, he would have been eager to support their application. He eupportedlhe recommendation of the Committee.

Councillor SHAW Gazasi pointed out that it was 12 years since Mr. Longdin had had an increase, and he supported the present proposal. Heauggested that there ought to be fixed a maximum amount of salary to which an official could reach. (Hear, hears) Councillor H. Rosanne supported the suggestion made by Councillor Shaw Green. He •added that Mr. Longdin had saved the Corporation upon architectural work alone what would have amounted to about £5,000 in architect's commissions. Since Mr. Vawser's time the population had increased by about 20,000 persons, and he did not think they-could fbe,called extravagant in sug- gesting a salary that was ,proposed to be paid then. The Sanitary Committee had had Mr. Longdin s services night and day at Longford, and they were now in this happy position that the selieme there had at last resulted in an unqualified success. ,(",Oh, oh," and " Hear hear.") There were only two persons in Warrington who believed otherwise, and they were Councillor Dixon and that venerable but silly old man, Mr. Di,,,rgle. (" Oh, oh," and laughter. Mr. Digg.fle from the back of the room : " Here I am.") The Committee were quite pie- pared to stand upon the results obtained by the scheme. He added that he believed Itr. Longdin had always acted honestly and faithfully in:regard to the purchase of materials. (Hear, hear.) Councillor F. W. MONK* also. -supported the proposal of the Committee.

Alderman BURGESS supported the proposal, and pointed out that Mr. Vawser was paid £430 a year, and besides had assistance costing £123 a year. Alderman BURGESS was proceeding to make some statement when a loud ejaculation of incredulity was heard from Mr. Diggle, who was amongst the spectators. The Alderman repeated Ids statement in spite," as he said," of the sneer." gut the'. sneer "being repeated, Alderman Burgess in his most stately manner remarked that if the sound came from the ,other end of the room they would have the room cleared. Councillor ROBERTS : it is not worth bothering about. Alderman linaciass : I don't know:; itdnay be Coun- cillor D;xon. Alderman Pz.arr was supporting the amendment when Alderman Sutton objected that Alderman Platt had spoken before. Alderman Platt thereupon expressed his amazement, that Alderman Sutton who had passed the Mayor's chair, knew so little about the standing orders of the Council. Alderman Sutton was ruled to be in the wrong both by the Mayor and the Town Clerk, but he persisted in believing that he was right. A vote was then taken as follows :—For the amend- ment : Alderman Platt, Councillors Stnethurst, Balton, Hill, Cannell, and Brown-6 Against the amendment: Aldermen Francomb, Sutton

div.head: MESSRS. MONKS, HALL AND CO. LAUNCH A. STEAMER AT LYTHAM.
div.p: MESSRS. MONKS, HALL AND CO. LAUNCH A. STEAMER AT LYTHAM.

On Saturday last, at noon, a steamer made to the I order of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Warrington, was successfully launched at the shipbuilding works of Messrs. R. Smith and Co.. Lytham. The steamer is to be used by Vie .firm for their iron and coasting trade. It will ran chiefly between Warrington and Liverpool and afterwards on the Ship Canal. It is steel-built and the dimensions are :—Length, 90ft. ; beam, 21ft. ; depth of the hold, 9ft. It is estimated to carry about 200 tons, with a draft of 81t. Gin., and will cost something over £3,000. The engines are compound—surface condensing ones, having cylinders 3in. by 201 n. with an 18in. stroke, and are 200 indicated horse power. At the invita- tion of the firm a considerable party proceeded, on Saturday morning, .from Warrington to Lytham, being conveyed in two saloon carriages by the 9.50 train. The party comprised the directors of the Company, managers of the various departments, and a number of friends. Mr. Hall was,unfortunately.un- able to be present owing to the illness of Mrs. Hall. Carriages were waiting at Lytham station to convey the party to the ship-yard, where everything was in readi- ness for the launch„ and where aconsiderable number of Lytham people had assembled. The ceremony of christ- ening the steamer " The Helvetia" was performed by Master Re Monks, -son of Councillor F. W. Monks, who broke the bottle of wine on the ship's side in orthodox style as soon as it began to move. The launch was ad- mirably effected, the vessel, on the dog shores being knocked away, gliding smoothly down the slips, and plunging freely and gracefully into the water amid the cheers of the assembly. Various members of the party afterwards went on board, and expressed their satisfac- tion with the workmanlike way in which the vessel was being finished. The engines and boiler although made are as yet to be fitted in,and it is expected that a month or five weeks will elapse before everything will be com- pleted. Captain Monks of Warrington is to take charge of the vessel, and he will have as engineer Mr. James ' Ward, his son-in-law, who is at present engaged on the steamer at Lytham as representative of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co. After the launch the party were conveyed to the Clifton Arms flotel,where a frst class dinner was provided. Mr. Monks, C.C., said they had only one toast and that was ' " Success to the Helvetia and her builders." He added that that was a new omterprise so far as the firm was concerned, and he believed it would be a successful one. They had all seen the steamer that day, and had reason to think that it would prove a well-built, quick-sailing vessel, and in every way adapted for the work it had to do. Th.y were looking forward, like other people, to progress being made as a result of making the Ship Canal,and in helping themselves they were assisting in the development of the trade of Warrington. He then submitted the toast which was heartily drunk. Mr. Edmondson, as head of the firm of Messrs. R. Smith and Co.,in responding said he had every faith that "The Helvetia" would be found to be as good a steamer as could be built, and he trosted it would lead to further' orders. The afternoon was pleasantly spent about the town, and in walks by the shore, tl company assembl- ing for tea at half-past four. Be 'ore leaving Mr. John Walker moved a cordial vote of thanks to Messrs. Monks, Hall. and Co., tor their invitation and entertainment. This was seconded by Mr. J. H. Knowles and heartily adopted. Mr. F. W. Monks briefly responded. Captain Monks added a few words expressing his belief in the success of the enterprise. At 5.30 the party left Lytham for Warrington, the two saloons being brought from Wigan to Warrington as a special train. The weather, though showery for a time, was afterwards fine, and the visit to Lytham proved a very pleasant one.
