THE SHIP CANAL.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON MAN. Jonathan Mercer, who resided at Rose and Crown-st., met with a fatal accident at Big-field, Runcorn, at a quarter to eight on Saturday morning. The deceased was a rope runner in the employ of the Ship Canal Com- pany, and at the time named he jumped off the engine to hook on some waggons. He was not sharp enoagh, however, and in trying to do so the buffers caught him and crushed him in the abdomen. He was taken to the hospital at Latchford, where he remained in great pain for half-an-hour, when death put an end to his suffer- ings. The inquest was held on the body at Latchford Hos- pital, on Monday afternoon.—Annie Miller said that she had been living with the deceased tor the last twelve months. He was employed on the Ship Canal as rope- runner on the engine Barry. She last saw Win alive on the 25th ult., at 6 a.m., when he was going to his work. Deceased lodged at the huts at Big-field. He came home on Saturdays, and stopped till Monday. She heard of the accident about nine o'clock on Saturday morning, but when she got to the hospital he was dead. He was a native of Garston.—Geerge Simpson, 47 hut,Big-field, near Runcorn., engine driver of the Barry, said that on the dayin question, at 7.40 a.m., he was engaged in moving earth from a navvy in the cutting at Norton. He had taken one full set of waggons out, and brought the empty ones in. He was just basking up to a full set of 19 waggons, which were ready to take out. De- ceased remained on the engine until within eight or nine yards of the first waggon, and then jumped off and went in the direction of the waggons with the intention of coupling them. As deceased was a long time in giving the signal to start he looked round, and saw him between the buffer of the waggon and the engine. The fireman jumped off and held him whilst witness loosed him. He was taken on the engine to the Latchford Hospital.—John Gibson, 14, Mersey-st., Runcorn, stated that he was working alongside the train of waggons on the day in question, and saw the deceased riding on the step of the engine until it had almost stopped. He then jumped off, and in trying to get be- tween the engine and waggons, the buffers caught him. —Ellen Teraroe, nurse at the hospital, deposed that de- ceased was brought to the hospital at 8.15 on the morn- ing in ,qttestion, suffering from severe injuries to the chest and abdomen. The case was hopeless from the first. He died at nine o'clock in great pain. He was partially conscious at the time of death.—The Coroner remarked upon the man's carelessness, and a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. THE SECOND ISSUE OF STOCK.

The Special Committee of the Manchester Corporation re the Ship Canal have recommended that the second issue of £1,500,000 of stock under the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 191, should be made through the Bank of England at an early date. The company are prepared to receive the money at dates most convenient to them, and the committees suggest three equal instalments of £.500,000 each in March, June, and September. It is proposed to increase the number of Corporation repre- sentatives on the Ship Canal directorate, to which it is not expected Parliament will object.

RIVER DEVIATION AT CADISFIEAD. The deviation of the Mersey in this neighbourhood is not yet finished. The work, however, is being pushed forward, and something like one hundred men are con- tinually working at the barriers, which are now almost removed. This deviation, when completed, will unite No. 2,3, and 4 cuttings of No. 7 section, which arc at present separated by the Mersey. Already near the upper barrier earth is being tipped into the river, to direct the water into the new channel.

MANCHESTER CORPORATION. In reply to remarks made by Mr. Alderman Bailey, at the meeting of the Salford Town Council, on Wednes- day, in relation to a petition to be lodged by the Cor- poration against the Ship Canal C.mapany's Bill, the Mayor stated that the Corporation were disposed to act in the most friendly way towards the, Directors of the Company. At the same time care must be taken to pro- tect the rights of the borough, and he thought the rights of the borough had not been protected as they ought to have been in relation to the Fairbrother-st. bridge. The petition, it was explained, was simply lodged in order to give the Corporation a locus stand, in the matter.

THE BALANCE SHEET. The balance sheet of the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany, Limited, made up to the end of last year, shows that the loan capital amounts to £3,406,300, and the ordinary share capital to £3,977,521, the five per cent. perpetual preference shares to £3,999,222, and other assets to £397,520; making a total of £11,780,564. The outlay upon capital may be thus summarized :—Pur- chase money of the Bridgewater Canals undertaking (with the amount of the stamp duty and additions), £1,777,701 ; land purchase, compensation, and expense, £1,119,818 ; construction of works, including plant (less receipts on traffic account), £6,956,147 ; depreciation in value of shares vested in trus- tees for the company taken over from contrac- tor under agreement terminating the contract

for works, £71,873; engineering and surveying, £97,321; interest on share and loan eapital (less balance of general interest account), £751,482; parliamentary expenses, £149,519; law charges and disbursements, £16,697; directors' fees, salaries, office and general ex- _ . .

, costs of issuing debentures, and inteiest on par- liamentary deposit, £242,726; while cash in bank, in hand, and invested (including £150,000 invested in Man- chester Corporation on mortgage at three per cent.— Bridgewater undertaking), the value of general stores and stock of material on hand, outstanding accounts owing to the company, and the present value of shares vested in trustees for the company, taken over from the contractor under agreement terminating the contract for works, aggregate £597,277.

DISASTER AT RUNCORN. A LOCK IN RUINS. NARROW ESCAPES: A MAN MISSING.

- - A south-westerly gale of great violence blew over Runcorn, on Monday, and was the cause of great damage to the Ship Canal Works in the river. According to the tide table the tide should have reached a height of 15ft. 9in. at two o'clock, but half-an-hour before that time had arrived the water, driven up the river by the force of the gale, had attained a height of 16ft., and when two o'clock arrived there would be 191 t. of water in the Channel. Those not acquainted with the river in its strong moods have no idea how the waves roll along. White-crested, and of considerable height, they roll and tumble and dash themselves against the banks with tremendous force, and spray flies in drenching showers all around. Monday was such a day, and the river traffic was conducted with great difficulty and danger. The sea wall of the Ship Canal appeared to stand the strain of the gale and the rush of the water in a manner calculated to give confidence to all concerned. High tide was reached, and the water commenced to flow back 1 to the sea in the teeth of the gale; the waves had moder- ated in size, although the water was still churned to foam ; but all dauger of disaster appeared passed, when suddenly the inner wall of the Bridgewater Lock, in course of construction npposite Runcorn Docks, was seen to arch up in a most mysterious manner, and then crashed down in ruins. . _ .

----- Through the violence of the gale there were fortunately not many men at work at the time, and many of those present saw signs of the impending destruction, and reached places of safety, while others had a battle with the waters, but were quickly rescued. Mr. Davenport, the sub-agent, was about to inspect the workings, and had to make a jump for life. He escaped scatheless. A man named Webb also jumped from a gantry on to the wall with no more serious result than a sprained ankle. When the men were mustered and the roll called there were three missing, and for some time there was doubt whether they were drowned and carried away by the tide, or buried in the ruins of the lock. Afterwards two of them turned up, but the third, a young man named Kinn, a native of Essex, who lived in Mill-st., Runcorn, is missing.

The water appears to have penetrated the wall at three places and thrown it up in two segments as if by an earthquake. One lot of bricks were reared up on end, and on the summit of the pyrmadical pile stood an empty waggon, a silent monument of the destruction- wreaking waves. As an eye witness observed the wall is cut as clean through as though it had been done by a knife. The only piece of plant which has gone down is a derrick, as the end of the wall which has collapsed was not the scene of very active operations. The Bridgewater Lock is intended to play a very im- portant part in the traffic of the port of Runcorn, which is very extensive and the feeder of the trade on the Bridgewater Canal. This lock Is to be the means of communication between the river and the docks, and as it will have to be used by schooners and barques in addition to large number of flats, it is designed of large size, for their accomodation. The length is 350 ft. and the width is 45ft. Two years had been spent upon its construction, as the work presented engineer- ing difficulties of considerable magnitude, and neces- sitated the employment of much skilled labour. The erection of large water tight dams have been necessary, in order that the sand might be excavated and the foundations of the walls placed upon the rocky bed of the river. The foundations of the walls are of concrete. Twenty-one feet wide at the base, the wall gradually narrowed until it was only seven at the top,and appeared strong enough to stand an earthquake. The upper por- tion of the lock wall that has been partly demolished was of blue brick, which would have been finished with huge coping stones of granite. So recently as Saturday , the foundations of the sill of the lock gate were placed in, and everything pointed to the speedy accomplishment of an important part of the undertaking,but on Monday 200 feet of one side was rent asunder in a manner that illustrates but too well the tremendous force of water ; and the carefully planned work of months is thrown in ruins in less time than it takes to describe it. An explanation of the cause of the unfortunate mishap is not forthcoming. It appears probable that the water has worked its way into the foundations, for not only is the brick portion of the wall wrecked but the concrete has been split into huge blocks whic:i have been hurled hither and thither by the eddying water. Altogether the damage done is of great extent, and it is probable that the first official estimate of £6,000 will be exceeded by £lO,OOO. Many months will elapse ere the damage is made good. The gale continued on Monday night and on Tuesday. but the river was not so turbulent and no further damage was done. On Monday also the river washed away a portion of the embankment at Weston Point. The embankment is made of" spoil," and the damage is of very limited extent, and Can quickly and easily be repaired.

JUVENILE COMPETITION AT THE WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.

On Saturday evening the first annual Apmpeti- tions and prize distribution took place at We Gym- nasium. Mr. Thomas Morris presided,and there was a fair attendance of spectators. The programme on this occasion was entirely composed of exercises and various kinds ot competitions by younger members of the Gymnasium. The exercises included , dumb-bells, bar bells, clubs and vaulting horse,and ' they were all gone through in a style which evi- denced a remarkable advance towards proficiency. The competitions were as follows :—High jumping com- petition—prize silver medal.-1., H. Bush, 4ft. lin. ; 24. G.Robertson and C. R. Doncaster,4fs. each ; 3, ‘l. Smith, and 11. 0. Crosby, 3ft. llin. each. Hurdle race—prizes, 2 silver medals.—First heat : J. Fierpoint, 4yds., 1 ;C. R. Doncaster, scratch, 2 ; second heat, H. Bush, scratch, 1 ; H. Massey, 3yds., 2; final heat, Bush, 1 ; Pierpoint, 2. Sack race—prizes, 2 silver medals.—First heat, H. Heywood, 6yds., 1 ; B. Podmore, 3yds., 2 ; second heat, P. Heywood, 3ydB., 1 ; F. McGregor, Byds., 2 ; final heat, Podmore, 1 ; Heywood, 2. Flat race—prizes, two silver medals.—First heat, J. Pierpoint, scratch, 1; H. G. Roberts, scratch,2 ; second heat,H. Fleywood,scratch, 1 ; H. Fox, scratch, 2 ; third heat, A. Mylechreest,3yds , 1 ;H. Massey, scratch, 2; final heat, Yfylechreest, 1 ; Massey, 2. Obstacle race—prizes, 2 silver medals.— First heat, A. G. Robertson, scratch, 1 ; J. Smith, scratch, 2 ; second heat, R. H. Heywood, 9yds., 1 ; H. Massey, 4vds., 2 • final heat, Smith, 1 ; Robertson, 2. The prizes were afterwards distributed to the successful competitors by Mr. Morris.

div.head: LORD SALISBCRI: AT EXETER.
div.p: LORD SALISBCRI: AT EXETER.

Lord Salisbury, speaking at a Unionist demonstration at Exeter Hall on Tuesday night, said the Government were summoned to judgment, but had not been told what was the issue upon which the trial must take place. The Radicals were making all sorts of promises at the expeese of the farmer and the squire, and also at the expense of the Eighth Commandment. Many causes had been at work to improve the condition of the labour- ing classes. Trade and industry had been encouraged by scientific discovery ; and the new Poor-law, in contrast to the old, had done much good, one of its lessons being that a man should, if possible, depend upon his own efforts. The only lasting benefit a statesman could con- fer upon a poor man was to give him ample opportunity for the exercise of his moral , and intellectual qualities, and this opportunity the Goverment had afforded in free education, which ha considered far better than the most lavish gifts the State could offer. He spoke with disfavour of parish councils, which would be certain to increase the rates ; hut said he should Probably be responsible for creating district councils. He looked upon Mr. Cham- berlain's scheme of insurance, if it could be carried out, as a hopeful method of alleviating the condition In the aged poor ; and said he was anxious to multiply the small properties in the country, fon he thought small holdings and the creation of yeomen the strongest bul- wark against revolutionary change. Ireland remained the burning question of the hour. It was the fate of Ireland that the general election, and possibly the next and the next after that, would be called upon to decide. He doubted whether the Radical Opposition had made up its mind as to what it would do on the Irish question, pointed out what he considered the dangers and perils of separation. and urged Conservatives and Unionists to sink all minor differences and fight persistently for the unity of the empire.

At Ilarlesden Police Court, on Thursday, a woman was charged with attempting to commit suicide and to murder her three children. They were all found in bed in the night apparently dead,but emetics Were promptly administered, and all recovered consciousness on Thurs- day morning.

But, unfortunately, there•aae. other cases in which it becomes a species ef whiteelavery, and that, not because of ordinary„but because of extraneous,,duties. Something iss known, in every town of the obligation under- which certain teachers labour to dance attendanceen. the parson as the chief manager of the school „but there are few town4aeople who have any iita,of the syste- matic way in which teachers of ,bothi sexes are called upon throughout the conntny,—aud especi- ally in ,:ennection with village- schools—to do a lot of work for which they amin no wise paid. The State has for many years found the money for twovthirds oh the cost of elementary education, and haa recently wads provision for meeting a large portion of the remaining % third. Under these aircumstances it has not auanaturally regu- lated, the work of school teachers.. But, unfortu- nately, whilstalie code and. time-table have been recognised as constituting the teacher's definition of duties, the clergyman or minister has in tho• sands of instances stepped in and insisted that; certain work,shall,in addltion, be done for him ,for nothing or next to nothing, under pain of dismis- , rah This, as it seems taus, isa species of tyralmy tempered by fraud ; and electors as well as teachers ought to resolve that it. shall be put an els', to. . The National Union of, Teachers have tak,m, the :matter up most vigorOusly ; and an important Re- port upon the subject has just been issued by the Executixe of that ozganisation. Referrinato the "system of parasitilal tasks. which has boon, fae- toned upon the teachers engaged in our elementary schools," the Report adds The teacheda must be organist, parish clerk, overseer, bellringer Sunday school superintendent,, school cleaner, secretary to all the clubs an institutes which may exist in the parish, or any combination of these duties, and, apparently last of all,teacher of the khool." From ,anaxalysis of the advertisements in "The School- , master" for 1890 it appeared that "'One hundred and seventy advertisements demanded as a con- dition of appointment that the applicant should be prepared to take organ or harraonium at the, services; 68, organ or choir; 28, organ, choir, andi Sunday school; 62, organ and Sunday school; 62, Sunday school alone; and 21, the choir alone." It would seem from inquiries that have been I instituted that there are over 10,000 teaches in the country who are performing Sunday duties for which they are either not paid—or paid, as is often understood, in the salaries which they. obtain as day-school teachers. Such a state of things is degrading to teachers and a fraud upon the tax- payers. It is sometimes said in defence of this iniquitous system that Sunday duty is net compul- sory ; but that is a delusion, as the teacher soon finds. To be fore- warned is to be forearmed. It is a desperate game to play ; and what if it should end in the dissolu- tion of the House of Lords itself? After tievoting Years of consideration to the Irish question, the People of this country will not be baulked, when they have given their decision in a constitutional fashion, by a handful of stupid and irresponsible tlen who mar everything they lay their hands up- ". LOCAL NEWS.
RUNCORN SEAMAN'S INSTITUTE. An enjoyable entertainment was given on Tuesday evening in the above institute, by the " Ole Kansas Minstrels." Mr. A. Ravenscroft officiated as accompanist.

CONCERT AT LACEY-STREET SCHOOL, WIDNES. On Thursday evening, a concert was given in the above schoolroom, in aid of the Oakland-street Brass Band. There was a very fair attendance, and Mr. J. Williamson presided. DEATH OF A WIDNES VOLITNTREE.

Sergeant Instructor Hills, of the Drill Hall, Widnes, has died after a severe illness, extending over sixteen months. Deceased was formerly a sergeant in the King's Own Border Regiment. THE Sr. JOHN AMBULANCE CLASS, RUNCORN. The examination of the third Ambulance Class, Association, in Runcorn' for first aid certificates, took place in St. John's Schoolroom, on Wednesday afternoon. It was conducted by Dr. Okell of Winsford, and passed off very well. KITCHEN RANGERS—GarIand Builders Ironmonger, War- rington.— Advt.

div.head: S&CRED CONCERTS AT_ RUNCORN.
div.p: S&CRED CONCERTS AT_ RUNCORN.

In aid of the Instrument Fund, the Runcorn Town Band, and Kingston Mills Prize Band gave two Sacred Concerts in Runcorn Public Hall, on Sunday. There was a large audience at both the afternoon and evening concert, for the music was of a high-class character.

LICENSING MATTERS AT RI7NCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Chas. White was granted temporary permission to sell at the Claren- don Hotel, under the license lately held by Fanny Lee. Wm, Dunbavant, at the Nelscm Inn, Rutland-st., under the license formerly held by his late father, and Charles Dutton, at Wilson's Hotel, lately held by George Wyatt Cooper. VICTORIA. ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES. In aid of Home Missions, special services were held lin this Chapel on Sunday, and large congregations at- tended. The morning preacher was the Rev. W. Pritchard, and in the evening the Rev. G. S. Meek occupied the pulpit. On Monday evening a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. B. Brown. The Rev. Joseph Rhodes, of Bristol, attended as a depu- tation, and delivered an address. The collections were satisfactory. . RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. On Thursday evening, a meeting of the ratepayers of the township of Runcorn was held in Bethesda School- room, Vicar-st. Sanction was given for a loan of £534 35., to be made by the Runcorn Burial Board, to repay to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners £534 35., expended by them in making and draining that portion of Victoria-road, in Runcorn, which ahuts on the Run- corn Cemetery. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Wood. I /UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. DEATH OP A RELATIVE OF DR. PRESTON.—A leading figure of the North of Ireland has just been carried off after a brief illness, by the fatal influenza, namely, Dr J. King Maconchy, who for nearly forty years has, been head surgeon of the County Down Infirmary. He was one of the most distinguished surgeons in the country, and had a British reputation. Dr. Maconchy was son of the late well-known Rector of Corlick, near Dublin; and he was brother-in-law to the present vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, the Rev. Dr. Preston. TEMPERANCE SUNDAY AT WIDNES.

Sunday was the day appointed by the Bishop of Liver- pool for sermons to be preached on temperance, in the diocese of Liverpool, and also for offertories to be taken in aid of the Church of England Temperance Society. In Widnes special services were held at all the churches, and the offertories realised a satisfactory sum. The preachers at the various churches were St. Mary's, Rev. Dr. Preston (Runcorn) ; St. Paul's, Rev. G. H. Garrett (vicar) ; St. Ambrose's, Rev. G. A. Le Bert and Rev. R. Meiklejohn ; St. Luke's (Farnworth), Rev. T. G. John- son and Rev. J. R. Jones. RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB ANNUAL MEETING.

There was a good attendance at the annual meeting of the above club, over which Mr. W. Ockleston pre- sided. The report and balance sheet were submitted by Mr. A. Riley, one of the joint secretaries, which showed that after meeting all liabilities, there was a balance in hand of between £3O and £4O. The member- ship had increased during the year, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., was re-elected president ; Mr. Ockleston was ap- pointed treasurer; and Messrs. W. Handley, and A. Riley were re-chosen as joint secretaries. A working committee, consisting of 13 members, was also elected. EVIIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York. Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. " Examiner ' Office. Bewsev-at.. Warrington.—Advt.

RUNCORN FREEMASONS AND THE LATE DUBE OF CLARENCE. In reply to their letter of condolence with the Prince of Wales, K.G., M.W.G.M.' &c., &c., on the occasion of the death of the Duke of Clarence, the members of the Fllesmere Lodge of Freemasons have received the follow- ing communication :—"Sir Francis Knollys is desired to convey to the worshipful master and brethern of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons the sincere thanks of the Prince of Wales for the warm fraternal sympathy they have expressed on the occasion of his Royal Highness's and the Princess of Wales's great bereavement. Sand- ringham, 27th Jan., 1892."

GEMS OF THII OPRRA COMPANY AT RUNCORN. Mr. Josef Cantor's "Gems of the Opera Company" made their first appearance in Runcorn on Monday even- ing, and scored a brilliant success. This was Mr. J. W. Temperley's initial effort at catering for the public amusement, and he is to be commended for his enter- prise in securing the services of so large and talented a troupe for his first evening concert. There was a large and fashionable audience present, and it is to be hoped that Mr. Ternperley will be encouraged to provide another musical treat ere the season ends. The artistes were Madame Laura Smart, Misses Lucie A. Jones, Aimee Roland, Dora Jones. and Bella Pride ; Messrs. P. Makinson' 'S. Kirkham John Peate, C. Makinson, R. Jones, T. Barlow, W. Lewis, J. Nevir, and Frederic Owens. The orchestra comprised solo violin, Mr. Thos. Shaw ' • clarionet, Mr. F. Norton ; horn, Mr. J. Lay- burn ;flute, Mr. V. L. Needham ; cornet,Mr, A. E. Hall; contra bass, Mr. R. Stewart; pianoforte and conductor, Mr. Josef Cantor. A Steinway grand supplied by Mr. Temperley was used. The programme was calculated to meet the tastes of the most exacting, and included excerpts from Lurline, Patience, Hugenots, Siege of Rochelle, Maritana, The Gondoliers, Sultan of Mocha, Ruddigore, and H.M.S. Pinafore. Both the songs and choruses were rendered in a most admirable manner, and the encores were enthusiastic and frequent,and two hours' pure enjoyment was spent. NORTHWECH DIVISION L/DERAL ASSOCIATION. In connection with this Association, a meeting of the Liberals of Runcorn north and south polling districts, was held on Thursday night, in the Union Hall, Regent-st. The business was of a formal character. Representatives on the general council of the Assoeiation were appointed, and also the chairman and secretaries of the various districts into which the town is divided. Eight vice presi- dents were also chosen. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. A RUNCORN CAPTAIN DROWNED. Mr. S Brighouse, county coroner, on Saturday held an inquest, at Bootle Police Court, on the body of Joseph Orme, captain of the flat Garston, who resided at Wright's-row, Runcorn. About 6.30 on Friday night the deceased fell into the Brocklebank ' Dock, when going aboard, between the flat and the quay. A dockgateman named Ilampson and a man named Charles Berthelis was nearly drowned in try- ing to get him out of the water. The deceased was eventually taken out alive, but died in the Bootle Hospital from the effects of his immersion. The jury found a verdict in accordance with the evi- dence, and commended Hampson and Berthelis on their bravery. RE-VALUATION of STOCK. Unheard of Bargains, at liverrs' 17, Sankey-street, Warrington,—Advt.

DEATH OF AN, OLD RUNCORNIAN. On Wednesday, Mr. T. Yarwood, lately of Thel- wall, but formerly of Runcorn, died at his residence, in his 73rd year. During his residence in his native town he closely identified himself with the Wes- leyan cause, and was a well-known Odd fellow. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankerat.. Warrington.— Advt. 200 CONVICTIONS. Bridget Kildare, the notorious St. Helens charac- ter, was charged with drunkenness, at St. Helens Police Court, on Monday. She pleaded guilty, and the Chief Constable stated that she had been con- victed on 199 previous occasions. She was fined 10s, and costs. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, SRBlcey-SG. Warrington.—Advt. AN UNFORTUNATE COINCIDENCE. One day last week, Mrs. Renshall, of Kemble-st., Prescot, whilst hanging clothes on the line in the kitchen, slipped off the chair she was standing on, and broke her leg. Rather strange that only a week or so ago her husband, Paul Renshall, fell in the street, owing to the slippery state of the foot- path, and broke his leg. GAS FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. WIDNES FREEMASONS. On Thursday afternoon, the installation of Bro. J. Goff as senior warden of the Equity lodge of Freemasons (1384), took place in the Masonic rooms Central Hotel, Widnes. After the installation had taken place, the brethren sat down to a banquet provided by Bro. Parkes, of the Central Hotel. A past master's jewel was presented to Bro. J. Walker in appreciation of his services to the Lodge. EVAN'S GREAT STOCKTAKING SALE now OD.-17 Sankey- , st., Warrington.— A dat.

NEWTON AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION. Mr. Robt. Stone has now returned from Scotland, and has signified his refusal to allow himself to be nominated for election to the County Council for ' the Newton Division. Mr. A. C. McCorquodals has not, as stated by a contemporary, been approached, nor is there any present intention of asking him. Another gentleman, whose name is withheld, has been asked, and his decision is expected shortly. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-J. and W. Durrov, Sankey-t., Warrington.—Advt.
DEATH OF THE REV. G. BOND, VICAR OF
FAIINWORTH.

The Rev. G. Bond, M.A., vicar of Farnworth, died at his residence at Roby on Monday last, and was interred at Farnworth on Thursday afternoon in an unostentatious manner. The vacant benefice of Farnworth has been offered to and accepted by the Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar of Rainford, who will be succeeded at Rainford by the Rev. John Bridger, organising secretary of the S.F.C.K. Mr. Williams was vicar of Widnes, from 1879 to 1888, and he was' a very popular preacher. HY-VALUATION Of STOCK. Unheard Of Bargains, at EVANS' 17, Sankey-street, Warrington,—Advt. Mn. T. W. LEW' M.P., AT ST. HELENS:

Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the Newton Division, addressed a meeting of his constituents resident in the St. Helens portion of the division, in the Moss- bank Schoolroom, St. Helens, on Saturday night. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. Henry Foster, who presided, was supported by Lieutenant-Col. R. Pilkington, Messrs. J. 0. Swift, E. A. Robinson, C. Culshaw, W. Brooker A. C. Davies, R. Jones, and others. Mr. Legh, M.P.:Lieutenant-Col. Pilkington, and other gentlemen addressed the meeting, and a vote of confidence in the Government was unanim- ously passed, EVAN'S GREAT STOCKTAKING SALE now 011.-17 Sankey- It., Warrington.—Adrt. div.head: FORBIDDING TIM BANNS AT 11 AYDOCK.
div.p: FORBIDDING TIM BANNS AT 11 AYDOCK.

The very rare occurrence of forbidding the banns of marriage, was witnemed at St. James's.Church, Gftydock, on Sunday, and caused a considerable amount of excitement. The vicar (Rev. W. Caton) was announcing, for the second time of asking, the banns of marriage between a young couple named Abbott and Smith, when the father of the prospec- tive bridegroom, Abbott, rose in his place in the church, and objected to the publicatiom of the banns. The vicar invited the objector to see him in the vestry at the close of the service, which he did, when it transpired that his objection was on account of the age of his son, who was only 19, whilst the girl Smith was only 16 years old. Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., and Lady Gerrard were present in the church at the time. EvIN'S GREAT STOCKTAKING SALE Il*w 011.-17 Sankey- at., Warrington. " SUNNYSIDE " HYDEOPATHIC ESTABLISHMENT, SOI7TLIPORT. This admirable institution, under the direction of Mr. Bernardo, has been built on the site of what was the well-known private hotel. " Sunnyside," which was successfully carried on in Saunders-street by Mr. Councillor and Mrs. Boocock for the last six years. The situation is all that could be desired. The house has a south-west aspect, and thus is in a favourable position for catching the sun's strongest rays, hence the derivation of its title " Sunnyside." The premises are fronting Saunders-street, Knows- , ley-road, and Adelaide-street; on the Promenade Extension, and are close to the new Marine Park ,1 and Lake, and Promenade, Hesketh Park, and Lord- street, as well as being almost the proverbial stone's throw from the centre of the town. The public rooms, corridors, halls, and staircases are heated by means of hot-water coils and pipes,the air admitted to the building being warmed before entering. Low pressure heating is the system used. Without doubt the Hydro is a first-class establishment, constructed and equipped with all the improve- ments which science and experience can suggest, and its unrivalled situation, with unbroken sea view and cpen,though sheltered, surroundings, and the excellent accommodation which is provided, will gain for it a reputation not exceeded by any similar place in the kingdom—or else we are sadly mistaken. Lawns for tennis and other outdoor games are provided. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Ada. LANCASHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The annual meeting of the Liverpool District in connection with the above society was held on Tuesday in the Crescent Chapel, Everton, Liverpool. The proceedings commenced with a brief devotional service conducted by the Pastor of the church, the Rev. F. A. Russell. The business meeting was pre- sided over by Mr. William Crosfield, J.P. Betore proceeding with the usual business, the Rev. R. J. Ward of St. Helens seconded, a vote of condolence with the relatives and members of the church of the late Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, which was carried, and ordered to be forwarded tp the Rev. James Spur- geon. The treasurer, Mr. Crostiekl, reported an increase in the income of the district fop the year 1891 of about £3OO. The secretary, the Rev. John Yonge, read the reports from the various aided churches in the Liverpool district, and the grants recommended for 1892 by the Executive Committee were discussed and ultimately approve I by the meeting. The ministers and delegates afterwards partook of an excellent tea, provided by the friends of Crescent Chapel. In the evening, a public ser- vice was held in the chapel, when a sermon was preached by the Uev. John Hunter of Glasgow. A collection was taken on behalf of the funds of the union. The following ministers and delegates at- tended from Warrington :—The Revs. John Yonge and John Davies, Messrs. J. Podmore, William Bes- wick, Thomas Hawthorn, A. Lang, and J. Kershaw. Ra-VsLusnos of STOCK. Unheard of Bargains, at Bvszin' 17. Sankey-street, Warrington.—Advt.

STREET ACCIDENT.—On Monday P.C. Mitchell, from Rainford, whilst walking along St. Helens-road, slipped on an iron grid and fell, breaking his shin-bone and Rut- ting his ankle out. He was carried into a neighbouring house. The police authorities were communicated with and Dr. C. Barlow sent for, who set the injured Hint?. The injured constable was afterwards conveyed to his home at Rainford in a cab. PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS.—At the Prescot Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday, Henry Forster, Horn's Smithy, was charged with stealing the sum of ss. from the dwelling- house of William Sutton, a carter, residing at Tarbock, with whom be had been lodging. He pleaded guilty. and was fined 205., including costs.—Richard Salt and John Catherall, colliers, Whiston, were charged with stealing a quantity of timber, valued at 55., from the premises of Richard Prescot, brickmaker, Whiston. Complainant stated that he had missed timber to the value of about £6 during the last few months. The I charge against Salt was dismissed, but Catherall was I fined 10s, and costs.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
DISGRACEFUL SCENE IN THE BOARD ROOM.

THE MEETING ADJOURNED. The monthly meeting of Runcorn Board of Im- provement Commissioners was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. H. J. Grice presided, and there were present Messrs. 11. White, 3. Taylor, W. Hankinson, B. Bisbrown, P. Smith, W. Fisher, W. Timmins, W. R. Wass, H. Coward. It. Abel, and F. Wis wall, W. F. A. Lake (clerk), E. Marshall (sec.); and M. Barker (surveyor). THE DEATH HATE.—NO INFLUENZA. The Medical officer reported that during January there were 48 deaths registered, of which 13 were due to bronchitis. The deaths showed an average death rate of 28.8, and exclusive of 4 inquest cases of 284. In reply to Mr. Lightburn, Mr. McDougall said he had not seen a case of modern influenza this year. MB. SMITH AND ISIS PATIENCE. Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minutes of the Highways and Buildings Committee, and said to put the matter in proper legal form there was a slight addition to be made which Mr. Lake would read.—Mr. Smith : Is he suggesting something that the members of the Board are not cognizant of ?—Mr. Taylor : If Mr. Smith will have a little patience.—Mr. Smith (excitedly) : I object. to Mr. Taylor askiry, me to have a little patience. Mr. Taylor has no right to talk of such a thing as my pat- ience.—The ChAirman got up to explain, but it Wail some time before he could obtain a hearing, and then Mr. Smith interrupted—The Chairman : Those who live in glass houses should not throw stones.—Mr. Smith reiterated that he should not allow Mr. Taylor to talk about his patience.—The Chairman : Mr. Taylor, will you please go on with your proposition.—Mr. Smith :He has finished.—The Law Clerk said if Mr. Smith objected it was fatal to the addition.—Mr. Smith : I do object.--1 Mr. Taylor : I move the minutes.—Mr. Fisher seconded, and the motion was immediately put to the meeting and carried.—Mr. Smith then asked a question, but was in- formed that the minutes were passed.—Mr. Smith: My dear sir, they are not passed.—The Chairman replied that they were, he had had plenty of time to move an amendment if he wished.—Mr. Smith : Plenty of time ! I have only just stood on my feet.—The Chairman : The minutes are passsd.—Mr. Smith : It is simply absurd.— The Chairman: I think it is simply absurd to waste the time of the Board in this manner. NOT HIS SUNDAY OUT. Mr. Smith then proposed the minutes of the Health Committee, recommending that the wages of William Carmen (disinfector) be increased from 18s. to 18s.—The Chairman : It is usual for the Chairman of the Commit- tee to move the minutes,—Mr. Smith : It is usual to make mistakes.—Mr. Lightburn said he would second the motion. If they (:outi get through the business quietly it would be for the benefit of all.—Mr. Smith : Don't talk so much then.—The Chairman : I hope the reporters will make a complete report of these proceed- ings.—Mr. Smith : I hope they will. It is not my Sun- day out now ; it is my privilege.—The minutes were passed.
THE FIRFI BRIGADE.
ject .

The General Purposes Committee recommended that the salary of the superintendent of the Fire Brigade be ncreased from £8 to £lO per annum.—Mr. Flaukinson proposed the adoption of the minutes, and remarked that Mr. Wright had been connected with the Brigade for 33 years, and the work had much increased in con- sequence of the growth of population and the increase in the number of fires.—Mr. B. Abel seconded.—Carried. Mr. Smith wished to know why a minute relating to the Market Inspector was not proposed, and he was told that it would be dealt with under " General business " but in consequence of Mr. Smith ignoring the ruling of the chair, business could not be proceeded with for five or ten minutes.—Mr. Wiswall moved the following re- commendation of the Parliamentary Committee: That a further sum of £3O be expended in the purchase of apparatus for the teaching of Science and Art, making £l9O in all.—The Chairman addressed a remark to Mr. Wiswall in an undertone.—Mr. Smith : I think it is unfair to members of the Board.— The Chairman : Will you please allow Mr. Wisvrall to finish. I asked him to move that this £3O be handed over to the School Board.—Mr. Wiswall moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded.—Mr. Smith said the agenda was not worth the paper it was printed on. It was apparent to everybody that th,• proposer was entirely ignorant of what he was proposing. He thought the business ought to be more above-board.—The minute was carried.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported that they had re- ceived on general account £1,009 16s. 4d. ; district fund £lO2 ss. ; loan account, £800; Library account £9 15s. 4d. Accounts amounting to £1,052 7s. Id. were recommended for payment.—Approved on the motion of Mr. Fisher.

PRIVATE IMPROVEMENTS.-MR. SUITT/ AND THE PROPERTY OWNERS. Mr. Lightburn moved that all private streetsrequiring completion be made and that in the event of any of such streets being made by this Authority on behalf of the owners, the expenses so incurred be declared private improvement expenses, and be payable by the owners by instalments within a period of seven or ten years with interest at a rate not exceeding five per cent, per annum until the whole amount be paid. Mr. Lightburn advocated his resolution amid continual interruptions from Mr. Smith. He argued that this would benefit the owners and the ratepayers. The Committee could borrow the money at 3 per cent. aud charge the property owners 5 per cent., which would pay for the necessary office work. There would also bs a charge of 2i per cent, for superintendence, which ought to be utilized in providing an assistant for Mr. Barker. There was too much work for one man.—The Chairman con- tinually called Mr. Smith to order, but with no effect. At last he told him that he was too pachydermatous to be dealt with here. "You won't listen to reason," he continued, and I am sure the members--Mr, Smith (loudly) : Speak for yourself. I am a member of this Board—speak for yourself, speak for yourself.— Mr. Taylor seconded the motion, but on it being pointed out that there was a Committee already appointed to deal with this question, Mr. Lightburn withdrew his motion.—Mr. Smith claimed to say something on this question. It was well known by the ratepayers of Runcorn that the people who owned these streets were people like Mr. Lightburn, Mr. Taylor, the ' Chairman, Mr. Lake, and Mr. Fisher.—The Chair- man interpolated a remark, which caused Mr. 'Smith to repeat several times, his voice rising with each repetition, " I say it, I say it."—Mr. Lake : I unfor- tunately don't own any property.—Mr. Smith: You are connected with this very body, and Mr. Philip Speakman that owns all these streets. He said let the people who owned the streets make them. His friend Mr. Imison had defeated a motion like that some time ago, and he would do the same.—The Chairman ruled Mr. Smith out of order ; there WAS nothing before the Board, he must give notice.—Mr. Smith replied lf they stifled discussion he would speak to the reporters, but the Chairman put an end to the discourse by cAlling upon the secretary to read the correspondence.

div.head: STORMY TERMINATION.
div.p: A STORMY TERMINATION.

Mr. Taylor said he could not sit there as a member of that Board to put up with such disgraceful conduct as a member had exhibited that morning. (Hear; hear.) He had been a member 6f that. Hoard somethirnt like 18 years, and that was really the first time that any mem- ber had Conducted t imself in such a diszraceful, un- gentlemanly, unmannetley,and unmanly manner, as one of them had that day. . •
Mr. Smith.—Pile it on. Mr. Taylor said he would sit with no man that would lower himself to such a degree as lie was sorry to find a member had done that morning. _ _ .

Mr. Smith.—Don't be sorry:" Mr. Taylor (continuing said if the ratepayers would choose such a man as their representative, he for one would resign his seat. Mr. Smith.—So will I. Mr. Wiswall.—Will you name the member? . ._.

Mr. Taylor.—l have no hesitation in doing so. I refer to Mr. Smith's conduct this morning. Mr. Smith.—That's right Mr. Taylor. The Chairman said he sympathised with Mr. Taylor. Was he prepared to move anything? Mr. Taylor regretted his inability to do so. Mr. Smith said he claimed that he was a man, and that Mr. Taylor was a brute, a beast, and a dirty blackguard, to make use of the expressions he had applied to him. I say so sir. I say so sir. (Mr. Smith shouted the last remark at the top of his voicel.—The Chairman: I move the adjournment of the meeting.—Mr. Wiswall seconded, and it was carried.—Previously the members had risen op their feet, as though about to retire in a body. As they now left the room Mr. Smith several times shouted "Be is a blackguard to call me unmanly," and then he quietly walked away alone.

div.head: ADJOURNED MEETING.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED MEETING.

The adjourned meeting was held yesterday morning, Mr. 11. J. Grice presided and there were present Messrs. Fisher. White, Wiswall, Coward, Bisbrown, Wass, Tay- lor, Lightburn, Abel, Hankinson, P. Speakman, C.C., Lake, (Law Clerk), Marshall. (Secretary), and Barker, (Surveyor).

div.head: INFLIFENZA..
div.p: THE INFLIFENZA..
A memorandum from th-e—i;;T.Government Board respecting the Influenza epidemic was referred to the Health Committee on the motion of Mr. Bisbrown.
TEE MARKET SIIPERINTENEENT.

The resignation of Mr. C. Dutton as Market superin- tendent was read.—The Chairman moved that the resignation be accepted and Mr. Dutton said it was due to him as an old servant that the expression of feeling should be conveyed to him.—Mr. Hankinson seconded and endorsed the Chairman's remarks.—Carried unani- mously.—The General Purposes Committee submitted a resolution fixing the salary of the Market Superintend- ent at £6O a year, and resolved that an advertisement be inserted in the local newspapers for applications.— The resolution was carried on the motion of Mr. Han- k i nson.
THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. Mr. Speakman said he had pleasure in informing the Board that he was in a position on the previous day at

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: the Cheshire County Council to put the crowniag stone upon the edifice that a great number of members of the Board had been working at so hard for a considerable time. By 45 votes to 15 a committee of inquiry had been appointed. -

WATERLOO BRIDGE. Mr. Lightburn referring to the shocking condition of this bridge pointed out that neither the Committee nor the Board were to blame, because they could not proceed until they had completed the agreement with Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co.—Mr. Wiswall advised the Board to go on with the road independently of that ob- struction. He did not think it was necessary to wait.— Mr. Lightburn said Mr. Wiswall's advice as a civil en- gineer must have great weight. —Mr. Wiswall said the carriage way could be made, and the parapet left as at present.

THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. The Chairman proposed that .it be an instruction to the Parliamentary Committee that steps be forthwith taken to raise funds by appealing to the public, on behalf of the establishment of a Technical Institute.— Mr. Wiswall seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Speakman and carried. DEEP DOCKS. On the proposition of Mr. Lightburn, Mr. Taylor was appointed a member of the deputation, which will on Thursday next wait upon the Ship Canal Company with respect to deep docks at Runcorn. Mr. Pritchard's name was also added. YESTERDAY'S SCENE.—ME. smun REQUESTED TO RESIGN. The Chairman said before concluding the pro- ceedings of the Board which were interefered witk in such an unusual manner yesterday, he felt it his duty as Chairman of the Board to call attention to the un- warrantable, unjustifiable, and disgraceful terms applied by Mr. Smith to Mr. Taylor, who was one of the most highly respected members of the community in which he resided, a gentleman who had devoted a large portion of the best of his days to the study of the in- terests of the ratepayers of Runcorn and who had been grossly insulted. He felt it his duty to take the feeling of the Board and to ask for its support. He would not ' ask that member to apologise, but that they should ' unanimously request him to resign his position, and he would move that.--Mr. Abel seconded.—Mr. Speakman said this was an uausual course to take, but at the same time he felt that it was justified.—The motion was car- ried unanimously.--The Chairman in the name of the name of the Board expressed regret to Mr. Taylor that such language should have been addressed to him.—Mr. Taylor said he never felt more grieved than he (lid to see such conduct as that which was exhibited by a member of the Board on the previous day, and he sin- cerely hnped no • member would witness such a scene again. (Hear, hear.)

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. Pritchard presided,and there were present the Rev. Canon Wood, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Handley, S. Taylor, A. Salkeld,and G. Moss (clerk). SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The School attendance Committee reported that 34 parents had been summoned and 29 appeared before them and were dealt with. The visitors reported that during January the numbers on the rolls was 3.959, increase 212 on corresponding period last year. The average attendance showed an increase of 156 and the per centage of attendance was 76, the same as in Jan. a st year. A Izmir OF WAY. In answer to Dr. McDougall, Mr. Bowyer, the senior attendance officer, said there were about 150 children from Mill Brow district attending Greenway-rd. schools. —Dr. MacDougall said he had asked this question because the footpath from Heath-road to Greenway-road had been ploughed up and the footpath was therefore stopped without the requisite legal steps having been taken. The new road was not completed, and with teams of horses constantly working on it was not safe for the children to use it. He moved that the attention of Major Orred be drawn to the matter, and he be asked what explanation he had to offer. kir. Handley seconded the doctor's proposition, which was carried. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT CONMITTEE.
On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, the resignation of Mr. R. T. Kenyon, assist- ant master at Green way-road school, was accepted.

THE SCIENCE AND ART COMMITTEE. With regard to the question as to the relation of the Science and Art Committee to the School Board, which was debated at the last meeting, Mr. F. A. Lake wrote and explained that the Science and Art Committee were under the control of and subject to the School Board.

div.head: AN ECCENTRIC METER.
div.p: AN ECCENTRIC METER.

The Clerk reported that the water meter at Green- way-road schools had been tested and found to register 1000 gallons for every 900 gallons that passed through. The Water Works Company had agreed to make a cer- tain reduction in the account, but it was resolved that the Clerk ask the Water Company for a further reduc- tion.

div.head: – MARRIAGES AT 1117NCORN.
div.p: - MARRIAGES AT 1117NCORN.

Two interesting marriages took place at Runcorn, on Thursday morning, at St. Edward's Roman Catholic Church at eleven o'clock. Miss Elizabeth White, third daughter a Mr. George White, of The Glen, Higher Runcorn, was married to Mr. Robert R. Noblett, of Chester. The bride, who was attired in lavender cashmere, wore a wreath of orange blossoms and a flowing veil, and in her hand car- ried a beautiful bouquet. She was attended by Miss Thompson and Miss Ada Thompson, of Mona, Higher Runcorn, who were dresed in corn flower blue dresses, trimmed with fur and with hats to match. Mr. George Noblett, brother of the bride- groom, was the best man, and the other groomsman was Mr. C. Noblett. The bride was given away by Mr. William Harvey, of Widnes, and the marriage ceremony was performed by Canon Lynch of Chester. Amongst the presents were :—Mr. and Mrs. White, two pictures; G. Noblett, over-mantle ;J. C. Noblet, dinner service; Mr. and Mrs. Ellis, clock ;Mrs. Mills, China cruet and decanters; Dent. Serjeant Gallagher, fish carvers; Mrs. Whitwham, electro-cruet ; Mr. J. McNulty, electro preserve dish; Mr. Rossitter, pair of decanters; Miss Holley, fancy fans; Miss Corcoran, one pair of salt cellars and preserve jars; Mr. Cotgreave, one biscuit jar; Miss S. Thompson, silver tea pot; Miss A. Thompson, silver-mounted ink stand; Mr. and Mrs. Harvey, hearth rug; Mr. and Mrs. Jones, sofa rug; Mr. C. LeCouteur, self-pouring teapot; Mr. Stubbs, water jug and teapot; Mr. Gandy, tumblers; Mr. and Mrs. Graham, chair cushion and pin cushion; Mrs. Rayner, cheese dish; Mrs. Newall, ornaments; Mrs. Clarke, sugar basin and cream jug; Master Geo. and Ada White, tray; Mr. and Mrs. Martin, crumb brush and tray; Mr. Smith, glass dish ; Miss Heatherington, ornaments; Mr. and Mrs. Thomas White, table cloth; Miss Hampson, two table cloths; Miss Hoyle, dozen spoons; Mr. Edwin White, bed linen. On the same morning at ten O'clock at Ellesmere-at. Methodist Free Church, Miss Elizabeth llampson, daugh- ter of Mr. James Hampson, of Cawilor-s., was married to Mr. Edwin White, second son of Mr. George White, of the Glen. The bride was attired in electric blue cashmere, with silk hat to match, and in her hand she ' carried a charming bouquet. The bridesmaids were Mrs. Harvey, Miss Flossie Newall, and Miss Ada White, and they were respectively attired in pale lavender, white, and terra coax. Mr. George Brereton was best man, and the other groomsmen were Mr. John Handley ' and Mr. George Rutter. The Rev. James Martin per- formed the wedding ceremony. The presents included : blankets. Mr. and Mrs. Harvey ; bed linen, Mr. and Mrs. Jones; photo Runcorn Docks, Mr. and Mrs. Martin ; sugar basin and cream jug, Mrs. Clarke ; vases, Mrs. Newalt ; butter cooler, Mrs. Stubbs ; set of glass dishes, Mrs. Rayner; set of glass dishes, Mrs. Gandy; toilet ' covers, Miss Royle ; tea tray, Master George and Ada White ; sugar basin, tea pot, and hot water jug, George Rutter ; lamp, a friend; pair of brackets and pictures, Mr. and Mrs. Handley ; table cloth ; Mr. Jas. Hampson; tea set, Mr. and Mrs. White.

div.head: DEATH OF LA.DY MARY FOX-POWYS.
div.p: DEATH OF LA.DY MARY FOX-POWYS.

The death is announced of Lady Mary Fox-Powys. It took place, on Saturday, at Bournemouth. The deceased lady was second daughter of the late and sister of the present Earl Gosford. She married, in 1862, Leopold, second son of the late and brother of the present Lord Lilford. She leaves issue six daughters. The deceased lady and her husband oc- casionally resided at Bewsey Old Hall, Bewsey, generally during the months of September, October, and November. She and her husband, the Hon. Leopold Fox-Povvys,accompanied by their daughters, frequently attended service at St. Paul's Church, and the Hon. Leopold Powys has several times read the lessons there. Lady Mary was highly respected for her kindness to the poor. Her eldest daughter was several years ago married to Captain Mulville, of the Guards. The interment of the deceased lady teok place on Tuesday at Bournemouth.
Four persons have been drowned at Kingstown' near Dublin, owing to the capsizing of a boat which was conveying an officer's servant and a seaman to H.M.S. Belleisle.... .

The mill premises occupied by Messrs. John Hill and Sons, at Bradford (Yorkshire) were, with the exception of a weaving shed, destroyed by fire on Wednesday morning. The damage is estimated at £15,000. • CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—The fourth entertainment of the season, in connection with the Prescot branch, was held in the Houghton-st., school- room on Monday evening. An excellent programme was rendered. The accompanist was Miss Harris, of Prescot. The chair was taken by the vicar, the Rev. H. Mitchell. The entertainment was very well attended.
SUDDEN DEATH OF MRS. THEWLIS.

On Thursday afternoon, about a quarter past three, Mrs. Thewlis, the widow of the late Alder- man Thewlis, formerly Mayor of Warrington, on entering the office premises of Messrs. Thewlis and, Griffith, Phenix Works, Mersey-Bt., was suddenly so overcome with faintness that she had to seat' herself at the foot of the stairs. She was discovered there presently in an alarming condition by Mr. Finch, sub-manager of the works, and Mr. Harris the manager hat. her removed to the house next door, of Mr. Forster, the caretaker. Dr. Spinks was promptly sent for; he came immediately and pro- nounced Mrs. Thewlia to be dying. She expired in an arm chair about half-past three. The cause of death, it appeared, was heart disease. The deceased lady resided at Latchford House, Latchford, and was nearly 70 years of age. Her husband to whom she was married some '27 years ago, died about seven years since. He was mayor of Warrington for the municipal year 188.5.6. He was formerly princi- pal of the firm of Thewlis and Griffith.
DEATH OF MR. GEORGE WOODS, OF

• I WARRINGTON. It is with much regret we announce the death of Mr. George Woods, managing director of the Long- ford Iron, Wire and Steel Company. Limited, which took place at Southport, on Wednesday morning. Mr. Woods had been ailing for a considerable time. In the course of last year, feeling his health failing ' him, he went to Llandudno, and stayed there a month, but 'he returned to Warrington not feeling any better. After being at home for some time he decided'to go to Smedley's Hydro- pathic establishment at Birkdale. For a short time the treatment there seemed to make him consider- ably better, and he was in hopes of coming back quite recruited in health and strength. But, the first beneficial effects having passed away, there was again a falling off, and, as he was advised by one or two specialists to take absolute rest, he took private apartments at Southport, and engaged a special medical attendant who was unremitting in his endeavours to effect an improvement. All efforts failed, however, and he gradually got weaker until he died, as stated, on Wednesday morning. During his stay at Southport several of his friends visited him, and Mrs. Woods has been with him all ~ along nursing him most assiduously. The cause of - death was anmmia, and it is not unlikely that bia• fatal illness was brought on by overtaxing himself in the past, as he was of a most energetic eisposi- tibn and never spared himself. At the time of his death Mr. Woods was fifty years of age. Re was a son of the late Mr. Joseph Woods, who for more than 40 years, was employed by Messrs. Rylands as a wiredrawer. He was a nephew of the late Mr. William Woods, jeweller, Sankey-street, and another of his father's brothers was Mr. Thos. Woods, who for many years, was employed by Messrs. P. Stubs and Co. As a boy Mr. George Woods was a scholar at St. Paul's Heath Side Schools, and for a year or two after leaving, that school was engaged,along with his father,at Messrs. Rylands. He then, however, returned to Heath Side Schools as a pupil teacher, and in course of time pro- ceeded to Saltley College, near Birmingham, to undergo a training for the post of schoolmaster. After passing through the coarse there, he received an appointment as second master of the Liverpool Blue Coat School. He held that post • for a few years, but having displayed promises of unusual abilities as a vocalist he went to Milan to be trained as a professional singer. It was at this time that Mr. Woods formed friendships with several men—such as Santley and Maybrick—who have since attained high distinction in the pro- fessional ivorld, and those friendships continued unimpaired throughout his later life. The aspirations after distinction as a vocalist were, however, somewhat abruptly put an end to by the development of an affec- tion of the throat, which, though not very serious in other respects, was fatal to the attainment of the highest excellence as a singer, and upon the advice of doctors, both in Milan and in England, Mr. Woods abandoned the career that he had decided upon. The deceased gentleman was of a resourceful and energetic nature, and soon shaped another career for himself. On returning to Warrington, be found that his brother Edwin, who had been employed at M,Jssrs. Rylands, had invented a machine for reducing wire three or four sizes at one operation. This was patented in the joint names of Messrs. George and Edwin Woods, and the first named of the brothers introduced the machine to Messrs. Richard Johnson and Nephew, of Manchester; Messrs. Edelsten and Williams of Birming- ham ; and Messrs. Ramsden and Camm, of Brighouse. Later on the two brothers were the means ef forming the Longford Wire Company, which first began opera- tions in April, 1875, At the commencement, Mr. George Woods, the commercial manager, was secretary of the Campany, and Mr. Edwin Woods, manager of the works, Latterly both gentlemen have held positions as managing directors. Quoting from an account of the compsany's works which appeared in our columns a few months ago, we may say of the two brothers that "they have carried the concern through a period of commercial depression, under which many older firms have come to grief. The company is now paying a good dividend, and is largely extending its business operations. The company began business at a ' perilous time for the English wire trade. German com- petition is keen now, but it was keener still in the later seventies, and it is no wonder that the new enterprise did not not at first meet with the success winch had been anticipated, Unlike, however, many firms which ven- tured into the same business about that time, and in later years, they held their ground tenaciously." Hav- ing developed special branches of wire production, the company's business under the joint direction of the de- ceased and his brother, has lately made such progress, that large extensions of the works are now being made, and there is every prospect of continued growth. Mr. Woods's activities were not by any means wholly in business. He was a Conservative in politics, though of a liberal-minded type, and frequently spoke from the platform. In all local affairs he also took a great inter- est, and as a rule had something to say worth hearing 'on any "burning "question. He frequently contributed to the local press—generally adopting a nom-de-plume— 'for though a Conservative he was active in exposing abuses, and ever ready to suggest reforms. The Ship Canal Scheme had in him an ardent and vigorons advo- date, and he was one of those who gave evidence on be- half of the Company's Bills before Parliament. He recently gave very valuable and interesting evidence as to the trade of Warringtoa before the Parliamentary ' Committee which considered the Bill in promotion of the proposed Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway. Mr. Woods's early proclivities were seen in his fondness for music. Ile was a prominent member of the local Musical Society, and was quite recently mainly instrumental in wiping off a debt of £l2O which had sadly crippled the usefulness of the Society. He likewise promoted and conducted a series of admirable concerts at the Conservative Club, which resulted in the Purchase of a piano. In disposition he was most kindly, genial, and straightforward; and it is therefore a matter of course to say that he had a large circle of friends who were warmly attached to him. It may be added that, thirteen or fourteen years ago, Mr. Woods married Miss Branson' the daughter of a solicitor of high repute in Sheffield. He leaves a widow, but no children. The funeral will take place to-day (Saturday). The cortege will leave the Central Station, Warrington, at 11.15 a.m., and the interment will take place at the Cemetery, at 12.

div.head: FRODSHAM,
div.p: FRODSHAM,

DEATH OF Mns. DIINSFORD.—Mrs. Dunsford, wife of Mr. F. W. Dunsford, chemist and druggist. died early on Thursday morning after a brief illness. The deceased lady was highly respected by all classes of the commu- nity. She dispensed her charities with a sympathetic hand, and spent much time in nursing the sick. PLEASANT EVENINGS.—On Saturday evening, an ex- cellent lime-light lantern entertainment had been pro- vided as a change from the ordinary concert series. The several connective readings were admirably dealt with by the Rev. P. Pizey, the lantern being manipulated with great success by Mr. Walter Robinson. There was an exceedingly large audience. FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—On Tuesday afternoon, between four and five o'clock, a fatal accident occurred to a man of the name of Powell, from Birkenhead, who was engaged with others at some repairs to the viaduct over the river Weaver at Frodsham Bridge. The de- ceased stepped on one side to allow the Manchester ex- press passenger train to pass, when he was caught by the engine of the Chester goods train, which knocked him down and fractured his head. The deceased leaves a widow and one child.

div.head: I'EA-13,L CASE.
div.p: THE I'EA-13,L CASE.
SURRENDER OF MRS,OS_RO.R.NE AND CHARGE OF
PERJURY.

Mrs. Osborne was arrested at 9.-5 on Thursday night, on landing at Dover. For some time back, it is stated, the lady volunteered to surrender to any process that might be instituted against her as soon as her health permitted. . At the Guildhall, London, yesterday morning, Mrs. Osborne was charged before the Lord Mayor, with hav- on the 19th of February last year, obtained £550 by false pretences from Messrs. Spinks, jewellers, Grace- church-St., London. Mrs. Osborne sat between her husband and a detective on the front solicitors' bench. She was weeping when brought into court. The Trea- sury solicitor intimated that no evidence would be offered, and the accused was, therefore discharged, but shortly afterwards was conveyed to Bow-St. At one o'clock Mrs. Osborne was placed in the dock at Bow-St. charged with perjury.--The magistrate remanded the accused for a week, and she was removed to flollowa:y Gaol in a cab, her husband accompanying her. No application was made for bail.

div.head: WARRINUTON.
div.p: WARRINUTON.

DEATH OF MR. FREDERICK Morn. The death took place on Tuesday of Mr. Frederick Muir. The deceased, who was only 23, had been an invalid for some time, lie was a well-known member of the Warrington Cricket Club. WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

A public meeting will be held in connection with this Association, in Wycliffe Hall, on Monday evening. An address will be delivered by Dr. Houston, Q.C., the candidate for the borough. Mr. W. Pierpoint will preside. All the electors of Wh.itecross, Bewsey, and Town Mall Wards are invited to be present.

- - - SUDDEN DEATH OF AN INFANT. About five o'clock yesterday morning, John Edward Lowe, a previously healthy child, aged 15 weeks, and, son of Edward Lowe, an engine driver employed by the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, and residing at 6, Stevenson-st., was found dead in bed. The child was not insured. It is supposed that the child died in a fit. No in- quest will be held. Y. M.C.A. LECTURE. An interesting lecture entitled "Egypt 6,000 years ago" was given by Mr. Kent in the Y.M.C.A. rooms last Wednesday evening. The chair was taken by Mr. C. H. Kerry. A vote of thanks was proposed to the lecturer for his very able paper and to the Chairman for presiding, by Mr. Stringer, seconded by Mr. Butler, and supported by Messrs. Bayley and Horton. • THE SATUILDA:r NIGHT CONCERTS. The sixteenth concert of the season was given in the Buttermarket-street Schoolroom, on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Strange. The TOORI was full, and a capital programme of songs, clarionet and concertina solos, and humorous recita- tions was gone through, many of the artists being encored. Amongst those who gave their services were Mrs. W. Strange, Miss M. E. Gallop, Messrs. Simkinson, N. Cook, A. Grounds, Hopkiss, W. Brob- bin, G. Whitfield, Miss J. E. Pigot accompanied on the piano.. The usual votes of thanks closed the prxeedings.

BALL AT CROFT. , A most successful ball, promoted by Messrs. .T. I Ball, of Southworth Hall, and Alfred Faulkner, of , Kenyon, took place at the Board School last night I week, when about fifty ladies and gentlemen were present. The schoolroom was most elaborately and tastefully decorated by Messrs. J. Daintith and Son of Croft. Messrs. J. Ball and A. Faulkner acted as M.C.'s The catering was carried out in a satisfac- tory manner by Mr. and Mrs. S. Daxon. of the Joiners' Arms Hotel, Croft, assisted by Miss Ball, of Newton. The music was supplied by several gen- tlemen from Leigh, and gave evident satisfaction. Tux CHESS CLUB. The Warrington Chess Club held their annual meeting at the Y.M.C.A. rooms on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance of members, and the Rev. Canon Dodd presided. The secretary reported the nature of the arrangement made with the Y.M.C.A., and much satisfaction was expressed at the excellent accomodation which has been placed at the disposal of the club. The Rev. Canon Dodd was re-elected president, and Messrs. Garland and Chandler treasurer and secretary respectively. The Committee, in addition to the gentlemen named, will consist of Messrs. 11. Tiorden, Dunn, and O'Sullivan. DINNER OF THE PAVING AND SEWEILA.GE COM.

div.head: MITTRE.
div.p: MITTRE.

The members of the above committee entertained Mr. Joseph Davies to a dinner, at the Town Hall, on Monday evening. For many years the lato alder- man was chairman of that committee, and once a year he gave the members a dinner, and the one on Monday evening was in recognition of his previous hospitality. There were present—the Mayor (Aid. Greenell), the Deputy Mayor (Aid. Francomb), and Councillors Ashton, Beaman, R. T. Fairclough, Robert Heaton, T. Flood, J. Hepherd, T. Hutchin- son, J. Muir, Henry Roberts, James Smethurst, and the Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor. The usual loyal toasts were proposed and responded to, and the health of Mr. Davies was submitted and warmly received. Songs were given, and the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner. WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK. A special meeting of the trustees and managers of the Warrington Savings Bank was held on Tues- day morning, for the purpose of repealing and an- nulling the present rules, and making new rules in lieu thereof, in accordance with the existing Acts of Parliament 'relating to Savings Banks. Major Pickmere presided, and there were also present— Aldermen Holmes and Chandley, and Messrs. Joseph Davies, G. Dakin, John Geddes, Robert Garnett, J. Peers, and J. E. Davies (actuary). The trustees and managers afterwards proceeded to examine the new rules, and the Actuary pointed out particular alter- ations. It was decided, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Alderman Chandley. "that existing rules of the institution be repealed and annulled, and that the new rules be adopted in lieu thereof."

div.head: SOCIAL GATHERING AT WYCLIFFE.
div.p: SOCIAL GATHERING AT WYCLIFFE.

On Thursday night there was a social gathering in connection with Wycliffe Sunday School gym- nasium, over 80 members and friends being present. The meeting was presided over by Mr. G. Brown, and there were also present Mr. A. Lang, Mr. G. Wallington, and Mr. D. Owen. The Chairman, in a brief address, said the gathering was held for the purpose of reviving a better feeling amongst the young men of Wycliffe concerning the gymnasitun. The programme which was submitted was an excel- ent one, and included piano and violin selections, solos, Sze., with games between. la the course of the evening suitable refreshments were dispensed. Thanks were due to the following for their ser- vices : —Misses Kershaw, Hackney, Booth, Ball, Wallington, and Fleming; Messrs. Clay, Path:core, Molyneaux, Buck, and the secretary, Mr. F. if Longshaw. THE ASSISTANT OVEICSEERSIIIP OF GRAPPEN- HALL.—TnE POLL.

The poll for the election of an assistant overseer, in place of Mr. Fairhurst, took place in the school, on Monday evening. The voting lasted from four o'clock until eight, but the proceedings were very quiet for the Brat three hours. During the polling, Messrs. T. Fairh urst,H. Burrows, A. Smith, T. Jones, and Evans gale up the contest, as there was no possibility of success. The presiding officers were Messrs. Lister-Kaye and T. E. Taylor, the overseers of the parish. The result was announced a few minutes after eight, and was as follows :—Mr. S. J. Woodcock, 120 votes; Mr. Wm. Grimshaw, 31; Mr. Martin Lyons, 13. After Mr. Woodcock had been duly declared assistant overseer,he thanked all who had supported him, and said that he would do all that he could to discharge his duties satisfactorily. He proposed a vote of thanks to the overseers for their kindness. The vote was seconded and carried and the audience dispersed. ENTERTAINMENT AT THB NATIONAL SCHOOLS.

On Monday evening a magic lantern entertain- ment was held in the National Schools, Church-st., the title of the subject being " A Tour in Norway." There was a fair attendance. The lecturer, the Rev. J. H. Garratt, of Widnes, was thoroughly con- versant with the subject of his lecture, and the scenes; which w i were excellently produced, were de- scribed in an interesting and instructive manner. The rev, gentleman, it has recently visited Nor- way, recommended t to the audience as a country in which there were many grand and strange sights to be seen. At the conclusion of the lecture which had proved very enjoyable, the Rev. C. E. Jack- son proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Garrett He said that temperance advocates in Warrington had a very uphill battle to fight, but that very fact only tended to make them strive the harder. Three hearty cheers were then given to the lecturer, after which the audience dispersed. The Rev. A. Meikle- john manipulated the lantern in a skilful manner. EMMANUEL REFORMED CHURCH OF ENGLAND SIINDKY SCHOOLS. The scholars of the above schools had their annual tea party last evening week, to which about 200 sat down. After tea, a magic lantern enter- tainment was given by Mr. C. Young, assisted by Messrs. Holt and Byfield, which was greatlyen- joyed, In the interval the distribution of prizes took place. The secretary's report was read by Mr. J. Allen, who said the school teachers were glad to i be able to report an improvement n the average attendance for the last 12 months, resulting in 37 scholars being awarded first class prizes, 28 second class, and 8 third class. They viewed with great pleasure the growth of the school in numbers, and especially the increased attendance of the young men, necessitating the opening of an additional class-room. During the past year the library had been augmented, and contained a valuable collec- tion of books. The Band of Hope work has been again taken up, Mr. Heron acting as secretary, and the weekly and public meetings have been well attended. The penny bank, held every Saturday evening, has been a decided success. The Mutual Improvement Class has, so far, had a very success- ful session.
