div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THEFT OH POTATOES. Patrick Ryan, carter, 1, Vernon Yard, was charged at the borough magistrates' court, on Monday morning, with stealing a quantity of potatoes. value 4s. the pro- perty of James Longshaw, greengrocer, 4 arid 6, Mill-st. The prisoner was employed to get a number of loads of potatoes in for the prosecutor, and he made away with half a sack of them. He was apprehended by D.S. Mon- aghan, and said he had committed the theft, but he was drunk at the time.-11e was fined 20s. and costs. THEFT 01' A COAT.

_ • • r'' At the Warriegton Police Court, on Wednesday, Mary e. = Copeley. 6, Tilley-st., wife of John Copeley, and Mary • Burke, wife of Mark Burke, were charged with stealing, or receiving, knowing it to have been stolen,on Monday night, a coat, the property of William Leslie, general dealer, 3, Mersey-st. It appeared that Mrs. Copeley went to Leslie's and offered a clock for sale, and next , morning Mrs. Burke brought the coat there for sale,upon which Mrs. Leslie immediately identified it as her hus- band's. Mrs.Copeley in the evening came and admitted she had stolen it, but begged Mrs. Leslie to say nothing about it. Detective-Sergeant Monaghan had, however, been communicated with, and the prisoners were both • apprehended. Mrs. Burke admitted having bought the coat from the other woman.—Copeley was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour, and Burke • was dismissed. f ' TERRI` Or BOOTS. ' Mary Pugh, daughter of a stocktaker at the Bewsey •at''' Wire Works, was charged at the Warrington Borough 1-111) Police Court, on Wednesday, with stealing the previous ,r 14 afternoon from the shop of Messrs. Boothman, Butter- -trite market-st., a pair of boots, value 2s. 6d. The Chief ft', Constable detailed the circumstances, and said she was seen by P.C. Turoer. to steal the boots quite openly from • the inside of the door. He apprehended her and it struck him. that'she was not altogether sound in mind, as she ' did not appear to know what she TVAS doing. Inspector Bpinks identified her as a woman who come to the police station sorpo time since, and asked to be locked up threatening (half 8141 was not he would do something. Weser She would have been sent to the asylum long ago if her Je.ther could have afforded to keep her.—The father - • corroborated the siatement as to her mentai condition, and sha was discharged on his promising to take proper . care of her.—the prisoner's brother came forward and in an excited manner said the prisoner would have to go Wile asylum.—The prisoner excitedly exclaimed: I stole the goods., Twill be sent to prison if you pleaee, (Turning to he4brother) VI will not go with you. 1 will not have his Presence beCause he annoyed me. The prisoner was htirried away before she could finish the sentence. MR. PERCY DAVIES IND 1115 SHE/FIELD DOG. • At thS 'Borough Police Court, on Monday, Percy ' . • DatieS, 'solicitor, Fir Grove, Latchford, was charged with having on the 23rd of January, a dog at large un- et:Marled. A constable deposed to the defendant's wife and a boy bringing the dog usamuzzled from the Central Station.—Mr. Davies: Was it a dog? Witness : I did not examine it.-14.r. Davies: Was it a cat? (Laugh- - ter.)—Witness: No it way not. It was a full grown • terrier dog.—Mr. Davies said he appeared for the pri- soner in this case. (Laughter.) He hoped their worships ,- would keep in mind in considering this serious charge • that he had never been there before. (Laughter.) About a month before Christmas, a gentleman promised him at Sheffield, to send him a St. Bernard dog. On . Saturday morning he received a note from him to say -•' • that he was sending him a dog by train. He supposed it was a St. Bernard dog. His wife brought the dog from the station. To conform to the law he should have had to send about a dozen muzzles to see which fitted. The .f-r: dog was addressed to Fir Grove, and the Railway Corn- pany could have been compelled to deliver it there ; • surely they would not have been liable for delivering the ‘. dog unmuzzled. It was a most unfortunate thing that this rabid muzzling order should be in force. There was no doubt it was a great deal of trouble to Mr. Hunt,and it was a most cruel thing. He asked Mr. Hunt whether • if he had known the circumstances he would have taken out a summons.—Mr. Hunt replied that he would not. The Bench dismissed the ease. MORR CRIIIILTY TO CHILDREN.—PARIINTS DRINKING, AND CHILDREN OUT IN THE SNOW. _

Another case of distressing neglect of children was before the Warrington Borough Court on Saturday. The parties who were placed in the dock in the case were Patrick and Catherine Bartley, of Hill-street, and they were charged with neglecting their four children, aged nine, seven, five, and one year respectively, in a manner likely to cause injury to their health. Mr. Basil Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians, and he stated that the woman had been summoned ' to appear on Friday, but she left the Workhouse, where alio was when the summons was served, and walked to Widnes. The case was a very bad one. On the 31st December, the woman applied to him for relief. He visited the house, 4, Hill-st., and found the children in a very destitute condition. The man complained of being ill, was supplied with food, and went back to work. He was in receipt of £1 a week at Messrs. Monks, Hall, & Co.'s works. D.S. Monaghan had told him that he had received complaints of the children being desti- tute. On another visit, when he knocked at the door, the woman used a disgusting expression, thinking it was one of her children. The defendants were at home, and had a pint of beer between them. The children were out in the snow. Last Saturday, the woman walked the children to Widnes, and brought them back on Tuesday morning. She again walked them to Widnes on Thurs- day, and back again on Friday. One of the children was wearing at the time boots three or four sizes too large for him, and had a sore on his heel.—lnspector Spinks said that on Wedaesday, the 20th January, he visited the defendants' house, in company with P.C. Bell. He found that there was no bedding upstairs, except straw. The children were lying on the floor, and there was no bed. Everything was very dirty.—D.S. Monaghan said that during the severe frost he saw the children out beg- ging. He stopped one of the boys in Sankey-street, and found that he had no shirt on. Ile was also bare-footed. The rain ran down the walls of the defendants' room up- stairs.—Mr.Ci itchley, the landlord of the Higher Angel, said that the woman frequently left the house and stayed away for a fortnight or three weeks, and the children were locked up in the bedroom.—Mr. Curry, the Work- house porter, spoke to seeing the youngest lad bathed. He was covered with sores, and his feet were all over blisters.—P.C. Bell said the male defendant's foreman told him that the male defendant was in receipt of £1 a week, standing wages. The foreman also said that the female defendant used to go to him asking for advances on her husband's wages, and on being refused abused him.—Alderman Burgess, the presiding magistrate, said that the female defendant was more guilty than the man, and she would be sent to gaol for three months. Bartley would be sent to gaol for six weeks, and, in addition, each of them would be fined £lO, or in default a further term of two months' imprisonment.

Shields, who had been before the Bench 30 times before, was ordered to find substantial sureties for his good be- 1 haviour. In addition to this, he was sent to prison for one month with hard labour. THErr.—George James, labourer, residing with his pareets in Knutsford-road, was summoned for stealing from the shop of Isaac Houghton, Mersey-st., a spade, I valued at 2s.—The prisoner said that he had been out of work for three weeks. He was in drink at the time. —The Bench fined him 10s. and costs. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and
Alderman Fran comb.

DRTINIC AND DISORDERLY.—Mary Tyrell, in Butter- market-at., on Saturday night, dismissed on promising to leave the town.—Mary Turner, in St. James's-street, the same -night, was dismissed on promising to behave better.—William Disdale, in Butterruarket-street, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Charles Aspinall, on the 23rd January, ss. and costs.—Wm. Darbyshire, in Lord Nelson-street, on the 24th of January, ss.—Michael Fogarty, on Saturday night, in Berry-yard. The pri- soner, who it appears, has a silver plate in his head,had got drunk in his own house. Ald. Francomb said a man had 'better get drunk in a well-conducted public-house than at home, before his children. He was dismissed with a caution.--Selina Outram, in Beer-st.,on Saturday night. Inspector Bowen said in Orford-avenue, a quar- ter of a mile off, he heard the prisoner screaming and shouting.—Alderman Francomb said she should do as the last prisoner did, stop in her own house, not get drunk outside and disturb the whole neighbourhood. She was fined ss. and costs.—Michael Quinn, in Tan- ner's-lane, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Patrick Thompson, in Haydock-street, on the 22nd ult., ss. and Costa. DRIINIC.—James Shelley, charged with being drunk on Pinner's Brow, on Saturday night, was dismissed.— John Riley, labourer, 8, Edelsten's Yard, for being drunk in Winwick-street on Saturday night, and maltreating a dog by kicking it, was fined 10S. IMMORALITY.—Mary Garretty, widow, of Ship Yard, charged with this offence on Sunday night was dismissed with a caution. FIGICTING.—John Donlan, labourer, 24, Silver-street, was charged with fighting on Pinner's Brow, on Satur- day night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Hardy and Amson. He was fighting with another man and had no shirt on, and went to his lodgings and was smashing everything. They called in P.C. Hardy to put him out and he struck and kicked him, also assaulting P.C. Amson who came to his assistance. He was fined 20s. and costs.—Henry Johnson, labourer, 11, Town Hill, and Patrick Crow, labourer, 11, Back Haydock-street, for fighting in Dolman's-lane, were bound over in £5 each to keep the peace and fined 3s. ed. costs each. DOGS AT LARGE UNMUZZLED.—WiIIiam Allman, baker 6, Tanner's-lane, John Bancroft, provision dealer, 54, St. James's-street, Anthony Conner,labourer, 29 Orford. street, John Evans, Bull's Head, Church-street, John Flannaghan, labourer, 16 Bldon-st., were fined ss. each for having dogs at large unmuzzled.—Gorge Fern, brush maker, 21 Church-st. was charged with a like offence. The defendant made a statement about finding a hair- pin on his windowsill, after the constable proving the case had called about the dog.—The constable asked with some indignation, and amidst much laughter whether the defendant meant to insinuate that he had been in the company of a woman at his door.—Sergeant Cheeny here stepped into the box and explained that he himself had picked up the hairpin and placed it on the window sill. (Laughter.)—The defendant was fined ss. —Wm. Gallop, refreshment house keeper,Buttormarket- st., Samuel Loy, pensioner, Horsemarket-st., Henry Nixdrof, coach builder, 2, Talbot-yard, John Rafferty, farm labourer, 2, Gorsey-lane, George Smallman, forge- man, 24, Eustace-st., and Alfred Woods, jeweller, 98, Bewsey-road, were each fined ss. for having their dogs at large unmuzzled. IILMORALITY.—Mary-07itifey—bd John Burns were charged with immorality, in Brown-st., the previous night, and also with having been previously convicted of a similar offence. John Burns was charged with aiding and abetting O'Riley in the offence in Brown-st. They were sent to jail, O'Riley for two months' and Burns for one month's hard labour. EDUCATION ACT CASES.-51r. George Riley, school at- tendance officer' prosecuted in the following cases ; Mary Bennett, Bewsey-road, Sc.; Patrick Carey, Dol- man's-lane ss. ; Thomas Furnough, Helsby-st., 2s. 6d, ; Richard Lowe, Tilley-st., 2s. 6d. ; John Clare, Stamford- st., had an order made on him' for his son to be sent to the Clio.—Wm. Pennington, Manchester-lane, had an attendance order made against him. - - - -

WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Pairclough (chairman),Alderman Wright,and Mr. E. M. Crostield. Daimat AND DISORDBRLY.—NIary McCombe, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-st., the pre- vious afternoon, was dismissed, and George Brown, charged with a like offence, in Mersey-st., on Tuesday night, was lined Sc. and costa. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—James Higgins was I charged with making two false answers in attestation on enlistinent, and was sent to gaol, f9r a month for eiteh
offence.

Tiltrusnar.—Before Alderman Sutton. DRUNK.—Mary France was charged under a warrant with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st. on the 6th of January. She was fined ss. ARMY DEsimriox.—William Naylor was charged with being a deserter in March last from the 73rd field bat- tery stationed at Ipswich. He was remanded to Strangeways jail to await an escort. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Dr..Gornall...

. . Two BEAM' lES. —Catheriae Bowden and Ellen Giblin, were charged that they being suspicious characters were found frequenting Mersey-st., for the purpose of Com- mitting felony the previous night. From the evidence of D.-S. Monaghan and P.C. Corbett it appeared that the defendants had got hold of a drunken man and were wanting him to sell his watch and his coat in a second hand dealer's shop in Mersey-st. The all went down towards the rubber works and Monaghan there saw Giblin snatch at the man's watch and ran away. Cor- bett apprehended her, and Monaghan apprehended Bowden. The latter was described by Monaghan as having been committed for robbery with violence and as being a desperate character.—She was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour, and Giblin to one month's imprisonment with hard labour. BAD CoNnucr.—Jane Mortimer was charged with im- moral conduct in Bridge-st., at a quarter past 11 on Thursday night, also with having been previously con- victed of a like offence. She was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour. ASSAULT —Patrick Donoghue, employed at Messrs. ' Monks, Hall, and Company's works, was charged with assaulting William Fulclough, on the 25th of Jan. —The complainant said he called upon ties defendant in the works to prove a charge he had made there that be was not married to the woman he was living with. This was not true, and he now produced his "marriage lines." The defendant on his asking for the explanation gave him a blow on the head, knocked him down and kicked him several times. He asked him ti let him up as he was on his knees, and he tore the shirt off his back.—Annie Burchall, a youug girl, corroborated.—The defendant said the complainant came to him and took him by the arm and said he had made the charge against him about his wife. He said he had only repeated what he himself had said. The com- plainant threatenc-d him, and at his suggestion they went outside to settle matters, and struck each other.— The Chairman asked the defendant what business it was of the defendant's suPposing the complainant was not married to the woman ?—The defendant replied that the complainant was lodging with him, and he thought it would not he proper to keep them in the house if they were not married.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £2O to keep thd peace for six months, and ordered to pay costs, 145., or go to jail for 14 days.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY. —Before Mr. John White, and. Mr. S. J.
Armitage. AN UN-Nrozzr.cn Doo.—James Moore for having a dog at large unniuzzled on the 17th of January, at Sankey Bridges, was fined ss. including costs.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
MONDAY.—Before Sir Richard M. Brook and Mr. A.
Thomas.

RIDING WITHOUT RHlNS.—Thomas Hopley, a carter, pleaded guilty to riding on a lurry without reins, at Norton, and he was fined 55., and costs Bs. 6d. DRUNK.—Thomas Millington was fined ss. and costs for being drunk. Tun SIIPPORT OF A Marm.—Andrew Heatherington, a man of very respectable appearance, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his mother, Jane Heatherington, who was chargeable to the Runcorn Union. The defendant agreed to an order of is. 6d. a week, and said he had always been ready to maintain her, and there must have been some mistake in bringing these proceedings. There was always a home with him for his mother.—The order was made for allowance, and for costs, 13s. 6d.

"Sum yore sin, wen aw war a smartish ring mon, Mi feyther an' th' nayburs aw sed, If aw rattled mi eliquint tang so deyd mitch, Aw shad losen aw th' teeth i' mi yed No deaubt aw'd a very greyt deeul to say, An' mi langwidge at times war but feaw ; But throo gooin' to Church aw've turnt o'er a stew leaf, Fer aw'ro. keepin' mi meawth shut neaw I" " Eawr Bashaw wuz one ez cud poo sairt mi rag, Wen he gammon't an' chaff't mi face, Till aw thowt molly a time aw shad purr his owd

yed, If he 1./mita purr me i'th same place ! But that joker may gammon ez much ez he likes— He just ez wed l cod an owd ceaw • For a Churchwarden's job is mi object i' An • aw'm keepin' mi meawth shut neaw I' " " Birley Bill—he's another ez nair lets mi be; An' wenever he fancies aw'm • tite,' Keeps on cawin' mi names quite a flagstaff i' length, An' a cheeky, noanreet Parasite I An' he cosses mi shootin', up hill an' deawn dale, , Ez only that beggar noze heaw ; But it's only like suds on an owd gonder's back, Per "aw'm keepin' mi meawth shut neaw 1" "Then that Mon wi' a Medal, an' Bachelor John, Wr ther lies an' ther trottin' hey tried To make mi a misery, aw to mysel, But at present "aw'm not mitch anny'd." Per aw that, to keep mi enrag't dander deawn, Hez bin very hard wark, aw'll alleaw ; But like Bashaw wi bowin', aw'm noan to be Dunn, Per "aw'm keepin mi meawth shut neaw 1" " Eaur Yethart, th' Owd Scholar, an' good Uncle George Made mi aware even wen aw're i' bed; But, by gyow ! lads, they rais't th' British Lion at last; An' they rued Wry yure o' ther yed. Aw frickent them gradely, an' one on urn's gone Into rayther deep mournin', shuz heaw ; But he'll 80011 tak' a turn, wen he heers the good news, That "aw'm keepin' mi meauth shut neaw 1" "its a boon to mysel', that aw'm quietent deawn, An' mi' temper's like that of a lamb ; Per neaw, thro' a fear it met Jigger i' print, Aw don't even whisper a Th' owd set 'ith' "Bull "snug will be blessin' the , change, ' An' the Saints ull be sheawtin' Hooreaw ! Wen ther" Cocker "—that's me ! 's gone ez mute ez a meause, An" aw'm keepin' mi' meauth shut neaw !" TILII 0' PEGS. Nyowton, God bless o'. February 2,1892.

DEA.TH Or MR. SPURGEON. Mattroxx, SUNDAY NIGIIT.—Mr. Spurgeon expired at twenty-three minutes past eleven o'clock. He remained unconscious up to the last. and Buffeted no pain. Besides Dr. Fitz Henry, Mrs. Spurgeon and Miss Thorne were present when he breathed his last. BUNTON', MONDAY, 8-50 A.M. The notice announcing the death Mr. Spurgeon posted upon the door of the Hotel Beaurivage was as follows :—" Mr. Spurgeon fell asleep in Jesus at 11-15 pan. All - relations and deacons of the telegraph immediately after

the sad event occurred. It appears that Mr. Spurgeon never recognised anyone after Saturday night, not even Mrs. Spurgeon. Dr. Fitz Henry says the cause of death was blood poisoning arising from congestion of the kid- neys, or in other words. Bright's disease. MaeToNe, MONDAY NlGHT.—Already over a hundred telegrams of condolence have been received by Mrs.Spur- geon, and the whole English colony here have called at the hotel, many leaving flowers, with which the body is covered.

• It has only just been decided to have the funeral at Norwood Cemetery, in accordance with the wish of the deacons and the church at the Metropolitan Tabernacle. The body will be sent to England as soon as possible, and the day of the funeral will be announced on Sunday at the service in the Tabernacle. Mrs. Spurgeon bears up wonderfully, but is too weak to go to England yet. MIINTONI9, WEDNEEIDI.2.-At half-past three o'clock this afternoon the leaden shell in which the body of the lat* Mr. Spurgeon is laid was sealed down and then en- closed in a beautiful olive wood coffin, the lid of which was afterwards screwed down. At four o'clock the seals were placed upon the coffin by the British vice- consul and the police commissary. On Monday next Mrs. Spurgeon will leave the Hotel Beau Rivage on a visit to an intimate friend, the Corn- mendatore Thomas Hanbur, who owns the beautiful Palazzo Orengo La Mortolo, near Ventimiglia, the pic- turesque gardens of which are well known to visitors to this part of the Riviera. Here Mrs. Spurgeon will re- main some time in order to recover her health after the loss she has just sustained. Ventimiglia, which is just ovelk the Italian border, is only about half an hour's drive from here.

The general committee of the Congregational Union of England and Wales met in London on Wednesday, and appointed the following gentlemen to act as a deputa. tion representing the Congregational churches at Mr. Spurgeon's funeral :—The Revs. E. Herber Evans, D.D. (chairman) ; John Brown, D.D., J. Guinness Rogers, Thomas Robinson, Messrs. Halley Stewart, M.P., D. Ford Goddard, Alfred J. Shepherd, William Holborn, and the Rev. D. B. Hooke (secretary). A resolution of sym- pathy with Mr. Spurgeon's family and.with the Baptist Church was passed. The following message was sent to Mrs. Spurgeon on behalf of the Baptist Union :—" ro Mrs. Spurgeon, Beaurivage, Mentone.—Just arrived from Egypt, and have heard with profound grief of the death of Mr. Spurgeon. I tender on behalf of the Baptist Union and myself deepest sympathy, commending you to the tender care of our dear Lord.—Dr. BOOTH, secretary Baptist Union."

Mr. Spurgeon, as a letter of his own tells us, had never 'known the fear of man, but when he discovered that his then young wife was agitated, as she well might be at the sight of that enormons congregation he felt that con- oern for her might perhaps unnerve him. He beckoned one of his deacons to come to him. This deacon, after a whispered conversation with the pastor, came to Mrs. Spurgeon' who sat immediately under the extemporised pulpit, and said, "Mr. Spurgeon would be glad if you would sit somewhere where he cannot see you. If you remain there, it may make him nervous. The other incident occurred at the close of the service and impressed itself upon the memory because it settled a point on which every mind had been intent—whether the preacher could possibly be heard at the extreme end of such a crowd. He had asked that the Doxology should be sung. After the last notes had died away My. Spurgeon' without any apparent effort, said" No, no, my friends, that won't do. There are great numbers of you who did not sing at all just then. I will have it again, and I will ask you all to sing. Mr. Organist let us have that again." The organist was seen in the far distance, with his hand to his ear as Mr. Spurgeon was speaking. At these last words he promptly turned to his instrument, and forthwith again the doxology re- sounded through the palace, this time with a much greater volume of sound, and with an effect that was truly magnificent. Mr. Spurgeon, in one of his addresses to his students, urged them to go always direct to the point in address- ing their fellow men. There was nothing gained, he said, by beating about the bush. It was not the practice of men of the world who wanted to gain any object to beat about the bush, and neither should it be the practice of men who wished to convert sinners. To illustrate what he meant by going direct to the point, he told how he had one day met a labouring man on a hot day rest- ing for a moment with a loaded barrow and wiping the perspiration from his forehead. " It's a hot day, my man," said Mr. Spurgeon sympathetically, " Yes, it is,' said the man, looking straight at Mr. Spurgeon," and I never seed a man look more like standing a pint of beer than you in my life." " That man," said Mr. Spurgeon, " went straight to the point." The following incident, which occurred some years ago, has the advantage of being true. At the weekly prayer meetings at the Tabernacle Mr. Spurgeon was in the habit of inviting anyone who was disposed to offer prayer. On one occasion, in reply to his invitation, a man following the humble occupation of a dustman rose to engage in prayer. He began, " Oh, Lord we are dust. This, in the circum it:knees, somewhat taxed the gravity of his hearers. He proceeded to thank the Lord" that He had put into the heart of His servant Charles Spurgeon to send him (the dustman) a leg of mutton." This was more than Mr. Spurgeon could tolerate. In a tone of indignation, not unmixed with humour, he peremptorily told the man to "sit down," ana his devotions thus came to a premature close. A correspondent writes :—A few years ago I heard Mr. Spurgeon preach at the Tabernacle. He was then in good health, and his high spirits were infectious. Nothing struck me more than the cheery tone which prevailed and the mutual good fellowship of preacher and congregation. One story he told on this occasion I well remember. He was explaining how it was he was always preaching with so much energy the truths of the Gospel to those who were perhaps as fully conversant with them as himself. "The fact is." he said in effect, "I am like the man who knocked at the wrong door late at night. After he had been knocking for some time a head appeared at a window and a voice was heard say- ing' What do you want?' I want Mr. Smith.' 'Then why do you come here disturbing me when Mr. Smith lives next door?' That's just it,' was the reply, ' Mr. Smith has no knocker, and so I have to knock loudly with yours to make him hear." On the point, whether the late Mr. Spurgeon could be heard by all the vast congregation of 25,000 persons when he preached in the Crystal Palace, a correspondent tells the fallowing story : Mr. Spurgeon, before the day for the sermon arrived, had doubts about making himself heard by so immense an assembly as was expected. Accordingly he went to the Palace shortly after noon one day to make a test speech. Standing on the spot from which he would preach, he recited in his well-known tones the following passage of Scripture : " This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." Having spoken these words, he left the building, appar- ently satisfied with its acoustic properties. A few days later a poor labouring man attended an " experience " meeting in the district, and with much confidence told how he had been converted. He said he was so bad that he thought he could not be saved. But he had spent a dinner hour in the Crystal Palace, praying behind one of the statues, and as he prayed he distinctly heard a voice from Heaven say, " This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." From that moment he was convertcd. Little did he know of Mr.Spurgeon, or Mr. Spurgeon of him.

div.head: PROLOGUE BY T. W. LEGH, MP.
div.p: PROLOGUE BY T. W. LEGH, MP.

The following prologue by Mr. T. W. Legh, the member for Newton Division, was spoken on the occasion of a recent Amateur Dramatic Performance at the residence of Mr. Bromley Davenport, 34.P.' Capesthorne, Chelford. Mr. Legh, it may be stated is the brother-in-law of Mr. Davenport : Once more the curtain rises on the play, And Capesthorne amateurs their skill display; Once more applause shall make these rafters ring While they not only act, but dance and sing ; Their varied talents to the world disclose, Draw tears from these, and laughter loud from those. ' And mine the task to try in halting verse, In dubious rhymes and lines that can't be worse, To bid farewell to eighteen ninety one; (I own for one I'm glad he's dead and gone). A year of strikes, of sackcloth, dust and ashes, Of influenza, panics, sales, and crashes ; Of crops destroyed, and months of beastly weather, Of snow in June, and ficods and fogs together; Of bills unpaid, and other bills obstructed, 0° cases #' nobly" by the Bar conducted. May better luck attend both me and you, In A.D. eighteen hundred and ninety two! Though without honour in my own county I'll venture on this startling prophesy : Boys will be boys ; each dog shall have his day ; When this is done you'll see a first rate play. Abroad the Turks shall greatly want for cash, Southern Republics go to endless smash, Russians and French exchange uncouth embraces, Cook's tourists find their way to distant places, Italian grinders flock to England's shores With German bandsmen, Jews, and other bores. The House shall meet, and reason's feast be spread , Much shall be said and heard but little Had. ' Ships by Canal to Manchester shall hurry, But nothing more be heard of Wilfred Murray. The Parnellites some priestly skulls shall crack. A grand old man shall show that white is black. One of these day's there'll be a fresh election, Each voter then shall back his own selection, Fury shall rage, and angry passions burn, But you once more your member shall return. The rates will rise, the plate go round on Sunday, And Tuesday as a rule will follow Monday. Yet ears of sow shall not silk purses make, Nor pint pot measures quarts or gallons take. No laws shall help to make the thriftless thrive, Nor two and two together count as five. This much I know and confident foretell; The rest you'll find in book of Zadkiel. Meanwhile for two short hours of fleeting time Dismiss all thoughts of care and toil and crime; Let talent, wit, and humour see fair play, And music reassert her magic sway ; Let the loud laugh that speaks the cheerful mind, Be heard from seats in front, and forms behind. I've done ; a fact you're doubtless glad to hear, Still let rue wish you all a glad New Year.
A. MINISTER'S BREACH OF PROMISE.

On Wednesday morning, a case of breach of promise of marriage, causing much amusement in court, came on for the assessment of damages at the Surrey Sheriff's Court. The plaintiff was a young lady named Dawsen, the daughter of a Norwich farmer, and the defendant was the Rev. James Stewart, vicar ef St. Ann's Church, Sutton. Defendant first met plaintiff two years ago at Yarmouth, and they became very fond of each other. He bought an engagement and keeper ring, and fre- quently took her to places of amusement. In June last, while having supper at Harris Silver Grill, in the Strand, he kissed her, and asked her to be his wife, and she consented. He took her to buy the furniture for the house he had bought, and the marriage was fixed for August last, but the defendant suddenly broke off the engagement. Plaintiff was awarded £250 damages.
DEATH OF SIR MORELL MACKENZIE.

Sir Morell Mackenzie, the celebrated physician, died on Wednesday night at ten o'clock, at his residence in Harley-st., London, from syncope following an attack of influenza. It had been known for some days past that Sir Morell was seriously ill, but no fatal result was ap- prehended. Sir Morell received the honour of knight- hood in recognition of his valuable services to the Emperor Frederik of Germany in the early stages of his last illness. He also received the Cross and Star of the Hohenzollern Order in 1888.. _

...,.. There were a large number of callers on Thursday morning at 19, flarley-st., to convey their sympathy to Lady Mackenzie, who is bearing up well in her sad and unexpected bereavement. During the morning telegrams of condolence arrived from all parts of the kingdom. Sir Morrell Mackenzie, M.D. (London), was born at Leytonstone, Essex, in 1837, and educated at the London Hospital Medical College, Paris, and Vienna. He founded (says "Men of the Time") the Hospital for Diseases of Ithe Throat, Golden Spuare. 1863; and in the same year obtained the Jacksonian prize from the Royal College of Surgeons for his essay on diseases of the larynx. He was soon afterwards elected assistant physican to the Lon- don Hospital, becoming in due course full physician, and was appointed lecturer on diseases of the throat. He was a corresponding member of the Imperial Royal Society of Physicians of Vienna, and of the Medical Society of Prague. and an honorary fellow of the Ameri- can Laryngological Association. Dr. Mackenzie was the author of numerous publications on laryngological subjects, and in particular of a systematic treatise in two volumes, on " Diseases of the Throat and Nose," which is acknowledged to be a standard work. It has been translated into Preach and German, and has had a very [large circulation both in this country and in America.

div.head: SKETCH OF HIS CAREER.
div.p: SKETCH OF HIS CAREER.

Charles Haddon Spurgeon was born at the village of Kilvedon, June 19,1534. His descent is somewhat re- markable. The Spurgeons of the olden time were driven from the Netherlands by the persecutions of Alva, when they settled in Essex, and became the firstfruits of a line of pastors each of whom was remarkable in his day and generation, while the line of succession has continued almost without a break. Preaching with Mr. Spurgeon was hereditary. At seven years of age he was smitten with the desire to preach like his father, and at sixteen the ruling passion of his life compelled the "boy preacher," then usher of a small school, to take services each Sunday, and others in the course of the week. It was the desire of many of his telations that Charles should enter one of the Independent Colleges,and under- go a training for the Ministry. As time went on, how- ever, he embraced what are termed the Anabaptist views, and eventually joined the congregation which had been presided over by the late Robert Hall, of Cam- bridge. It was during this crisis that he became a village preacher and tract distributor in the secluded village of Feversham, near Essex, and here the "boy preacher" delivered his first sermon. Shortly after- wards he was known as the pastor of a small Baptist Chapel at Waterbeach. His fame when only a lad was wafted to the great metropolis, and in course of time he was offered the pastorate of a chapel in New Park-street, Southwark, where the late Dr. Rippon once ministered. Mr. Spur- geon made his first appearance before a London con- gregation, in 1853, when he was nineteen years of age. His success was so unprecedented that at the expiry of ' two years it was found necessary to enlarge the building. Pending the alterations, he preached for four months in Exeter Hall, which became so crowded that, Sunday after Sunday, hundreds were turned away from the doers. With increasing popularity, the enlargement of the chapel in Park-street became insufficient ; the con- gregation continued to multiply with steady rapidity, and ultimately it was found necessary to hire the Surrey Music Hall for Sunday services. During this decade, in October, 1856, an accident occurred which was most appalling. At one of the services, when the building was crowded, some frantic Individual called out" fire," a panic resulted, and, amid other accidents, no fewer than seven persons were crushed to death. It was at this time that the large new chapel, designated the Tabernacle, was built. It was publicly opened in 1861, and for the last thirty years this central building has been associated with Mr. Spurgeon's name and the numerous good works which have accompanied his wonderful ministry. With regular congregations of about 6,000, and a communicants' roll of over 4,500, this living personality kept eyes fixed and ears open by his gleams of homely wit and simplicity of eloquence. For many years Mr. Spurgeon lived in the vicinity of Clapham, but on his health beginning to fail he was prevailed upon to remove further into the suburbs. His new residence was pleasantly situated on one of the hills of Upper Norwood, to the South-East of London. It has been described as a continuation of the hill on which the Crystal Palace stands, from which building it is situated about a mile in distance. Extensive views can be witnessed from the house and grounds. Mr. Spurgeon enjoyed fresh air to his heart's content, and used to remark, "Fresh air is more than medicine to me."

Mr. Spurgeon's home life was a busy one. It was there that Mrs. Spurgeon conducted much of the work of her" Book fund," which has now sent books to about 15,000 ministers. His literary contributions were also voluminous. They included "The Saint and his Saviour." "John Plough- man's Talk,"" 'lle Treasury of David," "The Metro- politan Tabernacle, its history and work," with countless collections of published sermons, such as—" Trumpet calls to Christian energy," "Farm Sermons," "The Present Truth," C. Many of his Writings give an ad- mirable idea of the peculiar combination of humour and religious exaltation which made the deceased a felt power wherever he went. Around the lengthened pastorate there sprang up from time to time m tny institutions, the principal one being the Pastors' College. The Sunday School contains over one thousand scholars, and, in addition to this, there are twenty-four Sunday and Ragged Schools connected with the tabernacle. They have done good work among the poor and neglected classes. There are twenty-eight mission stations, a Young Men's Christian Association, a children's and teachers' library, a Mission to Jews, a Baptist Country Mission for the Evangelisation of Vil- lages, a prosperous Band of Hope, and numerous home and foreign missionary societies. The .well-known Stockwell Orphanage accommodates nearly 500 boys and girls. It is situated in one of the healthiest of London suburbs, and covers about four acres of greund. This Institution has been maintained at an annual outlay of £ll,OOO since 1880. In unison with the Pastors' College, it will continue to perpetuate the memory of Charles H. Spurgeon. Mr. Spurgeon's attitude towards the Church of Eng- land under went considerable modification in the course of his life. At the commencement of his career, his references to the Establishment, both to its ecclesiastical and theological positions, breathed an antagonistic and, at times violently hostile spirit. But Mr. Spurgeon broke with the Liberation Society towards the end of his life, and as lately as May declined to grant the use of his building to the Liberationists. Their meeting was accordingly held in St. James's Hall, and the place of Mr. Spurgeon was taken by Dr. Clifford, the chief of the other section of the Baptist denomination. . . _ . . .

Mr. Spurgeon's conflict with his own denomination is differently viewed by parties both inside and outside tie Baptist Union. On the one hand he is regarded in the light of one of the cid prophets, valiantly protesting against flagrant error and corrupt teaching. On the other he has appeared lacking in sympathy, in breadth of view, in insight into moderate movements, and in understanding of present day problems. Whether this view found few or many supportors in the Baptist Union is a debatable point, but when in 1887 Mr. Spurgeon commenced formal hostilities against men whom he declared were on the " down grade," he failed to carry the Baptist Union with him, and accordingly retired from association with it, Three disputations were greatly regretted, although no one ever doubted Mr. Spurgeon's candour or honesty of purpose. Those who really differed with him mourn his loss, and it is felt on all sides that one of England's greatest personalities has been removed by the death of this truly remarkable man.

div.head: ST. HELENS GLASS TRADE.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS GLASS TRADE.
SERIOUS CRISIS.

The extensive alterations and improvements which are to be carried out in the various works for the manufacture of plate glass at St. lielens, of which details appeared a few weeks ago,have given rise to an extraordinary state of affairs at the Union Plate Glass Co.'s works, Pocket Nook, St. Helens. It will be remembered that the St. Helens manu- facturers are replacing the machinery hitherto used with the best and most complete it is possible to obtain in order to hold ground more successfully with their foreign competitors. The introduction of the new plant will have the effect of reducing the time and cost of production to about one-third the present amount in each case. It will also do away very largely with female labour in some of the departments, and it is understood that about 200 women have been discharged from the Ravenhead and Sutton Works of the London and Manchester Plate Glass Company. Considerable progress has been made with the alterations at the works of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers and at the London and Manchester Company's works, and, fortu- nately, at these places there has been little if any dlsagreement between the masters and the men. But at the works of the Union Plate Glass Company, Pocket Nook, a dispute has arisen, and there is a probability that the whole of the 600 hands employed thereat will Ibe thrown out of work for many months. The men allege that some weeks ago the firm reduced the number of each " set "of men employed in the grinding shed. and this naturally caused less work to be turned out. They accordingly made a request to the manager (Mr. B. Brearley) for the " sets " to be made up to their for- mer strength, and, according to the men's statement, this was done, but reductions were made in the wages of the emplosed men sufficient to pay the wages 'of those who had been restarted. An objection was raised to this course, and, failing a satisfactory arrangement, the firm last Friday posted notices intimating that the works would be closed after the present week. The grinding-shed men, however, took the matter in their own hands, and stopped on Monday, and their action has resulted in the stoppage of the whole of the works. On Tuesday a Press representative had an interview with Mr. Brearley, the manager, at the works ef the company at Pocket Nook. Mr. Brearley emphatically declared that there was no foundation for a statement by the men that he had asked them to work a week for nothing. Asked as to the origin of the dispute with the men, Mr. Brearley replied that the competition of foreign glassmakers was very keec, and the English glassmakers had felt it severely. The English makers had got behind with their machinery, and were unable to turn out the glass as desired. The working-men, however, seemed to have got an idea that the capital- ists could pay wages whether they were mak- ing money or not. But being behind in the machinery and paying good wages had brought about a crisis in the trade. The masters had tried to keep things going by working night and dav,thereby giving the men a chance of keeping at work.—Mr. Brearley said he pro- posed no reduction. The firm put four men on each " set" when the advance in wages was made, and they had latterly taken two off. The men had been told that work and prices had been worse ever since the advance was given, but they did not seem to appreciate the posi- tion in which the firm were placed. He could not say how long the works were likely to be closed.

RUGBY.

SALFORD v. WIDNIM-At Widnes, before 3,000 specta- tors. Brennan kicked off for the home team against the wind. Salford early asserted their superiority,and only a few minutes had elapsed before Barratt scored. Before the interval Miles and Nicholas also scored, but the latter failed at goal on each occasion. In the second half the game was evenly contested, and just on time Sudlow scored a fourth try for Salford, no goal result- ing. Final : Salford, four tries ; Widnes, nothing. WARRINGTON " A " v. BROD, 4ITON "A."—At Brough- ton, on a ground exceedingly heavy by the recent rains. Warrington started the scramble of the rival forwards, Smith ultimately removing the game to midfield. A fine kick by Sampson gained a lot of ground, and Lally from a pass by Lawless dodged through capitally. The pressure was relieved by Smethurst, but a bad pass was taken advantage of by Buckley, Molyneaux, Barnes, and Hampson dribbling to the Brotighton line. Brough- ton were hereabouts hard pressed, but Howe punting to Hamblett, the last-named almost dropped a goal. With the aid of the drop-out play was taken to the half way, until Davies, Buckley, Bailey, and Forster rushed into their opponents' quarters. Hers Lawless got finely away, but only a minor resulted. The play, which had been exceedingly poor, was again monopolized by the forwards, and eventually, from a kick by Hamblet t, the home custodian let in the visitors, Buckley rushing over near the posts for Sampson to cunvert. From the kick off Broughton looked very dangerous, but Bailey, Warburton, Barnes, and Davies headed a grand dribble past the centre line. The tome team retaliated, Smith scoring. Warrington were soon attacking, after this. Buckley, Daniels, and Hampson being notable, but the score remained unaltered at half time. Restarting, the first thing of note wasa dribble by Buckley and Lawless, which found the game being fought in Broughton terri- tory. By smart judicious kicks the danger was averted, until Hampson, Alolyneaux, Davies, and Forster re- sumed the attack. The game was entirely devoid of in- terest, owing to the style of play adopted by the home team and line outs and scrimmages followed with monotous regularity. For a long time these items were witnessed on the Broughton goal line, Warrington hav- ing hard lines in their attempts at scoring. Pack followed pack, Lally subsequently dribbling splendidly to the old position, where Sampson, receiving a long pass from Daniels, ran to the line, a minor being con- ceded. More scrimmaging and scrambling followed, but the contest was of such a description that further comment is unnecessary, and Warrington retired win- ners by 1-0-3 to 0-1-0. BROUGHTON RANGERS v. RUNCORN.

Runcorn were three short of their regular team,but the homesters were strong. When Faulkner kicked off there was a large attendance, and the first scrimmage was held in the home half. Abrains picked up from a scram- ble, and a fine bit of passing was seen between that player. Davies and Crompton, forcing the homesters to touch down to save disaster. The Rangers presently got a free kick, but this did not avail them much, as the Cheshire men were playing a fine game. Eventually the ball was carried to neutral ground. Medley now became prominent with a dribble, causing the Runcorn men to kick dead. Half time came with the score one minor each. Jackson started for the Rangers, and P. Riley re- turned,the game settling at centre. The visitors assumed the lead, and forced the Rangers to touch down twice,ia very quick fashion. The visitors for a time seemed to have the best of matters,the ball being continually in the Rancrers half. The Rangers defended fairly. Hirst got hold, putting in a nice run and kick, which transferred the play well in the Runcorn half, Davies being tackled nicely with the ball in his possession. The game was now very fast, the Hangers showing up well, but the visitors again went off with a rush, and ended by Hol- lingvrorth scoring. Towards the close Medley became prominent with a fine run, and the Rangers just missed scoring by Gresty failing to take the pass from Hurst. This the visitors followed by a brilliant run by Cromp- ton, who lost the ball when on the line, and the final soon came in a victory for the visitors. Result: Run- corn, one goal, two tries (nine points); Broughton Rangers, none. Teams :—Broughton Rangers: C. Ward- ley, back; Hirst, Hackin, and Gresty, three-quarter backs; T. Wall and Storer, half backs; J. Jackson, J. Fitton, R. Medley, J. Thomas, M`Gowan, J. Shaw, W. G. Campbell, T. Cleminson, and S. Oman, forwards. Runcorn: S. Eoughton, back; T. H. Davies, J. H. Crompton, and G. Pendlebury, three-quarter backs • S. Abrams and J. Hollhagworth, half backs; W. Faulkner, P. Riley, R. Dolan, A. Hampson, 0. Hughes, D. Massey, R. Reece, J. Davies, and G. Lee, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

This return match was played at Warrington. The fixture with Broughton is always sufficient guarantee fora large gate, and despite the unfavourable state of the elements on Saturday, there was a fair attendance. The first match had resulted in the unexpected defeat of Warrington, but the latter were determined to show that this form was all wrong. The Broughton men, with one exception, played the same team which had done such excellent duty in the first instance, and whereas Warrington were represented by nearly the same team, which first opposed the Broughton men, they suffered by the absence nf such players as John Bate, Webster, and Nevins.

It was 3.40 before a start was made, but Craven's kick-off being charged by Therniley, matters assumed a serious aspect for the visitors directly. Craven was not found wanting, and relieved finely to half-way, where James Bate kicked finely back, and the result of these exchanges was a determined attack n the railway goal. Jolley and Ashton joined in a dribble, which Shepherd cleared, but Teare, with similar tactics, once more placed the Broaghton men on the defensive. I3oscow was held with the oval in his possession, and from the scrimmage formed, fine passing by the Broughton halves saw D. Roberts running finely down the open, a faulty pass to Hassell spoiling a good chance. Broughton were now having a trifle the better of the argument, and a free kick being awarded, the Warrington goal was in jeopardy. The shot was a poor attempt, and a similar point being granted to Warrington, the kick wasproduc- tive of an excursion to the Broughton quarters, Berry, Jolley, and Holmes being prominent in following up. Piercy was at fault, and almost let Warrington in, but a clever dribble by Tomlinson and Munro, changed the venue to past the half-way flag. Bate and Antrobus, with neat passing, soon had the oval back at its original quarters. but an effort by the former received poor assis- tance from his companions. Shepherd saved his lines cleverly on one occasion, but Jolley, Turner, and Dono- hue, with brief efforts, all helped to maintain the attack. The Broughton backs, especially Craven, were in fine form, but a dodgy run by Heesom almost landed him a scorer. Donohue was prominent in some loose play, but his pass was a poor affair, and Broughton manipulated the chance proffered by a raid on the home goal. Boscow made his mark under difficulties, and the kick being seconded by pretty passing by Bate, Heesom,and Evans, the latter had a shot at goal which was short of the mark. The visitors again got the goal out of danger,but a return to the railway end saw -James Bate in a new character of dropping at goal, which realised the uncountable minor. Broughton were penalized for too strict attention to Bos- cow,whilst a fine run by Evans was cheered to the echo. The Broughton men were tested to the extreme, but Craven and Piercy came out with flying colours, and all the efforts were frustrated. Knowles, Jolley, and Thorniley dribbled well on one occasion, but the former was a trifle too rash in the final essay, and a minor was all that was notched. Barnes was now called upon for the first time, but the attempt was not a success, and play was at half way. A fine run by Craven was neutralized by Evans, but a clever cross dribble by Skidmore, Munroe, and Broadbent raised the hopes of Broughton to a high degree. Some fine exchanges be- tween Bate and Evans culminated in a third minor, whilst a fourth was forthcoming from a run by Bate. Judicious kicking by Turner, was seconded by the smart following up of Ashton, Berry and Knowles, and half-time was called with no substantial score. On resuming, Warrington early attacked, an infringement of the five yards rule allowing Evans to take the ball near the Broughton line. A short dribble by the visitors was responded to by the whole body of home forwards, and a try was claimed without success. Bate essayed

to cross the border by a pass by Antrobus, but nner. tackled well, and saved at times in a daring nota A fine punt by Hee,som was met by Hassall' bu.ntd° 04" accounted for this player in true style, -- Broughton goal was menaced. div.head: Ettters to tin Obttor.
div.p: Ettters to tin Obttor.
LIFE ASSURANCE POLICIES.

Sir,—Having had some experience with a large Indus- trial Life Office, perhaps I may be allowed to refer to the subject mentioned by Mr. Moorfield in a recent issue. Mr. Mo,rfield denounces, and rightly so, gambling, with human lives as counters, and it would be impossible for him to use language too strong in condemnation of this evil. When, however, he says that there is in England a gigantic system of this sort of wagering, I believe he is mistaken. None can deny that the evil exists, but it is less extensive than Mr. Moorfield thinks. He is of opinion that unholy wagering is caused by Companies using "own life 'S proposals for proposals "on the life of another." This I cannot admit. If, for instance, I desired to insure my father's life for an amount suffici- ent to cover the expense his death would entail upon me, with a Company using only one class of proposals— the "own life" proposal—he would have to give his consent and sign the proposal form. Afterwards he would be visited by an Inspector of the Company, who would test the signature, and ascertain what interest the intended payer had in the life proposed. If there were no interest, the case would be at once rejected. Although the policy would contain my father's name only, it would be known at the office of the Company that I was paying the premiums, and my insurable interest would be no greater if my name were to appear on the face of the policy. Still, I must admit that it would be better if the name of the person in whose favour a policy be granted were written on its face, as the law directs. This, however, would not stop gambling.—Yours truly, HENRY H. DUTTON.

div.head: PROPOSED RATEPAYERS ASSOCIATION FOR
div.p: PROPOSED RATEPAYERS ASSOCIATION FOR
NEWTON.

- - - - Sir,—l would respectfully suggest to the Newton ratepayers to call a public meeting with a view to form- ing a Ratepayers' Association. This need not be at all antagonieic to the Newton gentlemen acting as Com- missioners, but, on the contrary it wonld be the means of strengthening them and bringing them more in sympathy and touch with the wishes of their consti- tuents. The course taken by the Earlestown Commis- sioners, who are in the majority on the Public Hall question and also of filling up the vacancy is so extraor- dinary and so opposed to all rules of business and commonsense that to stand aside seems to be the greatest of folly. The Earlestown Commissioners appear to chuckle and say that the battle has been fought and won, the contract has been sealed, that the Newton people being in the minority are helpless &c. Whether all this be so or not I cannot say, but there is no telling what foolish thing will next be done. And by Newton having a centre and acting as a united body it is bound to have some voice in the matter. As it is it has virtually none; it does not appear to be even con- sidered in any important question. Besides, lam informed that there are many ratepayers in Earlestown i who do not approve of what s being done, and will not take kindly to this additional rate for the Public Hall. There are a number of important local questions which are being shelved in the present muddle, but are bound to be brought forward shortly, and I feel convinced an association of the kind I have named would be the means of doing much good. I Feb. 2nd, 1892.
"ACTION."

STANDING TO CLERGY. Sir,—ln yours of Saturday a correspondent "J. 5."1 draws attention to this unscriptural practice. Allow me to tell him that here five sixths of the congregation will not do it. He quotes what may have happened two hundred years ago ; he should give us authority for it in the New Testament. Let us have, as a fourth century divine said. a" Thus saith the Lord." We certainly read that even Peter declined accepting homage from Corne- lius. Paul and Barnabas said, "Sirs, why do ye these things ? We are also men of like passions with you" (not Ritualists or Sacrificing Priests) "and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the liv- ing God." (Not to processions, early celebrations, with fasting, genuflections,turnin,g at creeds and during Com- munion.) The beloved John was told by the Angel, "See thou do it not : lam thy fellow servant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus : worship God : for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of pro- Pllec9." What loyal subject, having come to do homage to our Queen, would offer acts of homage to her servants ? And ought our attention to be drawn thus to men, who, however sacred their office, are sinners as we are, when we come together to bow before the Judge who, as Saviour has promised if we meet in His name to be in our midst? St. Paul was content to write--" Ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake." Christ himself came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ramson for many." "Oh , no," says" J. S." and the Ritualistic clergy " are not your servants, but your lords ; you must pay us homage."" J. 5.," and his clique dare not meet me on a public platform and openly dis- cuss these matters; he will, however,have an opportunity (DV.) of hearing Mr. Moyes in Runcorn next Thursday, when I doubt not he will prove Ritualism to be nothing but Romanism. I advise" J S." to read the Angs- burg confession of A.D. 1530 and Bishop jewel's challenge. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, Feb. sth, 1892.

div.head: WARRINGTON HALF-lIOLIDAY MOVE-
div.p: THE WARRINGTON HALF-lIOLIDAY MOVE-
3IENT.

Sir,—Though I am not a shop assistant, I attended the meeting advertised to be held in Bold-st., on Tues- day night week. It was well attended, and Ido think that if they had taken each person's age who held up his hand, they would have found that the resolution was carried mostly by the younger end—some mere lads of 12 to 15.

Although Lam in favour of a half-holiday and shorter hours, I should, if I had been an assistant, have moved a resolution to the effect that all shops be closed the first five nights at 7.30, and Saturdays at eight o'clock. I think common sense tells us that the last two hours are the most unhealthy of all ; working in a close shop with say 40 to 60 gas burners going. Another thing ; I think, by a little considering the masters would find that they would almost do without gas, which is no little item in this town. Again, there is the market—is it going to be closed carnal'? There is another reason why I think closing as above is the best ; it is a well-known fact that our Saturday's trade is quite different to what it was a few years ago. We have now to deliver goods during the I middle of the week to the very people who used to block our shops on a Saturday evening. Again, I think most will agree that we should draw more money than we do. particularly from the working-man, who is unwise enough to stop at the public-house from noon on a I Saturday until the last thing of a Saturday night, before he will part with his few shillings to his wife, to buy in with. ram sorry to say it, but lam afraid there are some women as bad as the men. However, I wish the cause of the assistants the greatest success,but I do hope they will go in first for shorter hours all the week through. 'rhen try for the half-holiday. Before closing this I would like, Mr. Editor, to say a word about one of the speakers at the meeting. I don't know why he should try to stab the " new comers," as he calls them. Bless me !did he rail at his mother when she made him a " new corner p" Were they " old Warringtonians " that first started closing on Whit Monday? Didn't all the " new corners" agree to close last Christmas holidays, and did not the Warringtonians spoil it? Again, it is only the very old Warringtonian shopkeepers who close at seven ; and I think by the appearance of some, they are lingering on until the old coach comes for them. Why,Mr. Editor, this man spoke about Warringtonians, but let him tell us of a town that is more backward than this town with a population of 50,000. I suppose he was put in his present situation 60 years ago, ny his manner of speech. There is an old saving respecting two towns in Lancashire. Ashton- utider-Lyne, they often say, is 50 years ahead of StalY- bridge. I think Stalybridge is 50 years ahead of War- ington, and that some assistants, at 22, are very much ahead of some old Warringtonian assistants, at a very muob greater age.—Yours respectfully, ONE INTERESTED. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDkY, FEBRUARY 6. 1892
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDkY, FEBRUARY 6. 1892
THE QUESTION OF EVOLUTION.

Sir,—Although there has not been any discussion as yet beween Mr. Peers and myself, nevertheless, one or two things stand out pretty clearly. In spite of his per- sumed acquaintance with science, he is unable, unwill- ing, or afraid—l am not certain which is correct—to meet me on the qaeation of the origin of life. And secondly, although he has been calling me to come on and fight the battle of man's otigin, each advance of mine has been followed by the retreat of Mr. Peers. Mr. Peers,like the Unknown he swears by, recedes before the investigations of science. But he is a slashing writer for all that; and if he had only controlled himself until his opponent had laid aside the flag of truce, with which up to the present he has been covered, he would have had the advantage of measuring his strength in actual conflict.

Mr. Peers strongly reminds me of the old Highlanders who,claymore in hand,rushed impetuously on the foe, in utter disragard of all rules of fight, if haply they might smite to death. All the whilel have been attempting to arrange a discussion, he has been hewing at me, but with little effect. I have repelled his attacks where I thought it necessary ; but on the whole they have been a matter of indifference to me. How stands the result? Mr. Peers has retired, carrying with him the defences of the origin of life, and of the origin of man, into the "Citadel of the Unknown," and there we may leave
him. This is my fourth letter and for the preseut my last.

know better than to give myself away; in the minner my opponent wishes me to do. Mr. Peers plainly proposes to take for granted as a fact established beyond reason- able doubt that man is nothing more than a developed animal. My position was that the animal origin of man was not an established fact; that it was a question of controversy; and that I would argue as to the scientific probability of such a view. Mr_ Peers cannot have a very rational view of the subject proposed for discussion if he imagines for one moment that he will be allowed by one great assumption to virtually decide the question , before it has been discussed. The position he graciously ' offers me to defend is—" Prove the Biblical account of man's origin on the hypothesis that man—body, soul and spirit—is a developed animal." I decline this offer for very good and sufficient rea,sons—reasons which, unlike those supporting Mr. Peers's refusals, are at once lumin- ous and logical. One word more. Mr. reers's method of argumenta- tion—utrange mixture indeed of adjective and wrath, and ponderous, pointless satire—is not of such a nature SS to inspire confidence in his ability to discuss with care and moderation any question stretching ever so little beyond the ordinary correspondence of a newspaper. He will shine most where least thought is required, and where words—mere words, will count most. His is a [ guerilla warfare; and as to his influence let Cardinal Newman sum it up (I quote from memory) : The causes which incapacitate a man for understanding a thing happily incapacitate him also for opposing it.—l am, yours truly, Wilderspool.
W. 11. BUTLER.

LIBERAL MEETING AT BURIONWOOD. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. W. Neill, for the Newton division in the Liberal in- terest, was held in a room behind the Bridge Inn, Burtonwood, on Tuesday evening. Owing no doubt, to the very Inclement state of the weather, there was not a very large audience. Mr. G. W. Rawlins presided, and there were present with him on the platform Mr. W. Neill, the candidate, and Mr. S. Taylor of Eccleston Hall. The Chairman said he looked upon that meeting as the mast important one that had ever been held in Burton- wood, as he believed that the series of meetings they were now holding would lead up at last to them carry- ing a Liberal candidate for the Newton division. (Hear, hear.) At the last meeting they held in Burtonwood they had some six or seven present, and he must con- gratulate that meeting upon having a much larger num- ber present, and it only showed what staunch politici- ans they were to turn out on such a night as that. In introducing Mr. Neill to them he should like to say a word or two about what has passed in regard to his candidature. They did not want to have another Sir Geo. Errington, but they wanted a man of a robust type of Liberal which would satisfy all good Liberals, and to- night Mr. Neill came before them nob as a Whig, not as a Liberal dissentient but a..s a good Radical. (Hear,liear.) Burtonwood stood in a different position to-day from what it did at the time of the last election ; first of all it had a polling district of its own, instead of, as on the last occasion, being tacked on to Winwick. The game was in their own hands, and if they did not carry a Lib- eral candidate at the next election, they had only them- selves to thank for it. No man knew when the election would take place; all they knew was that when it did come, it would be a surprise to them, and they might take it for granted that Lord Salisbury would bring it upon them just at the moment when he thought they were not prepared for it. (Applause.) Mr. O'Brien moved the following resolution, "That this meeting of Burtonwood electors endorses the policy so ably advocated by Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues, for the better government of her Majesty's subjects in Great Britain and Ireland, records its conviction that the House of Commons is no longer in harmony with the will of the people, and considers that Parliament should be dissolved at the earliest convenient moment." Mr. W. Neill, in seconding the resolution said the present Government had made a point of breaking those very pledges which secured their return at the last election, viz., that there was to be no coercion in Ireland, and that local government would be granted to Ireland. Speaking of the work of the Conservative Government, he said lie was not going to run down the Local Govern- ment Act, as it was more or less a Liberal measure, but the fault the Liberal party found with it was that it be- gan at the wrong end. The Conservatives further passed an Allotment Act. The Act was very finely named, but , in practice it was perfectly inefficient—(A Voice: "A perfect sham.") They had: passed another amending that Act, which had proved as ineffective as the other. They passed another measure which he would acknowledge was a good one, viz., Free Education, a thoroughly Radical measure, but the Tories seemed rather ashamed of the name, free education : they said, no, assisted education. But there was one thing they prided themselves on, even more than these Acts about which they talked so much, that was the pacification ot Ireland. The reason why Ireland was quiet at present was not on account of the Coercion Act, but because of Mr. Gladstone's remedial act of 1881; it was only now that the tenants were beginning to feel the benefits of the beneficial and remedial act. ((fear, hear.) The Liberal Unionists as a party, had practically disap- peared. He could respect a good Tory, but a Liberal Unionist member or candidate was a man he csuld not respect. The Ressendale election was more important than any of the others that had gone before, and it seemed to him that that election was fought almost altogether on the question of Home Rule, because both candidates were local men, both of them were Liberals, and as far as he could make out the only difference between them was the question of Horne Rule; vet looking at the result, he thought they would find that what Rossendale thought to-day, the whole country would think at the next general election. (Applause.) He thought they would find at the next election, that it was on that question in particular that the fight would be founded. The Tories were now convinced, and they could not but acknowledge, that at present the country was with Mr. Gladstone. It was only by distorting facts that the Tories could hope to avert al overwhelm- ing, majority in Mr. Gladstone's favour. He thought that at the next election they would find that the rally- ing cry of the Tories would be" no separation." He loped when the next election came they would throw all their votes for Mr. Gladstone and induce others who might be wavering to follow them. With respect to an eight hours bill for miners, he had alreaay expressed himself as being in favour of that measure, and the more he considered that question the more he was in favour of it. One of the arguments he was met with in regard to it, was that the misers did not want the bill, as they did not work eight hours but the answer was, if they did not work eight hours, what harm would a bill do if they were in favour of it. But he believed they did work more than eight hours. He could find no one on the other side who did not agree that eight hours was quite as much as any man ought to work at such an occupation as coal mining, but they said such a measure should not be by legislation, but by agreement with their masters. He thought they wanted a reform in the registration laws. It seemed to him a shame that parties should be obliged to pay registration agents to look after their votes. He thought an officer should be appointed and paid by the State to attend to the regis- tration. (Hear, hear.) He was in favour of one man one vote, and an exteasion of the Employers' Liability Act. Be only hoped when the next election came, and it could not be far off, they would see their way to do all in their power to help back Mr. Gladstone into office, so that they might deal with those questions which were pressing, and pursue that course of social legislation, to increase the total sum of happiness, so as to raise the lower being, and make the lot of the toilers brighter and happier than they have been in the past. (Applause.) Mr. S. Taylor, Eccleston, spoke in support of the reso- lution, which on being put was unanimously adopted. The usual votes of thank a terminated the meeting.
SUNDAY AFTERNOON AT WESTON
POINT AND THE RESULT.

Before Sir Richard Brook and Mr. A. Thomas, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday. James Byrne grocer, Church-st., and Peter Smith, chemist and . druggist, High-st. and a member of Runcorn Board of Improvement dommissioners were charged with having on Sunday the 24th January been drunk in Greenwav-road. Mr. Byrne pleaded guilty and Mr. Smith not guilty. Joseph Campbell was also sum- moned for creating a breach of the peace at the same time and place. He was represented by Mr. Mad- dock, solicitor.—P.C. Booth said about II o'clock on the night in question he saw the three defendants walking down Greenway-road. Byrne and Smith were very drunk. After he had walked about a hundred yards, he heard a noise, and returning to the place found Smith bleeding from a wound at the back of his head which he said had been done by Campbell striking him with a stick.—There was a hole in Smith's hat. He and P.C. Dickenson took Smith to Dr. McDougall's surgery. —By defen- dant Smith : There was a pool of blood on the ground and some on his clothes. The blow must have been enough to daze anyone —P.C. Dickinson corroborated. He said Byrne was helplessly drunk and Smith was the worse for drink. The latter defend- ant had a pint bottle of whisky in his pocket.—P.S. Gosling said he saw Smith in Dr. McDougall's surgery, about a quarter to twelve. Ho had been stunned, but was evidently recovering from the effects of drink. This concluded the evidence in the case of drunken- ness. Mr. Smith said he was not .drunk. He was walking quietly down the road steadying Mr. Byrne, (who admitted he was the worse for drink), along somewhat, when the man Campbell struck him on the head with a stick and dropped him to the floor. The knob of the stick fitted into the hole of the Lit (produced).—Dr. McDougall deposed that he dressed the wound, which was a serious one. He thought Smith was not drunk although lie was under the influence of drink. The case against Campbell was then taken.— P.C. Booth said when begot up to the defendant's Smith charred Campbell With having struck him and he saw the slick lying on the floor. Campbell denied that he had struck Smith, alleging that he had failen.—By Mr. Maddock : He could not swear that Campbell struck Smith. —Mr. Smith then repeated his statement and said it was perfectly true that Campbell struck him with a stick.—Cross-examined by Mr. Maddock : He did not know Campbell and could no give a reason why the blow was given.—He went to Weston Point about half- past three. Be had no drink previously except the ordinary dinner beer. Mr. Byrne and he had tea with Mr. Orme. 'they left Weston Point about eight o'clock. Mr. Maddock contended that no assault whatever had hen proved. Campbell, if he could give evidence. would say that Smith and Byrne were both drunk, and se-ing the two men in a helpless condition he went to help them along the highway. Smith admitted that it took them the extraordinary time of two hours to walk two miles. At Runcorn Smith became riotous, and pushed Campbell about, and in the scuffle his head got cut in the w# described.—Sir Richard Brook said the case against Campbell would be dismissed ; there was not sufficient evidence of a breach of the peace. In the other cases there was no doubt both were drunk, and Smith would be fined ss. and costs Us. 6d., and Byrne ss. and costs Be. 6d. • . NEGLECTING HIS Crutnacw.—At the Lyrnm Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. P. Norris and Dr. Brabazon, Joseph Whitehead, a labourer, was charged with wilfully neglecting his three children. The case was adjourned till the 18th March, to see how prisoner treated his children in future. WESLEYAN BAND OF EIOPE.—The usual monthly public meeting of the above Band of Hope was held in the schothoom on Monday evening. A service of song, entitled "John Broom," was given, Mr. Brigg being the reader. Songs and hymns, in which the audience joined were sung, and solos rendered by Albert Moston, Nathaniel Rogerson, and George Percival. Mr. Thorpe was in the chair, while Miss Marian Thorpe was the accompanist. The meeting concluded with the Bene- diction.
