MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIA.TION. On Wednesday evening in connection with the above society, a paper entitled" The old world and the new," was read by Mr. T. Gandy. Mr. Parker presided, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Gandy gave his hearers an excellent account of his observations IL America gained during his long re- sidence there. An animated discussion followed. Afterwards the discussion was also resumed on Mr. Parker's paper " The Great Labour Question," which was left over from the previous week.

div.head: PENICETH HALL FAUX!.
div.p: PENICETH HALL FAUX!.

An interesting event was witnessed on Thursday, at Penketh Hall Farm. The new tenant to this farm —Mr. Ditchfield, who has just arrived—and all the farmers of the neighbourhood, assembled on Thurs- day to lend a helping hand with the ploughing. No less than 5,3 teams hailing from Prescot, Sutton, Bold, Sankey, Cuerdley, Penketh, &c.,were present, and a good deal of work was done during the day. Mr. Ditchfield is a gentleman much respected by those who know him. On Friday the teams went to Mr. Chas. Kelmll's farm at Cuerdley to give assistance. CHILDREN'S ENTERTAINMENT. Last evening week, in connection with the Wes- leyan Day School, the annual entertainment of the junior children was given in the schoolroom. There was a very large attendance,the room being crowded to excess. The first part of the programme consisted of songs, recitations, drill. marching, &c., contri- buted by the scholars, was gone through in a most successful manner, which reflected great credit on the teachers. After a short interval, during which the scholars were provided, with refreshments, the second part of the programme was commenced. It consisted of a musical piece, entitled "Cock Robin." This is a children's operetta,by M. C. Gillington and F. Pascal. The efforts of the scholars met with much applause from the audience. The following are the names of the scholars who took the various parts, viz., Cock Robin, Alfred Clarke (Albert Whit,e took the singing assigned to this part) ; Jenny Wren, Emily Plumpton ; the Cuckoo, Flossie Wat- son ; the Fly, Hilda Randall, and J. Watson; the Owl, Albred Foxley ; the Rook,Herbert Davies ; the Bull, Sam Tucker; the Sparrow. Albert Sampson. There was also a chorus of birds. Mrs. Wilson con- ducted the entertainment, whilst Miss Seed ably accompanied on the piano.

div.head: WARRINGTON Y.M.C.A. VERSUS ST. HELENS Y.11.C.A. DEBATE ON FOREIGN IMMIGRATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON Y.M.C.A. VERSUS ST. HELENS Y.11.C.A. DEBATE ON FOREIGN IMMIGRATION.

An interesting debate between the above named associations, on the subject" Should England be the happy hunting ground for the impecunious foreigner," at St. Helens on Tuesday evening. Warrington took the affirmative, and was repre- rented by Messrs. W. H. Butler, W. H. M. Isles, H. B. Crowder, J. Ainsworth, I. Storey, and S. B. Stringer. St. Helens took the negative, and was represented by Messrs. J. 11. Pickersgill, J. R. Turner, T. R. Jackson, W. Moss, W. E. Seddon, and W. Lightfoot. Mr. Butler led off in the affirmative. We, he said,who sent out 25,000 emigrants per year to other shords could not consistently complain at foreigners immigrating to ourshores.We owed much to the energy of impecunious foreign immigrant. He had been to us in many respects a means of valuable education, and a source of wealth. Mr.. Pickersgill replied. He argued that whilst the foreigners immigrated here to a country already overcrowded our emigrants went out to new lands. With regard to the energy of the foreign emigrant, the Gnly push he had been able to dis- cern in him had been the pushing of the English- man out of his situation by working for a less rate I of wages. The impecunious immigrant tended to make life much more severe for us here; and did not benefit our trade, and should therefore not be allowed to come to our shores. Mr. Isles said we were indebted to the foreigner for much of the skill we possessed, and in that sense the foreigner had been to us a source of wealth: Mr. Turner argued that immigration requires regulating; the impecunious foreigner ought not to be allowed to land in a country already overcrowded. Mr. Crowder advanced arguments similar to Mr. Isle's, and said we would be much impoverished if the foreigners departed from our midst. Mr. Moss argued that the impecunious foreigner interfered by competition with the improvement in the condition of the Englishman, and therefore ought not to be allowed to come amongst us. Mr. Ainsworth, believed in free trade in labour ; it was simply a case of free trade versus protection, tolerance versus intolerance, charity versus selfish- ness. Much had been said of the immigrant Jew, and especially with regard to the persecution of the Jews in Russ'a. They apparently inferred that because the Russian Jew was persecuted Ile must necessarily be a worthless creature. He thought it could be proved that instead of the Russian Jew being so he was really the only—or almost only— representative of true industry and perseverance that Russia possessed. Was it English. he argued. to condemn a man for something over which he hes no control? Surely a man is not to be held respon- sible for the place of his birth, and neither is lie to be trodden underfoot because he is poor. Mr. Jack-

div.p: BRIktSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. (MIX ED.)

Aw feel aw—Coad—SWeiif--an; dialect, too I It's a fine thing, is learnin'. Somewheere i' one o' Ben Brierley's books sonieboey says id teks no reawm up, " an' th' bailies connot fot it, theaw I sees."

• Wod has this to do wi' swearin' ? Aw've sin some o' th' wonderful things as it's done i' my time sich as mekkin' a lad or lass nod own id parent i' street, an' tINV mon say as id dud a v arra good thing for th' owd fooak theere, becose th' lad or lass wod ha' disgraced 'era. An' t' ether week id dud summat moore wonderful i' Derma, an' aw'll tell yo' abeawt id. (Eh, aw should feel relieved iv th' printer wod just let me coss a little bit here, an' at intervals I) Yo' may remember as aw towd yo' some tooathri week sin' as Darrun were famous for id breed o' salmon, as id were off th' skoo' maps, an' as id showed id culture bi gooin' in for some grand lec- tures at a penny ap;ece. Neaw it's gettin' id name up in another roped. It's this way: They hey some nosces Darrun, an' they hey some Aristockeracy (capital A. Mester Editor) ; this Aristockeracy took id in id heyd last month to give a Nosses Ball, sooa they printed some tickets, an' things, an' leet th' noospapper chaps know as they could come an' hey a peep heaw nice th' reawm wor, an' tickets were on sale at sich a place. Thad were kind o' ti Aristockeracy. Th' nosses ordered new frocks for tk' big do, an' one on 'em sterted tekkin' lessons i' dancin', for yo' see they med sure as they were goin', bein' a Nosses Ball; but worn'd they capt when the; were coolly towd as they wodn'd be expected—id were aboon them ! An' yo'd be capt, too, iv yo' knew th' fuss as hes bin med abeawt th' Darrun noospappers, for they seemed to expect th' Nosses to be theere, an thad is rididklous, isn'd id? An, nod only bein' theere. but ackshally eytin' at th' same table o' th, same stuff as th' Aristockeracy—nay, even dancin wi' th' Aristockeracy! Aristockeracy as is eddicated up to Dick, some on 'em hevin' hed as mich as a penny a week spent o'er th' job; Aristockeracy as toils nooan, nor spine, but licks Solomon into fits as far as clooas gooa ; Aristockeracy as is sprung fro' tradesmen i' good circumstances ! It's stillness to expect id. Yet these noospapper chaps tawk abeawt snob- bery, fergeddin' otogether as eddication teyches fooak their reights—thad is—iv a mon or woman is a snob or a snobess, or brutal, or brainless, they've a reight to show id—iv they pay for th' pleasure o' Going' sooa. . Aw these Darruners lies shown hi,

Aw darsay th' Nosses an' other fooak bi th' scoore, or th' hunderd, 'll quote this verse o' Tennyson's: "What profits now to understand, The merits of a spotless shirt; dapper boot—a little hand— If half the little soul is dirt ?" Excuse th' mention o' this case, but id does show wod eddication may leead to; iv yo' dorn'd think as eddication lies owt to do wi' id, think on as yo' con expect nowt fro' a pig bui; a grunt, nor mek a silk poss fro' a sow's ear.

There's a " fast " female o' th' name co Nelson, fro' America—an' bi' " fast " aw dorn'd meean one as is " loose "—as is showin' th' Frerch i' Paris heaw to live on next to nowt; aw suppooase hoo'll come across th' Channel as soon as boo's med o'th' brass hoo con mek theere. Well, hoo'll nod ha' mich to be seeasick oft iv boo does ; some o'th' noospappers is freetened on her teychin' werkin' boak to live on th' fresh air, becose al' employers 'II be sure to let 'ern live on nowt else ; yigh, they'll deawn wi' wages abeawt ninety per cent. streight off, an' put thad i' their own pockets. These noospapper chaps doesn'd seem to know as a chap corn'd live on owt healthier nor fresh air; yo' know fresh air isn'd as indigestible as poork chops or herd boiled eggs, nor as windy as peighs an' new baked shop breead. It's a thing as con be digested bi th' waikest stum- mick tooathri seckonds, is fresh air, beawt th' aid e' gastrick juice ; an' it's olez fresh, an' there s plenty on id. No deawt id is 'dulterated a bit i' some parts o'th' conntry wi' smook fro' th' werk- ' shops • but as soon as fooak ged to living' thad rooad there'll be no werkshops (3' ony soort—l•appen ; though they will want summat i'th' way o' clooas to put on,an' aw reckon they'll hey to werk for 'em. Id will be grand then, an' no mistake, becose there'll be no occasion to waste an heawr an' a hole every day on dinin',an' aw hooap id'll come to pass, an' as there'll be no" corners " formed to buy up o' th' fresh air, or to float id. Aw know some o' th' comic ;Nippers 'll be tellin' us as iv this young A merican faster gooas on a week or two there'll be another poem on th'" Death of Nelson " for some poet to write. Well, we shall see.

Am aw i' favour o' writers hevin' titles? To be sure aw am. Besant's bin on th' subject for months —happen for years—an iv ony chap deserves " Sir," at th' front ov his name it's him, iv nobbut on ackeawnt o' wod" All sorts and conditions of men," did tor't geddin' th' People's Palace gooin'. in th' East End o' London. Ay, an' Sir Char'es Dickens wod ha' seawnded wed, au' id owt to ha' bin sooa. We should ha' liked " Pickwick" just as weal as we do iv a Earl hed written id, an aw daresay Sir Charles Dickens wod ha' med jusc, as good a job o' " David Copperfleld " as plain Charles Dickens did ; happen he'd ha' cherged a bit extry for every book he wrooat at after,an' iv he'd ha' done aooa th' pub- lishers an 'us-sels wodn'd ha' minded a bit extry forth' pleasure we should ha' felt. Aw could reel off a list o' tooathri scoore chaps as owt to ha' bed titles long sin', but they were passed o'er for brewers, promoters o' companies, an' others as ne'er benefittedonybody a ha'poth. A better time may be coming. an id may be possible as some week yo may see at th' top o' this column thad startlin' announcement "Mixed bi Sir Turn o' Dick o' Bobs —or happen bi then id'll be Sir Thomas of Richards of Roberts. Aw've promised th' wife a new bon net wen this big event nomes off, but hoo hesn'd said as hoo'll wait for id till then.
As this is such a pleasant subject you happen ex• case me iv aw mention id ageen later on.

div.head: CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT AT NEWTON CO-OPERATIVE STORE.
div.p: THE CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT AT NEWTON CO-OPERATIVE STORE.

At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie (chairman), A. C. McCorquo- dale, W. Mitchell, and T. D. Grimke-Drayton, Wm. Hayes, lately employed by the Leigh Co-operative Society, as manager of their branch shop at Newton, was brought up on remand charged with embezzling sums amounting to ..£lO 4s. 6d., the property of that society, he having on the 13th of June last received .£l2 9s. 61.' from Mr. William Longton, and only accounted for .£lO Ss. 9d., on the 24th of June £5O , from William Ellam and only accounted for .C 45 land on the 27th of June £3 Os. 9d. from Wm. Hall, for none of which he accounted. Mr. Calvert, soli- , citor, of Leigh, appeared for the prosecution, and ! ' Mr. Swift for the defendant. Mr. Calvert said the case had been adjourned three weeks to enable the defendant to go through the books and accounts. —Mr. Swift said the defendant was going to adopt a particular course, by his ad vice. The evidence of Mr. Boydell, secretary to the , Society, given at the previous hearing of the case, was read over ; and in reply to Mr. Swift he stated that the Society had a considerable sum of money , in hand belonging to the defendant. Mr. Swift ; Which they intend to retain ? Mr. Boydell : Nothing decided. By Mr. Swift : The amount is a little over £35. Mr. Swift: He agreed to give them security for £.50, and they thought cash was better than his boyd, and he has been paying them Bs. a week for a time, and then 2s. Mr. Boydell, further examinad for the prosecution, said the prisoner's salary was 255. a week, out of which he kept 2s. a week. The prisoner had been with the society 10 years. He had a wife and three children. Mr. Swift: Although the society have felt bound in the interests of the members to take these proceedings they do not press the case. Mr. Boydell: That is rather a peculiar way of putting it. Our people do not like to press for the heaviest penalty. By Mr. Swift: The prisoner has given me certain ex- planations which are not satisfactory to the society. There are undoubtedly very grave irregularities on his part, more, than that. He has told me he borrowed one item, £5, and paid it back. If he paid it back, put the money into the till, and gave me a check, the counter- foil check would appear in my books; and if he gave the original check to any outsider that would mean that he would have to account for the money. He has given me the names of some people to whom he says he has given checks. I have seen sotre of these people and they admit tnat he has given them checks, either in place of some they have lost, or extra checks. We 'don't think that is proof that he repaid the money. Mr. Calvert said the society did not wish him to press the case, and he left it in their worships' hands. Mr. MeCorquodale : The society won't be losers. They have money in their hands for security. kii
Mr. Calvert said that was perfectly true, but Mr. Boydell was under the impression that the monies em- bezzled amounted to considerably more than £35. That

,as his information. Mr. McCorquodale : We are only. dealing with the sum here. The prisoner was formally charged, and pleaded guilty. Mr. Swift said his client desired him to say that he sincerely regretted what he had done, and it was essen- tial in the interests of the members of co-operative societies that such practices should be put down ; but he had honestly intended to repay the monies; and to the best of his belief he had made them up. He had been ten years in the employ of the society, and there had been no irregularity in his conduct till last year, though he was left in entire charge of the shop at Newton. As 2s. a week was deducted from his salary for security, he was only in receipt of 235. a week, and he had heavy expenses' and a wife and three children to support. He had lost his position and character, and the society would not lose a single penny as they had more security in hand than would cover the £35. The Bench, he thought, taking into account his forfeiture of this amount, and under all the circum- stances, would consider he had already been sufficiently punished. Mr. Swift, in reply to the Bench, said the prisoner had given a bond for £5O, and the condition was that if he did not satisfactorily account for all monies he would forfeit the entire amount.
Mr. Calvert : The society never considered whether or not they would return hits money. Mr. McCorquodale : By that the society are making £2O. _

Mr. Swift: If the Society think the defendant is suffi- ciently punished they can give some of it back. The Chairman: If they are going to keep this £2O it is a pretty severe punishment to start with.

„e pun's. The conditions of the bond were read by the Bench. Mr. McCorquodale ; He has 255. a week, and if he embezzles sixpence he forfeits the whole amount he has paid as security. I should be very sorry to be a servant under that society. Mr. Calvert: The Secretary wishes use to point out that it is the common form of bond of all co-operative societies. _
Mr. McCorquodale : I have seen a good many bonds but I never saw one like this. It was remarked on the Bench that the longer and more faithful the service of the man the worse his posi- tion.

Mr. Calvert: Instead of that the amount never gets up to £5O. It was 40 odd pounds the week before he was dismissed, and the society repaid him £lO. He has had two repayments. The Chairman, addressing the prisoner, said he had committed a most serious offence, but the Bench, tak- ing all the circumstances into consideration, and believ- ing he had made all the reparation he could and was sorry for what he had done, would simply order him to pay the costs and bind him over to come up again when called upon.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. "By AN OCCASIONAL CORRBSPONDRNT." For the first time since he succeeded to the bar- onetcy, and certainly not for many years previ- ously, Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., took his place on the Bench at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. His father was chairman of the Bench up to his death, and it would appear that the present baronet now intends to fulfil his magisterial functions.

The Vicar of Runcorn is an eminently practical man, and he has displayed this trait in a new way by publishing the following precautions against Influenza :—" Keep yourself in as 'good general health as possible. Dont be frightened, but culti- vate a good conscience. Eucalyptus Oil is said to be a good disinfectant. If you think you have the influenza, go to bed and send for the doctor. All through, trust in God."

In connection with the Church Army House, at Runcorn, the Vicar has just commenced a tempor- ary labour scheme for the help of those out of em- ployment. Work at chopping and bundling wood is given to men on application to the Captain, and as the "Parish Sfagazine "observes, they will not make a fortune, but they will not starve. The bundles are sold at 3s. 6d. a hundred and " the term s are strictly cash down."

div.head: BY IN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY IN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

Mr. Grimkb-Drayton has a peculiar notion of his own with regard to the eight hours question, and one which, I think, is not shared by anyone else in a similar position. This notion of his he disclosed last week at a Tory meeting at Golborne, and it was to the effect that, if the colliers received the advan- tage of a proposed bill for an eight hours working day,the price of coal would go up. If his prognos- tication came true, he tried to instil into his aud- ience that coal could be procured in America, shipped to England, and sold cheaper than the Eng- lish coal, and still at a profit, fie had a colliery in America, he said, and in certain eventualities, he hinted that he would try the experiment. In a vague way this shows what Mr. Grim ke-Drayton thinks about the eight hours bill for miners, but I fancy in practice,his American idea would not turn out quite so rosy,as in theory he would have us be- lieve.

The fact of a Liberal candidate being in the field for this division, appears to have put Mr. Legh on his mettle, and instead, as on other occasions,of be- taking himself to the land of the brigands,he is do- ing his utmost to ingratiate himself with all classes at home. First, he has been down into the bowels of the earth at Haydock, and endeavoured to put himself right with the miners ; then he attends divine service, also at Haydock, where, by the way, the miners are in strong force ; and, lastly, he pre- sides at a Smoking Concert, in the Conservative stronghold. We cannot say that we see very little of our member, for during the last two months we have had him constantly with us, but I fancy, had there been no opposition, his appearance amongst us would have been very much at intervals. How- ever, " All's well that ends well," and we shall see what his rival, Mr. Neill, has to say for himself on Saturday night.

Whilst referring to Mr. Legh, I may mention that that gentleman had a novel experience on Sunday at Haydock. As I have said, he was present at service in the church, being accompanied by Lady Gerrard ; and during the time the Vicar was pub- lishing the banns ot marviage between a young couple, a collier bluntly objected to the banns. It is said that both Mr. Legh and Lady Gerrard were for the moment greatly surprised, but they after- wards enjoyed the incident.

I cannot conceive what has come over our usually quiet and sedate body of Commissioners, a body .vhich at one time was described as "a happy family." Something has evidently gone ,wrong with the machinery, or Mr. McMahon and Mr. Ratcliffe have on two occasions been wound up the wrong way. At the last meeting they both objected to .£25 being taken out of the rates, and devoted to Technical Instruction. Then Mr. MacMahon found fault with the Technical Instruction Committee, and made a statement to the effect that the Com- mittee was a self, elected one, and in this he was upheld by Mr. Ratcliffe. This was only a small ember, which during the intervening month has smouldered to some purpose, and on Monday broke out into a flame which utterly consumed both Mr. MacMahon and Mr. Ratcliffe. I don't know what their object is, but if they think the sympathies of the Earlestown ratepayers are with them, in their objection to apaltry £25 for the education of the rate- payers, they are sadly mistaken, and they will find out their mistake on their next appeal to the ratepayers.

To say that Mr. MacMahon had to eat humble pie is putting it mildly, and Mr. Ratcliffe, seeing that he and his confrere had dug themselves a pit, very wisely kept to a certain extent, in the back- ground. When Mr. MacMalion makes a statement in public, he should first consider carefully the whole facts, and then when cl-allenged he will not have to practically withdraw what he has said, and hide his actions behind an application which he itnew it was impossible to grant. lam surprised that he should have agreed to spend £7,000 on a public hall, and object to spend ..E25 for educational purposes.

For the seecond time within a. very short period. Colonel McCorquodale has tendered his resignation as a member of the Board of Commissioners and for the second time, the Board have refused to accept it. I should be very sorry, and I know lam not alone in this, if Colonel McCorquodale should per- sist in resigning, as he is an old and very able mem- ber of the Board. He is a gentleman who hates such things as acrimonious discussions, or scenes at the meetings of the Board, and should anything of the kind happen to occur when he is present, he has a peculiar knack pf averting the storm, and restoring tranquility. For the sake of the township and the reputation of the Board, I hope he will be induced to reconsider hW 4e;i4op, , • , Peer r r 0j0..f

A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Federation held at Birmingham on Wednesday ha° under consideration reports from Cumberland, the Forest of Dean, and parts of Lancashire, setting forlh that miners in these districts had been asked to accepta reduction of wages, the owners asserting that they were forced into taking this step owing to surplus coal being_ sent into their markets from other districts and sold a: " unfair prices. It was decided to hold a conference 01 miners' representatives in Manchester on February 11! t° consider a proposal to meet the difficulty by ceaslng work at all collieries for two or more weeks.
4eP Work has been resumed by the helpers in the SOOT land shipyards, an agreement having been effected vi,o` the masters on Tuesday.
